The Services Guide
Data, Schemas, Orchestrations, and Agent Composition
Volume II · Data & Architecture
A Deep Dive Into the 38 Cataloged Services Across Seven Practices

The middle volume of the APEX Trilogy — paired with the Sellers Guide (Volume I · positioning APEX-accelerated Services) and the Deployment Guide (Volume III · deploying Services on the Microsoft Platform). This book is about the data and orchestration that make every Service real, and how the APEX framework accelerates the building of those Services: client SOR systems landed into Bronze, conformed to Silver, served from Gold, called by Agents through MCP, and orchestrated by n8n on the laptop or Azure Logic Apps Hybrid in production.

WROX-STYLE EDITION · SERVICES VOLUME
Keven Markham · VP Enterprise Transformation · Deloitte's Microsoft Technology & Services Practice · May 2026

How to Use This Book

What APEX Is — read this first

APEX is a framework that accelerates the building of services and agents on the Microsoft Platform. It is the architectural substrate Deloitte's Microsoft practice uses internally to deliver Services faster, more consistently, and with more rigorous governance. APEX is not a product and is not sold. What clients buy are Services — the 38-Service catalog enumerated in Part VI, each a productized envelope with a KPI commitment, scope, persona model, and two-contract Independence-compliant commercial structure. The Service is the contractable unit; the framework is the means.

When this book says "APEX," read "the APEX framework." When it says "Service," read "the productized envelope clients actually buy." When it says "Service architect uses APEX to build RC-E2E-03," read "the architect uses framework primitives — medallion · MCP · LEDGER · agent runtime · orchestration parity · trust envelope — to build the Service the client contracted for." The distinction is structural, not stylistic; the two-contract Independence model (client ↔ Microsoft for platform · client ↔ Deloitte for Services) makes the Service the contractable unit, not the framework.

The APEX library is now three volumes. The Sellers Guide answers how to position APEX-accelerated Services; the Deployment Guide answers how to deploy those Services on the Microsoft Platform; this volume — the Services Guide — answers the question between them: what data drives each Service, how the APEX framework shapes it, and how Agents compose over it through orchestration.

It is the volume the architects ask for after the seller has won the deal and before the deployment lead opens Bicep. It is also the volume the agent maintainers, schema owners, and MCP catalog editors return to repeatedly. If the Sellers Guide is the menu and the Deployment Guide is the kitchen wiring, this book is the recipe — and like recipes, it lives or dies on its handling of ingredients.

Audience

  • Service architects designing a new service composition or onboarding a new client into an existing Service — the catalog deep dives in Part VI are the reference, with Parts II–IV providing the data substrate.
  • Data engineers building the Bronze → Silver → Gold pipelines per Service — Parts II, III, and IV are the core; Appendix A indexes every schema referenced in the book.
  • MCP catalog editors exposing Gold-mart access to agents — Chapter 13 plus Appendix B (the full MCP tool catalog) are the reference.
  • Orchestration authors writing the workflow JSON per scenario — Part V plus Appendix D.
  • Agent maintainers who need to know which schemas an agent reads, which MCP tools it calls, and which Service envelopes it serves — every Part VI chapter has the per-Service composition map.

How the Book Is Organized

Part I — Foundations of Service Data. The data model the rest of the book builds on: why Services are data-first, the Bronze → Silver → Gold medallion in Microsoft Fabric, the canonical schema families (SCML, MERML, PROML, EHRML, ECRML, etc.), and how MCP exposes Gold to agents.

Part II — Bronze Tier · Client Data Sources. The source-of-record inventory by industry (POS, ERP, EHR, CRM, IoT telemetry, etc.), Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence as the real-time hub, ingestion pipelines + tokenization, PII classification, and the mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock identity.

Part III — Silver Tier · Canonical Models. The conformance layer: how raw Bronze rows become canonical Silver entities, the schema library deep dive, and Microsoft Purview as the lineage and quality control surface.

Part IV — Gold Tier · Decision-Ready Data. Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse patterns for serving Gold, per-Service Gold marts, and the MCP tool surface that makes Gold reachable from agents.

Part V — Orchestrations. The workflow design patterns (DAG, fan-out, HITL, fan-in), n8n on the laptop, Azure Logic Apps Hybrid on Microsoft platform, and cross-Service composition (e.g., RC-E2E-03 reading SCML.Lot owned by RC-E2E-09).

Part VI — Service Catalog by Practice. One chapter per practice covering all 38 Services. Every Service profile follows the same template — data sources, silver schemas, gold marts, agents composed, MCP tools, orchestration shape, KPI attribution path. RC-E2E-03 (Pricing & Revenue Decision Service) is the worked example throughout.

Note — How to read this book non-linearly

If you are working on a specific Service, jump to its profile in Part VI first; that profile names the schemas, MCP tools, and orchestration patterns it depends on, with cross-references back to Parts II–V. If you are designing infrastructure for any Service, start with Part I, read Parts II–IV in order, and treat Part VI as the catalog of consumers of what you are about to build.

Conventions

This volume inherits the conventions of the other two: callouts for Note · Warning · Best Practice · Try It Out · Objection · Independence; code blocks labeled by language; Microsoft platform components named at the resource-type level (Microsoft.Fabric/capacities, Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces, etc.). Where the Deployment Guide spells out "Azure Container Registry" rather than "ACR," this book follows the same disambiguation.

Schema names follow the APEX framework convention — uppercase prefix (SCML, MERML, PROML) followed by an entity name in PascalCase: SCML.Lot, MERML.Markdown, PROML.Pricing. Bronze tables are prefixed br_, Silver with the schema name itself, Gold with g_: br_pos_transactions → SCML.Inventory → g_inventory_position_daily. The pattern is uniform across all 38 Services.

Independence — Same boundaries apply

The two-contract structure from the Deployment Guide carries through this volume. Client SOR data flows under the client's Microsoft platform contract; schemas, MCP tool definitions, and orchestration JSON are Deloitte-authored artifacts shipped to the client tenant via the same mirror boundary that ships agent images. Throughout this book, the relationship is described as "Deloitte's Microsoft practice," "DMTSP," or "Microsoft-native deployment." Never partner, alliance, or strategic alliance.

Part I

Foundations of Service Data

Picture a Tuesday afternoon at a grocery chain's regional headquarters. Marisol — store operations manager for the Pacific Northwest — gets a Microsoft Teams notification that two trucks of fresh produce, headed for forty stores, had a refrigeration excursion in transit. The Pricer agent has already done the math: shelf life is now shorter, the operations team needs to decide which stores should accept early arrivals and which should drop the load, and somebody has to authorize markdowns before tomorrow's open. The card on Marisol's screen recommends, with reasoning, that 23 stores accept and 17 stores drop. She approves in 90 seconds.

Everything Marisol saw on that card — the SKUs, the shelf-life math, the per-store velocity numbers, the cost-of-goods, the proposed markdowns — came from her own company's data, but not in the shape her own company stores it. It travelled through three folders before it reached her: a folder that preserved every byte from D365 and the IoT sensors as they sent them; a folder that translated those rows into a consistent business vocabulary; and a folder packaged specifically for the decision she was about to make. Part I is the story of those three folders, plus the wires that connect the agents to the third one.

By the end of Part I you will know why APEX-M is organized this way (it is not the only architecture that could work, but it is the one that survives audit, schema drift, and cross-Service composition without crumbling); what sits in each folder and how Microsoft Fabric holds them; how the dictionary of business concepts (the canonical schema library) is the linchpin that keeps Silver stable while sources change; and how agents reach into the third folder through a standardized contract called MCP rather than writing SQL of their own. The five chapters below build that picture in order — each grounds the next.

Chapter 0

Foreword — Why Services Are Data-First

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Frames the Service as a data flow first, an agent composition second, and a Bicep deployment third.
  • Sets out the three rules that make every Service profile in Part VI legible.
  • Explains why a Service's KPI envelope is anchored on the data model, not on the agents.
60-second read
  • A Service is a flow of data first; agents and orchestration are stations along the flow.
  • Three rules: every Service has the same data shape · Bronze/Silver/Gold are not optional · agents read only Gold.
  • The KPI envelope lives on the data model, not the agents — build the KPI Gold mart first.

0.1 The Service Is the Data Flow

Walk into any APEX engagement and you will hear three different short answers to the question "what is a Service?" The seller will say it is a productized envelope with a KPI commitment. The deployment lead will say it is a Bicep module that composes Container Apps over Layer 1. The agent maintainer will say it is a set of agent images and prompts. All three answers are correct. None of them is the answer that gets a Service to ship.

The answer that gets a Service to ship is: a Service is a flow of data, with the agents and the orchestration as the stations along the flow. Bronze rows arrive from client SOR systems. Silver conformance produces canonical entities the agents understand. Gold marts make those entities decision-ready. MCP tools expose Gold to agents. Orchestrations call agents in sequence. Decisions get attributed back to the audit chain. The KPI envelope is the measurable difference between the input flow and the output flow.

Every other view — commercial, deployment, agent — is downstream of the data view. If the data flow is wrong, the most beautiful Bicep in the world will deploy a Service that misses its KPI. If the data flow is right, even crude orchestration usually produces the audited outcome the Sellers Guide promised.

0.2 The Three Rules

Three rules thread every chapter of this book and every Service profile in Part VI. State them up front so the rest is legible.

0.2.1 Rule 1 — Every Service has the same data shape

All 38 Services in the catalog land Bronze, conform to Silver, serve Gold, expose MCP tools, run orchestrations, and write LEDGER rows. The shape is uniform. What differs from Service to Service is which SOR systems land into Bronze, which canonical schemas the Silver layer uses, which Gold marts get built, which MCP tools get registered, which agents compose, and how the workflow branches. The shape is invariant.

This is what makes the catalog feasible. A Service architect onboarding HLS-E2E-04 (Prior Authorization) does not learn a new architecture; she fills in the same template with HLS-specific schemas (EHRML, CMSML) and HLS-specific orchestration. The architect onboarding TMT-TEL-RAA-04 (Revenue Assurance Variance Close) fills in the same template with TMT-specific schemas (BRMML, GLML).

0.2.2 Rule 2 — Bronze, Silver, Gold are not optional layers

It is tempting, when a client SOR exposes data in a clean shape, to skip Bronze and land directly into Silver. It is also tempting, when Silver looks Gold-shaped already, to skip the Gold mart. Both shortcuts produce Services that work for one client and break on the second.

Bronze is the immutable record of what the client system actually said. Silver is the canonical conformance to APEX schemas. Gold is the decision-ready denormalization for an agent to query in O(1). Each tier exists because each carries a different commitment: Bronze commits to fidelity, Silver commits to conformance, Gold commits to query latency. Collapsing tiers collapses commitments.

Warning — The "we'll just land directly into Silver" trap

This sentence appears in every engagement. Reject it. The next client's SOR will be different from this client's SOR; the Bronze layer is what absorbs that variance. Without Bronze, every new client onboarding mutates Silver, and the schema library stops being a library.

0.2.3 Rule 3 — Agents do not query Bronze or Silver

Agents in APEX read Gold. Always. The MCP tool surface is built against Gold marts, and the agent's prompts assume Gold-shaped facts. There are two reasons for this rule, both load-bearing:

  • Latency. Bronze is high-fidelity but high-fan-out — joining Bronze rows for one decision can scan hundreds of millions of records. Silver is canonical but still normalized; an agent traversing Silver joins five tables to assemble a single fact. Gold is denormalized for the question the agent asks; an agent gets the answer in one query.
  • Audit. The LEDGER row records which Gold mart the agent read and at which row hash. That hash is reproducible — the row is in Gold and the row is in the lakehouse and the lakehouse is in Microsoft Fabric. If agents read Bronze or Silver directly, the audit reconstruction loses a hop and gets fragile.

The exception that proves the rule: the mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock identity (introduced in the Deployment Guide) does reach into a PII-tokenized Silver column at HITL-approval time, but only after writing a LEDGER row that says it is about to. That bypass exists for one specific commitment — re-identifying a tokenized customer for a regulatory artifact — and it is auditable.

0.3 Why the KPI Envelope Lives on the Data, Not the Agents

The Sellers Guide commits a Service to a KPI envelope. RC-E2E-03 commits to GM +3.2pp, DoH −28%, Markdown-to-Clear +41%. Notice what those numbers measure: they are differences in the data. Margin per SKU per store, days-on-hand per SKU per store, markdown lifecycle counts. Those numbers are realized by Gold marts that compute them, not by agents that talk about them.

This matters for how the architecture is sequenced. When you onboard a new client into RC-E2E-03, the first thing you build is the SCML and MERML Silver layer over the client's POS + ERP + competitive-pricing feeds, and the Gold marts that compute the KPI baseline. Only after those exist do you compose the agents over them. Agents that decide markdowns without a Gold-mart-computed baseline have nothing to attribute their decisions against; the KPI envelope cannot be measured without the data view.

Best Practice — Build the KPI Gold mart before the agents

For any new Service onboarding into a tenant, the first deliverable is a Gold mart that emits the Service's KPI envelope from the existing data. If that mart is built and the numbers come out flat, the agents have not even run yet — and the data architecture is already proving where the value is hiding. This is the cheapest and earliest commercial signal in the engagement.

0.4 What This Book Is Not

This is a Service-and-data book. It is not:

  • A commercial book — read the Sellers Guide for envelopes, ECIF eligibility, persona briefs, and the Wave model.
  • A deployment book — read the Deployment Guide for Bicep modules, the three-layer cake, the two-registry boundary, and Day-Zero onboarding.
  • A data-platform book about Microsoft Fabric internals — Microsoft's Fabric documentation covers the engine; this book covers what to put on it.

If you are asking "what does this Service sell?" you want the Sellers Guide. If you are asking "how does this Service deploy?" you want the Deployment Guide. If you are asking "what data does this Service read, what shape does it produce, and how do agents traverse it?" — you are in the right book.

Key Takeaways

  • A Service is a data flow first; agents and orchestration are stations along the flow.
  • Three rules: every Service has the same data shape; Bronze/Silver/Gold are not optional; agents read only Gold.
  • The KPI envelope lives on the data model, not the agent — which is why the first deliverable in an onboarding is the KPI Gold mart.
Chapter 1

Bronze → Silver → Gold — The Medallion in Microsoft Fabric

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Defines each medallion tier — fidelity (Bronze), conformance (Silver), decision-readiness (Gold) — and what each commits to.
  • Maps each tier to its Microsoft Fabric and Microsoft platform components by resource type.
  • Establishes the per-tier write/read contracts that the rest of the book references.
60-second read
  • Bronze = fidelity (raw SOR, append-only, no agent reads). Silver = conformance (canonical APEX schemas). Gold = decision-readiness (denormalized, agent-queryable).
  • Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse hosts Bronze + Silver; Warehouse + Direct Lake hosts Gold; KQL DB handles streaming Bronze.
  • LEDGER (Azure SQL/Postgres) and Cosmos DB sit outside the medallion — different planes, different commitments.
Plain-English primer — before the technical detail

Think of your company's data like the mail that arrives at your home. The mail comes in many shapes — bills, junk, a letter from your aunt, an Amazon package. When you bring it inside, you have three folders:

  • Folder 1 — "as it arrived": every envelope and package, exactly as the postal carrier dropped them. You don't open anything yet. If you ever need to prove what someone sent you on Tuesday, this folder is your evidence.
  • Folder 2 — "sorted": you open each item and put it where it belongs — bills together, personal letters together, packages on the kitchen counter. Same mail, just organized by what it is rather than who sent it.
  • Folder 3 — "ready for the next thing I'll do": the bill that's due Friday goes on top of the pay-this-week pile; the package goes near the door to return tomorrow. Everything is shaped for an immediate decision.

APEX-M's data architecture works the same way. Bronze is "as it arrived" — every byte from every source system, preserved exactly. Silver is "sorted" — the same information cleaned up and put into consistent shapes regardless of which source it came from. Gold is "ready for the next thing" — the data shaped specifically for the one question an agent or operator is about to ask.

The three folders aren't a luxury. Together they let you (1) prove later what any source actually said (Bronze), (2) work with the data consistently across many uses (Silver), and (3) get fast, decision-ready answers without re-organizing every time (Gold). The rest of this chapter and Ch 1B explain exactly how each tier works and why the boundaries are where they are.

1.1 The Three Tiers, Side by Side

Bronze · fidelity

What it is — the immutable record of what the client SOR system actually said.

No conformance, no enrichment, no joining. One row in equals one row stored.

Silver · conformance

What it is — Bronze rows mapped to canonical APEX schema entities.

SCML, MERML, PROML, EHRML, etc. Conformance, deduplication, type stabilization, foreign-key resolution.

Gold · decision-ready

What it is — Silver entities denormalized into agent-queryable marts.

One mart per question agents ask. O(1) reads. KPI baselines materialize here.

1.2 Microsoft Fabric Mapping

Each tier maps to a specific Microsoft Fabric resource type. The MVP and the Deployment Guide treat Microsoft Fabric capacity as a tenant-shared Layer 1 resource (Microsoft.Fabric/capacities), with per-Service workspaces inside it.

TierMicrosoft Fabric componentStorage formatPrimary access
BronzeMicrosoft Fabric Lakehouse · raw zone · or Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence Eventstream + KQL DB for streaming sourcesDelta Parquet (batch) · Delta + checkpointed events (streaming)Append-only writes from Microsoft.DataFactory pipelines or Eventstream sinks
SilverMicrosoft Fabric Lakehouse · curated zone · partitioned by date and entityDelta Parquet · Z-ordered on common join keysSpark notebooks (transformation) · Microsoft Fabric Warehouse (T-SQL) · Microsoft Purview lineage
GoldMicrosoft Fabric Warehouse · Gold marts · or Microsoft Fabric Direct Lake for Power BIDelta Parquet served via Warehouse · materialized viewsMCP tools (agent-facing) · Power BI (operator-facing) · semantic models

The non-Fabric paths exist for specific commitments: Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server or Azure SQL Database hosts the LEDGER (append-only audit, hash-chained) because per-row insert latency and WORM enforcement are not what Lakehouse optimizes for. Azure Cosmos DB hosts agent session state when an HITL approval has to survive a multi-hour wait without burning a Container App revision. The Bronze/Silver/Gold pipeline does not write to either; the agents and orchestration do.

1.3 The Per-Tier Contracts

1.3.1 Bronze contract

  • Write. Append-only. No updates, no deletes. A correction is a new row with a corrected timestamp.
  • Schema. Whatever the SOR sent. Type-cast minimally; preserve every field even if APEX never reads it.
  • Retention. Bronze is the source of truth in case of any downstream rebuild. Retain ≥ 1 year for STAGE; ≥ 7 years for PROD (often longer for regulated industries).
  • Read. Only by Silver-build pipelines. Agents do not read Bronze.
ADR · architecture decision
ADR-001-01 · 2026-04-15 · accepted

Decision: Bronze is append-only. Corrections produce new rows with corrected timestamps; the original "wrong" row stays.

Why: Two reasons. Audit reproducibility — a regulator (or a careful internal reviewer) reconstructs decisions made on day X using the Bronze that existed on day X, not the "fixed" Bronze of today. Idempotent rebuild — the §8.2 Silver rebuild contract requires Bronze to be deterministic input; mutable Bronze breaks the contract.

Trade-off rejected: Mutable Bronze (with audit columns recording the old value). Cheaper storage; harder reproducibility. The win-rate on this trade-off shifts toward append-only as soon as a regulated workload is in scope (HLS/HIPAA · TMT/SOX · ER/PHMSA · etc.) — and 5 of 7 practices in the catalog are regulated.

1.3.2 Silver contract

  • Write. Idempotent rebuild from Bronze; deletions only by re-derivation, never by direct DELETE.
  • Schema. A canonical APEX schema (SCML, MERML, etc.) — the schema library is the contract surface.
  • Conformance. Type stability, naming consistency, foreign keys resolved to canonical IDs, units stabilized (every monetary field is the same currency, every weight is the same unit).
  • Lineage. Every Silver row is traceable to its Bronze origin row(s) via Microsoft Purview lineage.
  • Read. By Gold-build pipelines and by analysts. Agents do not read Silver directly.

1.3.3 Gold contract

  • Write. Materialized from Silver on a schedule (Microsoft Fabric Pipelines) or on event (Microsoft Fabric Eventstream → notebook trigger).
  • Schema. Per-Service. The Gold mart is shaped exactly to the question the agent asks; it is the answer-shape, not the entity-shape.
  • Latency. The agent reads Gold in < 200 ms. If a Gold query takes longer, the Gold mart is wrong-shaped — denormalize further.
  • KPI. The Service's KPI envelope is computed on Gold and emitted to the LEDGER for attribution.
  • Read. By agents (via MCP tools) and operators (via Power BI semantic models).
Note — Real-time Bronze for streaming sources

For real-time signals (POS terminals, refrigeration telemetry, network fault feeds), Bronze is Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence Eventstream sinking to a KQL DB rather than a Lakehouse. The contract is the same — append-only, full fidelity, no agent reads — but the substrate is event-grade. Silver builds run on a windowed cadence (every 1–5 minutes) rather than a daily batch. Chapter 5 walks the RTI pattern in detail.

1.4 What Lives Where, Concretely

For RC-E2E-03 (the running example):

FILE LAYOUT — RC-E2E-03 medallion zones
Microsoft.Fabric/capacities/contoso-fabric-lab01/workspaces/rc-e2e-03/
  bronze/
    br_pos_transactions/        # raw POS events from client point-of-sale
    br_refrigeration_telemetry/ # raw IoT sensor stream (RTI Eventstream)
    br_erp_inventory/           # raw ERP inventory snapshots (daily)
    br_competitor_pricing/      # raw competitor feed (CSV ingest)
  silver/
    SCML.Inventory              # conformed inventory positions
    SCML.Lot                    # FSMA 204 lot provenance
    MERML.Markdown              # conformed markdown decisions
    MERML.Elasticity            # SKU-store elasticity coefficients
    MERML.Competitor            # conformed competitor pricing
  gold/
    g_excursion_decision_panel  # per-event mart for The Analyst
    g_markdown_proposal_basis   # per-SKU-store mart for Demand Checker + Finance
    g_kpi_rc_e2e_03_daily       # KPI mart — GM, DoH, markdown-to-clear

Notice the asymmetry: there are four Bronze tables (one per source), five Silver entities (canonical conformance and joins), three Gold marts (one per agent question, plus the KPI mart). The fan ratio — Bronze:Silver:Gold — is roughly 1.3:1.5:1 for RC-E2E-03 and is similar across the catalog. Silver is where conformance work concentrates; Gold is where Service shape concentrates.

Key Takeaways

  • Bronze is fidelity (append-only, no agent reads). Silver is conformance (canonical APEX schemas). Gold is decision-readiness (denormalized, agent-queryable).
  • Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse hosts Bronze (raw zone) and Silver (curated zone); Microsoft Fabric Warehouse + Direct Lake hosts Gold; Real-Time Intelligence handles streaming Bronze.
  • LEDGER and Cosmos DB sit outside the medallion — the medallion is the analytics-data plane; LEDGER is the audit plane; Cosmos DB is the agent-state plane.
  • Each tier carries a different commitment: fidelity, conformance, latency. Don't collapse the tiers.

1.5 OneLake Security in User Identity Mode (GA)

The medallion contracts in §1.3 carry security policy with them — Bronze can hold raw lot data with PII or PHI tokens; Silver canonicalizes; Gold projects per agent question. Until April 2026 the SQL analytics endpoint enforced read security via SQL GRANT / REVOKE on tables. Microsoft Fabric's OneLake Security in user identity mode (now GA) replaces that pattern.

In user identity mode, the SQL analytics endpoint passes the signed-in user's Microsoft Entra identity through to OneLake, which evaluates row-level, column-level, and object-level security defined inside the OneLake Lakehouse — not by SQL GRANT / REVOKE. SQL permissions still cover non-data objects (views, stored procedures, functions); table reads are governed exclusively by OneLake security roles.

  • Centralized governance. Define policies once in OneLake; Power BI, notebooks, lakehouse, and SQL analytics endpoint all enforce identically. APEX-M's Tier-3 and Tier-4 PII / PHI rules live in OneLake roles, not in SQL.
  • 1:1 identity mapping across producer and consumer. When an APEX-M service workspace consumes the canonical Silver via OneLake shortcuts (per §1B), the principal referenced in a producer's OneLake security role must have Fabric Read on the consumer artifact too — group memberships do not resolve across the boundary.
  • Writes still happen through the Lakehouse page. All writes are governed by workspace roles (Admin / Member / Contributor); user identity mode is a read-time enforcement model.

The apex-m.data_lake_fabric.DataLakeFabric implementation honors user identity mode by always opening the SQL analytics endpoint with the operator's Entra Agent ID OBO token (per Deployment Guide §5.1.1), never with the deployment-time delegated identity. This guarantees that an HITL approver looking at customer-facing data sees only what their workforce identity is entitled to see, not what the agent's runtime identity could read.

1.6 The Primary-Workspace Pattern

APEX-M deployments adopt the primary-workspace pattern documented in Microsoft's OneLake security best practices: one primary workspace per practice owns the canonical Silver entities; per-service workspaces consume that data via OneLake shortcuts.

Microsoft.Fabric/workspaces/
  rc-canonical/                               (primary workspace — RC practice)
    Lakehouses/
      scml-silver/                            (SCML.Inventory · SCML.Lot · SCML.Movement · SCML.Receipt)
      merml-silver/                           (MERML.Markdown · MERML.Elasticity · MERML.Competitor · MERML.Promotion)
      proml-silver/                           (PROML.Pricing · PROML.DiscountRule)
      crmml-silver/                           (CRMML.Customer · CRMML.Loyalty · CRMML.Interaction)
    OneLake security: roles defined here, propagate via shortcut

  rc-e2e-03/                                  (per-service consumer)
    Lakehouses/
      service-bronze/                         (Bronze landing for RC-E2E-03 sources)
      service-gold/                           (Gold marts: g_excursion_decision_panel etc.)
    OneLake shortcuts → rc-canonical Silver tables (read-only consumer)

  rc-e2e-04/                                  (per-service consumer)
    same pattern; shortcuts into rc-canonical for shared Silver entities

  ...one workspace per featured RC scenario...

This is the recommended baseline architecture for OneLake security at scale. Three properties matter:

  1. Single source of security. Roles defined on the primary workspace propagate via shortcuts — there is no "secondary" copy of the security policy that can drift.
  2. Cross-service composition without cross-service writes. RC-E2E-03's cold-chain agents read SCML.Lot via a shortcut into rc-canonical (where RC-E2E-09 owns Silver writes per §17.4). RC-E2E-09's MCP tool surface remains the public interface; the shortcut is the data path. No service writes Silver tables it doesn't own.
  3. Scale. Per Microsoft's GA limit (Jan 2026), Fabric workspace identities scale to 10,000 per tenant — well beyond what a typical APEX-M deployment needs, but the headroom matters for enterprise rollouts.

The wizard's render endpoint emits Bicep that creates the primary workspace first, then per-service workspaces with shortcuts wired into the primary. Operators do not provision workspaces by hand. See apex-m/infra/bicep/platform/fabric.bicep (TBD — Phase I.4 follow-up).

Best Practice — primary-workspace ownership

Use the same Fabric capacity owner for the primary workspace and every consumer workspace under it. Mixed-owner setups break user identity mode for cross-workspace reads — the consumer workspace's SQL analytics endpoint cannot run in user identity mode if its owner differs from the producer's.

Chapter 1A

Microsoft Fabric — Deep Dive

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the four-level Fabric hierarchy (Tenant · Capacity · Workspace · Item) and shows where APEX-M anchors each Service.
  • Inventories every workload that lands in OneLake — Lakehouse · Warehouse · Real-Time Intelligence · Data Factory · Power BI · Data Activator — with the APEX use for each.
  • Drills the Real-Time Intelligence stack (Eventstream → Eventhouse → KQL · Activator) that powers APEX scenario triggers and the new Microsoft-hosted MCP servers for Eventhouse / Activator.
  • Establishes the workspace pattern APEX-M uses across the 38-Service catalog and the capacity SKU envelope per tenant tier.
90-second read
  • Four-level hierarchy: Microsoft 365 Tenant → Microsoft.Fabric/capacities (regional + SKU + CUs) → Workspace (RBAC + Git + deployment pipelines) → Item (Lakehouse · Warehouse · Notebook · Pipeline · Eventhouse · Activator · Semantic Model · Report).
  • OneLake is one per tenant — automatically provisioned, governed by tenant-level policies, built on ADLS Gen2 with Delta Parquet as the universal table format.
  • Five workloads land in OneLake: Data Engineering (Lakehouse · Spark) · Data Warehouse (T-SQL) · Real-Time Intelligence (Eventstream · Eventhouse · KQL · Activator) · Data Factory (Pipelines · Mirroring · Dataflow Gen2) · Power BI (semantic models · Direct Lake · reports).
  • Mirroring brings live SOR data (D365 · Azure SQL · Snowflake · Databricks · Cosmos DB · Fabric SQL DB · open mirroring for any source) into OneLake as Delta Parquet — no ETL, no scheduled refresh.
  • Direct Lake serves Power BI semantic models directly from OneLake Parquet — no import, no DirectQuery latency. Direct Lake on OneLake (current default) supports tables from multiple Fabric items.
  • OneLake shortcuts let workspaces reference data in other workspaces (or external clouds — ADLS Gen2 · S3 · GCS · Dataverse) without copying. Cross-cloud reads are first-class.
  • Two new MCP servers (March 2026 preview): Eventhouse remote MCP and Activator remote MCP. Agents now read and write Fabric RTI through MCP — the same protocol APEX uses for Gold marts.
  • Capacity is the billing & throttling boundary. F-SKUs (F2 → F2048) determine concurrent CUs; bursting/smoothing absorb peaks; surge protection caps background jobs; pause/resume halts billing.
Concept first — Fabric is one platform with five jobs

Microsoft Fabric replaces an alphabet soup of services that used to live separately — Synapse, Power BI, Data Factory, Azure Data Explorer, Real-Time Analytics, Data Activator. The product Microsoft now ships is one platform that holds all of them. For an APEX architect, that consolidation means one place to provision (one capacity), one place to govern (one tenant's Fabric admin settings), one place to read from (OneLake), and one place to publish out from (Power BI Direct Lake against the same data the agents are reading via MCP).

The chapter is long because Fabric has many parts. The mental model that keeps it manageable is: capacity is what you pay for; workspaces are how you scope teams; items are what your engineers actually build inside workspaces. Everything else — Eventstream, Activator, Mirroring, Direct Lake, OneLake shortcuts, the new RTI MCP servers — is one type of item or one capability of the platform.

Read §1A.1 (the four-level hierarchy) once. Then skim §1A.2 through §1A.10 as a feature tour — most engagements use four or five of those features, not all of them. Come back to whichever section your engagement is actively asking about. §1A.11 (workspace topology) and §1A.12 (capacity SKUs) are the two sections every engagement needs.

1A.1 The Four-Level Hierarchy

Per Choose a Microsoft Fabric deployment pattern, every Fabric deployment is shaped by the same four levels. APEX-M anchors at each level distinctly:

LevelWhat it isAPEX-M anchor
TenantThe Microsoft 365 / Microsoft Entra ID tenant. Identity boundary. Tenant-level Fabric admin settings, Conditional Access, sensitivity labels apply across all capacities and workspaces.The client tenant per the two-contract Independence model. Tenant settings (private links · Conditional Access · sensitivity labels) are enforced by the client; APEX-M consumes the contract.
Capacity (Microsoft.Fabric/capacities)Regional + SKU-bound compute pool. F SKUs (F2 → F2048) measured in Capacity Units (CUs). Billing & throttling boundary. Pausable/resumable.One capacity per APEX environment (Lab v0.1 · DEV · STAGE · PROD), sized per tier (§1A.12). Pause non-PROD outside business hours to keep zero-cost dev (memory note: laptop tier is free entirely).
WorkspaceCollaboration container. Four roles (Admin / Member / Contributor / Viewer). Git integration. Deployment pipelines. Belongs to one capacity at a time.One workspace per Service in the 38-Service catalog (e.g., apex-rc-e2e-03-prod). Per-Service Git repo. Per-Service deployment pipeline (Lab → DEV → STAGE → PROD).
ItemThe actual data & analytics objects: Lakehouse · Warehouse · Notebook · Pipeline · Eventhouse · KQL Database · Activator · Semantic Model · Report · Dataflow.Per Service: Bronze Lakehouse · Silver Lakehouse · Gold Warehouse · Gold Direct Lake semantic model · Eventstream(s) · Activator rules · Power BI report tile set.

Same-region capacity migration is straightforward; cross-region migration requires re-creating most items. APEX-M pins each environment to a single region (chosen at Lab provisioning time) and never moves a Service workspace cross-region — it re-provisions in the new region instead.

1A.2 OneLake — One Data Lake per Tenant

Per OneLake — the OneDrive for data:

  • One per tenant. You cannot create multiple OneLakes; you cannot delete OneLake. Every Fabric tenant has exactly one.
  • Built on ADLS Gen2. OneLake exposes ADLS Gen2 APIs and SDKs — every workspace appears as a container, every item as a folder. Existing ADLS tooling (Azure Storage Explorer · AzCopy · Spark) works unchanged.
  • Delta Parquet is universal. Lakehouses, Warehouses, KQL Databases — all tabular data lands in Delta Parquet. A Spark job and a T-SQL job writing to the same Lakehouse contribute to the same physical Delta tables.
  • Governed by tenant default. Sensitivity labels · Conditional Access · Microsoft Purview lineage all apply automatically to anything in OneLake.

For APEX-M this is the single most important Fabric property: OneLake unifies the medallion (Ch 1) and the agent's MCP tool surface (Ch 13) onto the same physical store. The Bronze Lakehouse, the Silver Lakehouse, and the Gold Warehouse are different items in different workspaces, but they all live in OneLake — agents reading Gold via MCP and humans reading Gold via Power BI Direct Lake see the same Delta Parquet bytes.

1A.3 Capacity SKUs and Capacity Units

F SKUs determine the maximum CUs a capacity can deliver per second. APEX-M's reference sizing per environment:

TierCapacity SKUCUsPower BI Viewer free?APEX use
Laptopnone — Docker Compose onlyn/an/aFree; Postgres + DuckDB stand in for OneLake; n8n stands in for Eventstream
Lab v0.1F2 (smallest)2NoOne workspace, one Service, single-developer; pause when not in use
DEVF88NoMulti-developer, single-Service end-to-end
STAGEF3232NoMulti-Service · production-shape data volumes · perf testing
PROD (small tenant)F6464YesF64 is the threshold — Power BI Viewer license becomes free for the tenant; common APEX-M PROD entry point
PROD (large tenant)F256 – F2048256–2048YesMulti-practice deployments · enterprise consumer counts · isolation per practice via separate capacities
Note — F64 is the Power BI license inflection point

Per Microsoft's licensing rules, on F64 and larger capacities users with the Viewer role can access Power BI content with a free license; on smaller capacities Viewers need Power BI Pro / PPU. For APEX engagements with broad analyst populations (the merchandising-director persona, finance-business-partner persona, store-ops persona), F64 is the smallest PROD SKU that doesn't require per-user Pro licenses. Below F64 the cost calculus needs explicit Pro licensing in the Cost envelope (§30.1.6).

Bursting and smoothing (per throttling policy): bursting lets jobs exceed the SKU's CU/s temporarily to finish fast; smoothing spreads compute cost over a longer time window so spikes don't trigger throttling. Surge protection caps background-job consumption to keep interactive (agent / report) latency healthy. APEX configures surge protection in PROD to leave headroom for agent-call concurrency.

1A.4 The Five Workloads

Every Fabric item is part of one of five workload families. APEX-M uses each:

WorkloadItemsAPEX-M role
Data EngineeringLakehouse · Notebook · Spark Job · Apache Spark PoolBronze + Silver tier homes (Ch 1, Ch 8). Notebooks run conformance jobs; Spark powers heavy-lift ELT.
Data WarehouseWarehouse (T-SQL) · SQL analytics endpoint · Stored proceduresGold marts where T-SQL semantics matter (Ch 12). Native Microsoft Entra auth · row-level security · column-level security.
Real-Time IntelligenceEventstream · Eventhouse · KQL Database · KQL Queryset · Activator · Real-Time DashboardScenario triggers (Ch 5). Event-driven workflows. KQL anomaly detection. Activator-driven HITL alerting.
Data FactoryData Pipeline · Dataflow Gen2 · Mirrored Database · Copy JobBronze ingestion (Ch 6). Mirroring from D365 / SQL / Snowflake / Databricks (§1A.7). Copy jobs for batch SOR pulls.
Power BISemantic Model · Report · Dashboard · Paginated Report · MetricsLayer 08 Experience plane — Gold marts surfaced via Direct Lake (§1A.8) to merchandising directors, finance leads, store ops.

1A.5 Lakehouse vs Warehouse — When Each

Both store Delta Parquet in OneLake. The choice is about compute primitive:

PropertyLakehouseWarehouse
Primary computeApache Spark (Python · Scala · SQL)T-SQL (MPP engine)
Read endpointSQL analytics endpoint (auto-generated, read-only T-SQL)Native T-SQL (read + write)
WriteSpark jobs · Notebooks · Pipelines · Mirroring · Eventstream destinationT-SQL INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE · stored procedures
Schema enforcementDelta schema (lenient by default)Strict relational
Cross-table transactionsSingle-table ACID via DeltaMulti-table ACID
APEX useBronze · Silver — high-volume, schema-on-read tolerable, Spark-driven conformanceGold for Services where multi-table transactions and stored-proc business logic are required (e.g., RC-E2E-04 Loyalty redemption ledger, RC-E2E-09 lot-trace deletes)

Most APEX Services use Lakehouse for Bronze + Silver and a Lakehouse-backed Gold; Warehouse-backed Gold is reserved for Services that need stored-proc semantics or multi-table transactions. Either way, the agent's MCP read tools (Ch 13) read via the SQL analytics endpoint — read path is uniform.

1A.6 Real-Time Intelligence — The APEX Trigger Plane

RTI is the Fabric workload most central to APEX scenario architecture. The pipeline is fixed:

Real-Time Intelligence canonical flow
External event source
  │  (Event Hubs · Kafka · IoT · REST · Service Bus · Azure SQL CDC ·
  │   Fabric workspace events · OneLake events · job events · Microsoft 365)
  ▼
[ Eventstream ]
  │  - Schema alignment, timestamp normalization, partitioning
  │  - SQL Operator (GA Mar 2026) for stream processing
  │  - Routing fan-out to multiple destinations
  ▼
[ Eventhouse → KQL Database(s) ]
  │  - Auto-indexed, time-series optimized
  │  - Multi-table per database; multiple databases per Eventhouse
  │  - KQL queries: filter · aggregate · join · anomaly detection · time-series
  ▼
[ KQL Queryset ]                       [ Activator ]
  │  - Reusable saved queries           │  - No-code rule engine
  │  - Drives dashboards, alerts        │  - Subscribes to query / event
  │                                     │  - Triggers: Teams notify · email · Power Automate · Pipeline · Notebook
  ▼                                     ▼
[ Real-Time Dashboard ]               [ APEX scenario start ]
  - Live tiles, sub-second refresh     - Activator → Logic Apps Hybrid →
  - Power BI integration                 agent fleet (per Ch 14, Ch 15)

APEX-M wiring per Service:

  • Eventstream as the scenario trigger. RC-E2E-03's cold-chain excursion fires when an IoT temperature reading crosses threshold; the Eventstream filter routes the event to the Eventhouse for forensic preservation and to Activator for immediate scenario dispatch.
  • Eventhouse as the analytical mirror of Bronze. Time-series volume that would overload a Lakehouse (RC-E2E-09 lot scans · TMT-TEL fault telemetry · ER-PU-04 distribution events) lands in an Eventhouse instead. KQL is the read primitive for agents that need temporal analytics.
  • Activator as the Day-1 HITL alerter. Year-1 maturation arc: Activator-driven adaptive cards in Microsoft Teams replace the agent's HITL composer. As the LEDGER fills (Year-2), the agent takes over composition; Activator becomes a redundant alerter rather than the primary path.
  • KQL Queryset alerts turn arbitrary KQL queries into Activator triggers — APEX uses these for cross-Service composite signals (e.g., excursion rate-of-change combined with regional weather forecast).

1A.7 Mirroring — Live SOR Replication

Mirroring is Fabric's zero-ETL replication primitive. Source data lands in OneLake as Delta Parquet, kept in continuous near-real-time sync with the source. APEX uses Mirroring as the default Bronze ingestion path (Ch 6):

Mirrored sourceAPEX-M Bronze use
Microsoft Dynamics 365D365 Customer Service · Field Service · Sales · Commerce as SOR for HLS-E2E-04 (prior auth) · TH-AIR-02 (IROPS) · TMT-TEL service-channel data
Azure SQL Database / Managed InstanceMost enterprise OLTP SORs land here — RC pricing master · HLS claims · ER outage tickets
Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL / MongoDocument SORs (catalog content · agent-state cold storage)
SnowflakeCo-existence pattern for clients with existing Snowflake estate (per Sellers Guide Appendix F)
Azure Databricks Unity CatalogSame — co-existence with Databricks Lakehouses
Fabric SQL DatabaseApplication data created inside Fabric itself
Open Mirroring (any source)For sources without a built-in connector; provider writes Delta Parquet directly to a designated OneLake folder

The benefit for APEX is structural: no ETL pipeline owns the Bronze landing. The source system owns its data; Mirroring keeps the OneLake copy synchronised; the Silver conformance Notebook (Ch 8) reads the mirrored Delta Parquet. When the source schema evolves, the mirrored Bronze schema evolves automatically; only the Silver layer requires conformance updates.

1A.8 Direct Lake — Power BI Without Data Movement

Direct Lake is Power BI's third storage mode (alongside Import and DirectQuery). The semantic model reads Delta Parquet directly from OneLake — no import refresh, no DirectQuery latency. Two flavors:

  • Direct Lake on OneLake (current default) — semantic model can include tables from multiple Fabric items (multiple Lakehouses · Warehouses) within and across workspaces. No fallback to DirectQuery.
  • Direct Lake on SQL (legacy) — semantic model bound to a single SQL analytics endpoint with DirectQuery fallback for unsupported queries. Migration path documented in Direct Lake in Power BI Desktop.

APEX-M uses Direct Lake on OneLake for every Service Gold-mart semantic model. The merchandising-director persona's daily P&L review · the finance-lead's margin-attribution dashboard · the store-ops weekly digest — all Direct Lake. The agent reads the same OneLake Parquet via MCP; the human reads the same Parquet via Direct Lake. Convergence cost: zero ETL between agent path and human path (§29.5).

1A.9 OneLake Shortcuts — Cross-Workspace and Cross-Cloud

Shortcuts are virtual references to data that lives elsewhere in OneLake (same tenant, different workspace) or in external storage (ADLS Gen2 · S3 · GCS · Dataverse). Reads transit the shortcut without copying bytes.

APEX-M shortcut patterns:

  • Cross-Service Gold reads. RC-E2E-03 Pricing's Gold mart shortcut to RC-E2E-09 Lot Provenance's Gold mart — no duplication, ownership stays with the producing Service workspace.
  • Co-existence with Snowflake / Databricks. Per Sellers Guide Appendix F, clients with existing Snowflake estates can shortcut Snowflake-via-Iceberg into OneLake; APEX agents read through the shortcut without forcing a migration.
  • Cross-cloud consumer data. Client has POS data in S3 · clickstream in GCS · sensor data in their on-prem ADLS — three shortcuts into the apex-rc-e2e-03 Bronze workspace, agent queries hit them transparently.

1A.10 Microsoft-Hosted MCP Servers for RTI (preview)

Per the March 2026 release, Fabric Real-Time Intelligence ships two remote MCP servers — Microsoft-hosted, callable over HTTP — that let agents read Eventhouse data and create Activator rules using the same MCP protocol APEX uses for its own Gold-mart MCP host (Ch 13):

ServerEndpointCapabilitiesAPEX use
Eventhouse Remote MCPMicrosoft-hosted HTTP · per EventhouseSchema discovery · KQL query generation · data sampling · natural-language-to-KQLThe Briefer agent uses the Eventhouse MCP to explore time-series anomalies without APEX writing custom KQL tool wrappers · The Analyst can request "spikes in last 24 hours" without an MCP tool definition for every metric
Activator Remote MCPMicrosoft-hosted HTTP · per ActivatorCreate monitoring rules · manage alerts · trigger actionsThe Operations Lead, when staging an HITL approval, can install a follow-up Activator rule ("alert me if this excursion repeats") without leaving the agent context

Per Build AI agents for Real-Time Intelligence, both MCP servers are Microsoft-hosted (no Container Apps to operate). APEX-M's Loader (Services Guide §14A.8) registers these MCP endpoints via MCPStreamableHTTPTool — the agents see them as ordinary tools alongside APEX's own MCP catalog.

1A.11 Fabric Domains — The Data-Mesh Mapping

Fabric domains are logical groupings of workspaces by business unit or subject area. They support delegated governance (per-domain admin can manage their own workspaces) and surface in the OneLake catalog for discovery.

APEX-M's recommended domain map:

DomainWorkspaces groupedWhy
apex-rc (Retail & Consumer)apex-rc-e2e-03 · apex-rc-e2e-04 · apex-rc-e2e-05 · apex-rc-e2e-07 · apex-rc-e2e-09RC practice owns governance over its Service workspaces
apex-hls (Health & Life Sciences)apex-hls-e2e-02 · apex-hls-e2e-04 · apex-hls-e2e-06 · apex-hls-ls-03HLS practice — separate Trust envelope (PHI), separate KV requirements
apex-erER-MN-02 · ER-OG-02/03/05/07 · ER-PU-04Energy & Resources

1A.12 Throttling, Bursting, Smoothing, Surge Protection

Capacity management mechanics every APEX architect must know:

MechanismWhat it doesAPEX-M tuning
ThrottlingApplied at capacity level when CU consumption exceeds SKU. Throttled capacity sees degraded performance until consumption normalises.Monitor via Fabric Capacity Metrics App. Notification at 80% set on every PROD capacity.
BurstingLets jobs temporarily exceed the SKU's CU/s to finish fast. No additional cost — just better latency.Default-on. APEX agent calls benefit because Spark conformance and Direct Lake refresh windows complete sooner.
SmoothingSpreads compute cost over a longer time window so spikes don't trigger throttling.Default-on. Smoothing is what makes occasional Eventstream surges (incident-storm scenarios) survive without throttling neighbour Services.
Surge protectionCaps background-job consumption to leave headroom for interactive (agent / report) latency.Configured per PROD capacity. APEX sets background-job ceiling to ~70% of CUs so agent calls never starve.
Pause / ResumeHalts billing on a capacity entirely.Lab v0.1, DEV: paused outside business hours via Bicep deployment script. PROD: never paused.
Autoscale Billing for SparkMoves Spark Engine compute outside the allocated CUs (per-Spark-job billing).Enabled on PROD only when conformance Notebook windows are predictable enough to budget.

1A.13 The APEX-M Workspace Pattern

APEX-M follows the multiple-workspaces-multiple-capacities deployment pattern (per deployment-pattern guidance). One workspace per Service, with three workspace tiers per Service:

APEX-M workspace topology · per Service
Tenant: contoso.onmicrosoft.com
└─ Domain: apex-rc
   ├─ Capacity: cap-apex-rc-prod (F128, East US 2, paired West US 3)
   │  ├─ Workspace: apex-rc-e2e-03-prod
   │  │  ├─ Lakehouse: bronze (mirrored from D365 + IoT eventstream destination)
   │  │  ├─ Lakehouse: silver (canonicalized — SCML schema family)
   │  │  ├─ Lakehouse / Warehouse: gold (per-Service marts; Direct Lake serves)
   │  │  ├─ Eventhouse: rti (cold-chain excursions, sensor stream)
   │  │  ├─ Eventstream: excursion-events (IoT → Eventhouse + Activator)
   │  │  ├─ Activator: excursion-triggers (event → Logic Apps → agent fleet)
   │  │  ├─ Notebook(s): silver-conformance.ipynb, gold-build.ipynb
   │  │  ├─ Pipeline(s): nightly-gold-rebuild
   │  │  ├─ Semantic Model: rc-e2e-03-direct-lake (Direct Lake on OneLake)
   │  │  └─ Reports: merchandising-director-daily, finance-margin-weekly
   │  └─ Workspace: apex-rc-e2e-04-prod
   │     └─ … (similar layout)
   ├─ Capacity: cap-apex-rc-stage (F32)
   │  └─ Workspace: apex-rc-e2e-03-stage  (deployment-pipeline target)
   └─ Capacity: cap-apex-rc-dev (F8)
      └─ Workspace: apex-rc-e2e-03-dev   (deployment-pipeline source)

Properties of this layout:

  • Per-Service blast radius. A throttling or perf event in apex-rc-e2e-03 cannot affect apex-hls-e2e-04, because they live in separate capacities (one per practice; one Service per workspace).
  • Per-Service Git + deployment pipeline. Each Service workspace pairs with a Git repo branch and a 3-stage pipeline (DEV → STAGE → PROD). Promotions move semantic-model definitions, notebooks, pipelines.
  • Cross-Service composition via shortcuts. When RC-E2E-03 needs RC-E2E-09 lot data (cross-Service), it adds a OneLake shortcut to RC-E2E-09's Gold lakehouse — no physical copy, ownership stays correct.
  • Shared canonical workspace. Schema family Lakehouses (SCML / MERML / EHRML / etc) live in apex-shared-canonical; per-Service workspaces shortcut to them.

Key Takeaways

  • Fabric is a four-level hierarchy: Tenant → Capacity (Microsoft.Fabric/capacities) → Workspace → Item. APEX-M anchors one workspace per Service inside a per-practice capacity inside the client tenant.
  • OneLake is one per tenant, built on ADLS Gen2, Delta Parquet for everything tabular. The medallion (Bronze/Silver/Gold) and the agent's MCP tools read from the same physical store.
  • Five workloads compose: Data Engineering · Data Warehouse · Real-Time Intelligence · Data Factory · Power BI. APEX uses each for distinct responsibilities.
  • Real-Time Intelligence is APEX's scenario-trigger plane: Eventstream → Eventhouse / KQL → Activator → Logic Apps → agent fleet.
  • Mirroring is the default Bronze ingestion path — D365, Azure SQL, Snowflake, Databricks, Cosmos DB, open mirroring. No ETL required.
  • Direct Lake on OneLake serves Power BI semantic models from OneLake Parquet directly; agents and humans read the same bytes.
  • Microsoft-hosted Eventhouse + Activator MCP servers (March 2026) let APEX agents query RTI via MCP without bespoke tool wrappers.
  • F64 is the Power BI Viewer license inflection point — APEX-M PROD entry SKU for tenants with broad analyst populations.

Catalog Drills

  1. For your engagement's primary tenant, draw the four-level hierarchy with concrete names: tenant · capacities (one per practice) · workspaces (one per Service) · key items per workspace.
  2. Pick one Service. Identify which workload(s) it uses and why. If it doesn't use RTI, ask whether the trigger is event-driven; if it doesn't use Direct Lake, ask why the human path is different from the agent path.
  3. For your client's existing data estate, inventory which sources can be Mirrored vs which require open mirroring. Estimate the Mirroring cost saving vs an ETL pipeline (CU/s × hours).
  4. Draw the OneLake shortcut graph for one cross-Service composition (RC-E2E-03 needing RC-E2E-09 lot data). Identify ownership boundaries — which workspace owns the bytes, which workspace consumes via shortcut.
Chapter 1B

Medallion Architecture — Deep Dive · Why Canonical Lives in Silver

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Goes beyond the Ch 1 surface — explains the architectural reasoning behind APEX-M's medallion: why Bronze is preservation-shaped, why Silver is canonical-shaped, why Gold is decision-shaped, and what would break if any one were re-shaped.
  • Drills the classes of source variance Bronze absorbs (system variance · schema variance · semantic variance · temporal variance · governance variance) and how each is dissolved at Silver.
  • Walks the 1:N fan-out pattern — one Silver canonical row supplies many Gold marts; one Gold mart joins many Silver schemas. The canonical anchor is what makes the fan-out tractable.
  • Specifies the contract each tier owes the next, the read-discipline rule (agents read Gold only · humans read Gold only · Silver is internal), and the lineage chain that ties an operator decision back to the SOR row in Bronze.
90-second read
  • Bronze preserves what the SOR said — every per-source variation, every duplicate, every field name oddity, every rate-of-change. Lossless on purpose. Bronze is for forensics and lineage; agents never read it.
  • Silver dissolves source variance — multiple Bronze sources (D365 · Snowflake mirror · IoT stream · on-prem SQL) conform into one canonical schema per business concept. Stable contracts that survive the SOR's schema changes.
  • Gold answers questions — decision-shaped marts denormalised from Silver. One mart per question the agent asks. Direct Lake-served for Power BI and MCP-served to agents.
  • Canonical lives in Silver, not Bronze, because: Bronze must preserve source-specific shape · canonicalising at Bronze would lose information needed for audit · canonicalising at Gold would force every Gold mart to redo the conformance.
  • Canonical lives in Silver, not Gold, because: Gold marts are denormalised answer shapes that change frequently with Service evolution; the anchor of stable meaning must outlive any particular Gold mart.
  • The fan-out: one Silver row often feeds 3–8 Gold marts in different Services; one Gold mart usually joins 2–6 Silver schemas.
  • Read discipline: agents read Gold only (via MCP) · humans read Gold only (via Direct Lake Power BI) · Silver is producer-side internal · Bronze is forensic.
Plain-English primer — why three layers, not two

If three folders sound like extra work, here's the thinking. Imagine you're a chef in a busy restaurant. You could try to skip a step — go straight from "groceries dumped on the counter" to "plated dish for the customer." But chefs don't work that way. They have a prep station in the middle.

At the prep station, the chef:

  • Chops the onions the same way regardless of whether they came from Supplier A or Supplier B.
  • Standardizes the herbs into the kitchen's house mix, so any recipe can grab from one container.
  • Labels and dates everything so anyone in the kitchen can use it consistently.

That prep station is Silver. The groceries on the counter are Bronze. The plated dish is Gold. The chef doesn't put the prep station after plating — that would mean re-prepping for every order. The chef doesn't put it before delivery — that would mean inspectors couldn't trace a complaint back to the original supplier's onions. The prep station sits in the middle precisely because that's the only place it does the most work for the least cost.

In APEX-M, "the prep station" means: one consistent shape per business concept, regardless of which source system the data came from. Once you have that consistent shape, every downstream question (every Gold mart) is fast to build. This chapter explains the same idea in formal terms — sections §1B.1 through §1B.10. Read the primer once; the rest will land easily.

1B.1 The Five Classes of Source Variance Bronze Absorbs

Every APEX-M engagement encounters the same five variance classes. Bronze's job is to absorb each without dissolving any of it — preservation is its only contract:

Variance classExampleWhat Bronze does
System varianceRC client has D365 Commerce in NA region · D365 Customer Insights in EU region · legacy SQL POS in APACThree Bronze landings, source-system tagged. No merge yet.
Schema varianceOld POS schema has CustomerID as INT; new POS schema has CustomerKey as GUID; same business conceptBoth fields preserved verbatim. Schema-version stamp on every row.
Semantic varianceD365 "active customer" = bought in last 12 months; SQL POS "active customer" = bought in last 24 monthsBoth definitions preserved as source data; no normalisation in Bronze.
Temporal varianceD365 mirrored ~5min cadence · POS landed 4h batches · IoT eventstream sub-secondEach lands at its own cadence; per-source ingest_ts column.
Governance varianceD365 fields have built-in sensitivity labels · POS fields have none · IoT has open accessBronze applies four-tier PII classification (Ch 7) at ingest; per-field classification stamp; downstream tiers respect.

If APEX-M canonicalised at Bronze, four of the five variance classes would be lost. The auditor's question — "show me the exact SOR row that drove this decision on 2026-03-14 at 14:23:07" — would have no answer if Bronze had already normalised the field names away. The forensic contract requires verbatim preservation.

1B.2 Silver — The Anchor of Stable Meaning

Silver is where the business concept stabilises. Three rules govern what lives in Silver:

  1. One canonical schema per business concept — not per source system. A SKU is a SKU whether it came from D365 Commerce, SQL POS, or an Excel master. Silver has one canonical SKU schema (MERML · per Ch 2); the conformance Notebook maps each Bronze source's representation to it.
  2. Stability over evolvability — the Silver schema may evolve, but only via additive changes (new optional columns) and explicit deprecation cycles. A breaking change to a Silver schema is an ADR-level decision that ripples to every downstream Gold mart in every Service consuming that schema.
  3. Producer-side · internal — Silver is read by Notebooks and pipelines that build Gold. Silver is not exposed to agents (MCP reads Gold) or humans (Power BI reads Gold). The discipline is enforced by Microsoft Fabric workspace permissions plus OneLake security.

The conformance Notebook (per Ch 8) is the producer that consumes one or more Bronze sources and produces a Silver canonical row. Three transforms typically happen:

  • Field renaming and type coercion — CustomerKey GUID ← CustomerID INT with surrogate-key mapping. last_purchase_ts UTC ← regional timestamps converted.
  • Semantic normalization — "active customer" semantically defined for the Silver schema (e.g., "bought in last 12 months") and computed regardless of which Bronze source originally produced it.
  • De-duplication and merge — when the same business entity appears in multiple Bronze sources, Silver produces one canonical row with the merged attributes, with a source_systems_g array recording every Bronze source that contributed.

1B.3 Why Canonical Must Sit at Silver — The Counterfactuals

The medallion is a three-tier answer to a fundamental tension: preserve raw fidelity for audit · answer fast for decisions · without paying both costs every time. Three counterfactuals make the placement of canonical obvious:

1B.3.1 What if canonical were at Bronze?

Bronze would lose source-specific shape, defeating its forensic contract. The auditor's "show me the exact field as the SOR sent it" becomes impossible to answer. Schema evolutions in the SOR (D365 release upgrades · POS replatform) become destructive at ingest. The four PII tiers (Ch 7) which depend on per-source classification become harder to enforce because the field names have been remapped before classification reads them. Net: every regulator-facing engagement loses the lineage walk.

1B.3.2 What if canonical were at Gold?

Each Gold mart would have to redo the conformance from Bronze. Different agents would see different "canonical" shapes — RC-E2E-03 Pricing's canonical SKU would differ from RC-E2E-05 OSA's canonical SKU even when they're the same business concept. Cross-Service composition (RC-E2E-03 calling RC-E2E-09 lot data per §17.4) requires schema reconciliation between Gold marts, which is exactly the friction Silver dissolves. Net: every cross-Service composition pays a translation tax.

1B.3.3 What if there were no canonical layer at all?

Agents would read Bronze directly. Each agent prompt would need to know every source-specific oddity (D365 field names vs POS field names vs IoT field names). Prompt versions would multiply uncontrollably (a per-source variant for each conceptual prompt). The eval framework (Ch 28.5) would have to maintain golden sets per source rather than per business concept. Net: the agent maturation arc (Year 1 → 2 → 3) becomes intractable because the surface area is multiplied by N source systems.

Canonical-at-Silver is the only placement that absorbs source variance, preserves audit fidelity, and gives agents a stable contract. The medallion is not three arbitrary layers — it is the smallest topology that solves all three requirements simultaneously.

1B.4 The 1:N Fan-Out — Silver to Gold Marts

One Silver canonical row typically feeds many Gold marts. Worked example for the Silver Order row in MERML:

Silver MERML.order canonical row → downstream Gold marts
Silver MERML.order
  │
  ├── RC-E2E-03 Gold · markdown_decision_panel
  │     (joins MERML.order × MERML.sku × MERML.store × WOSFML.shelf_life)
  │
  ├── RC-E2E-04 Gold · loyalty_attribution_panel
  │     (joins MERML.order × CRMML.customer × CRMML.segment × GLML.margin)
  │
  ├── RC-E2E-05 Gold · osa_gap_panel
  │     (joins MERML.order × MERML.sku × MERML.store × WOSFML.task)
  │
  ├── RC-E2E-07 Gold · returns_fraud_panel
  │     (joins MERML.order × CRMML.customer × MERML.return × CRMML.payment_device)
  │
  └── RC-E2E-09 Gold · lot_provenance_panel
        (joins MERML.order × MERML.sku × WOSFML.lot × QMSML.attestation)

One canonical Silver row · five denormalised Gold answers ·
each Gold mart shapes the answer to one decision-question · joins
2-6 Silver schemas per mart · supports both agent reads (MCP) and
human reads (Direct Lake Power BI) from the same Parquet bytes.

The reverse fan-in is also true: one Gold mart typically joins 2–6 Silver schemas (per the parentheticals above). Silver schemas are composable; the canonical contracts each schema offers mean a Gold mart's joining logic is straightforward — no per-source translation, just joins on canonical keys.

1B.4.1 Worked Example in Code — One Excursion, Three Forms

Pseudo-code makes the three forms concrete. Below: an IoT temperature reading lands at Bronze (verbatim), passes through Silver canonicalisation (a Notebook), and emerges in a Gold mart row The Pricer reads via MCP. Three transformations · one event · three forms.

Python pseudo-code · Bronze landing
# IoT temperature sensor posts to Event Hubs · Eventstream routes to Bronze
# Verbatim · no transformation · just stamp ingest metadata + PII classification

def land_to_bronze(raw_event: dict) -> None:
    bronze_row = {
        # === ORIGINAL PAYLOAD — every field preserved as the source sent it ===
        **raw_event,                           # device_id, temp_c, ts, store_id, …

        # === APEX-added metadata ===
        "ingest_ts_t": utc_now(),              # when we received it
        "source_system_s": "iot.eventhub",     # which source
        "source_partition_s": raw_event.get("EnqueuedTimeUtc"),
        "classification_tier_i": classify_pii(raw_event),   # 1, 2, 3 or 4
        "schema_version_s": "iot.v3",          # source schema version at ingest
    }
    append_to_delta(table="bronze_iot_temps", row=bronze_row)
    # Bronze writes are append-only · no UPDATE · no DELETE · ever.
Python pseudo-code · Silver canonicalisation Notebook (runs every 5 min)
# Read recent Bronze rows · canonicalise to SCML.excursion_event · merge with D365

def build_silver_excursion_events(window_start: datetime) -> None:
    iot_rows = read_bronze("bronze_iot_temps", since=window_start)
    d365_rows = read_bronze("bronze_d365_events", since=window_start)

    # CANONICALISE — one row per business-concept event, regardless of source
    for iot in iot_rows:
        # Resolve canonical IDs (surrogate keys)
        facility_id = resolve_facility(source_key=iot["store_id"], source="iot")
        asset_id = resolve_asset(source_key=iot["device_id"], source="iot")

        # Find the matching D365 event for this physical asset (if any)
        d365_match = find_match(d365_rows, asset=asset_id, ts=iot["ts"], window=60)

        # Build the canonical Silver row
        silver_row = {
            "event_id_g": uuid7(iot["ts"]),                      # canonical PK
            "facility_id_g": facility_id,
            "asset_id_g": asset_id,
            "temperature_c_d": iot["temp_c"],                    # numeric, SI units
            "observed_at_t": parse_to_utc(iot["ts"]),            # always UTC
            "severity_score_d": compute_severity(iot["temp_c"]), # business logic
            "source_keys_a": [                                   # forensic links
                {"system": "iot", "key": iot["device_id"]},
                {"system": "d365", "key": d365_match["EventID"]} if d365_match else None,
            ],
            "schema_version_s": "SCML.excursion_event.v2",
            "silver_ingest_t": utc_now(),
        }
        merge_to_delta(
            table="silver_scml_excursion_event",
            row=silver_row,
            merge_on=["event_id_g"],   # idempotent re-runs are safe
        )
SQL pseudo-code · Gold mart materialisation (runs hourly)
-- Build the decision panel The Pricer will read.
-- Joins SIX Silver schema families · denormalised into one wide row per event.

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW gold.g_excursion_decision_panel AS
SELECT
    -- From SCML — the excursion event itself
    e.event_id_g,
    e.facility_id_g,
    e.observed_at_t,
    e.severity_score_d,

    -- From MERML — what SKU lots are in the affected asset
    s.sku_id_g,
    s.sku_name_s,
    s.lot_id_g,
    s.lot_quantity_d,

    -- From WOSFML — shelf-life math
    sh.expiry_date_dt,
    DATEDIFF(day, CURRENT_DATE, sh.expiry_date_dt) AS days_remaining_i,

    -- From SCML — cost-of-goods for margin calculation
    cog.unit_cost_d,

    -- From GLML — current margin per category
    gl.margin_pct_d,
    gl.period_id_g,

    -- From MERML — recent velocity (units/day)
    v.velocity_30d_d,

    -- Decision-shaped derived column
    propose_markdown_pct(
        days_remaining   => DATEDIFF(day, CURRENT_DATE, sh.expiry_date_dt),
        velocity_30d     => v.velocity_30d_d,
        cost_of_goods    => cog.unit_cost_d,
        target_margin    => gl.margin_pct_d
    ) AS recommended_markdown_pct_d

FROM    silver_scml.excursion_event   AS e
JOIN    silver_merml.sku_lot_inventory AS s   ON s.asset_id_g = e.asset_id_g
JOIN    silver_wosfml.shelf_life       AS sh  ON sh.sku_id_g = s.sku_id_g
                                              AND sh.lot_id_g = s.lot_id_g
JOIN    silver_scml.cost_of_goods      AS cog ON cog.sku_id_g = s.sku_id_g
JOIN    silver_glml.margin             AS gl  ON gl.product_category_g
                                                  = s.product_category_g
                                              AND gl.period_id_g = current_period()
JOIN    silver_merml.velocity_30d      AS v   ON v.sku_id_g = s.sku_id_g
                                              AND v.facility_id_g = e.facility_id_g
WHERE   e.severity_score_d > 0.5
  AND   sh.expiry_date_dt < CURRENT_DATE + INTERVAL '7' DAY;

-- Materialise this view into a Delta table for fast Direct Lake reads
-- · refreshed hourly · partitioned by observed_at_t · Z-ordered on facility_id_g

Three code samples · one event · three forms. The Bronze code keeps every byte. The Silver code translates source-specific shapes into one canonical row. The Gold view denormalises six Silver schemas into the answer-shape The Pricer reads. Each transformation is small and explicit because the canonical layer (Silver) absorbed the variance once.

1B.5 The Per-Tier Contracts

Each tier owes the next a specific contract. Violating the contract is an ADR-level event:

TierContract to the next tierViolation example
Bronze → SilverVerbatim preservation · per-source-system tag · PII classification stamped · row-level provenance preserved · schema evolution handled non-destructivelyDropping a field at Bronze ingest "because it's never used" — breaks the lineage walk · forecloses future schema use cases
Silver → GoldCanonical schema by family · semantic normalisation done · merge of duplicate entities · row-level lineage trace back to Bronze · stable column contracts (additive evolution only)Changing a column's data type at Silver — breaks every Gold mart joining on it · breaks every agent prompt referencing it
Gold → AgentDenormalised answer-shape · one mart per decision-question · MCP tool exposure with row-hash registry · Direct Lake-served · Trust-envelope-respectingAn agent reading Silver directly — breaks the read-discipline rule · introduces source-coupling into the agent prompt
Gold → HumanDirect Lake semantic model · sensitivity-label inheritance · row-level security (per persona) · low-latency readA Power BI report joining across Silver schemas — bypasses the agent-readable Gold mart · creates parallel definitions of "decision"

1B.6 Read Discipline — Who Reads What

ReaderBronzeSilverGold
Auditor (forensic)✓ via lineage walk · primary forensic surface✓ as intermediate evidence✓ as decision-final evidence
Silver conformance Notebook✓ producer✓ writer—
Gold build Notebook / pipeline—✓ producer✓ writer
APEX agent✗ never✗ never✓ via MCP
Power BI / human operator✗ never✗ never✓ via Direct Lake
Microsoft Sentinel detection✓ specific KQL access for audit-trail walks——
Microsoft Purview Data Map scan✓ classification✓ lineage✓ business catalog

The read-discipline rule is enforced by OneLake security policies (per §6A.5 of the Deployment Guide). Agent identities are granted Viewer + OneLake security policy on Gold tables only; the policy denies them Silver and Bronze. The same applies to operator personas.

1B.7 Lineage Chain · From Operator Decision Back to SOR Row

The full lineage walk that the auditor exercises for any APEX-M decision:

Forensic lineage chain · single decision
OPERATOR DECISION (HITL approval timestamp · who approved · what action)
   ↑ (LEDGER row reference · four-stamp anchor)
AGENT INVOCATION (LEDGER row · agent_id · prompt_version · model · output)
   ↑ (MCP tool calls · per call row-hash registry entry)
GOLD MART READ (mart name · query hash · row hashes returned)
   ↑ (Microsoft Purview lineage walk · auto-tracked transformations)
SILVER CANONICAL ROW (schema family · canonical entity ID · merge sources)
   ↑ (conformance Notebook lineage · explicit Bronze→Silver mapping)
BRONZE SOR ROW (source system · ingest timestamp · verbatim payload)
   ↑ (Mirroring source manifest · D365/Snowflake/SQL change feed)
ORIGINATING SOR (D365 transaction · POS event · IoT reading)

Purview's automatic lineage covers Bronze→Silver→Gold transitions in Microsoft Fabric. The Bronze→SOR step is Mirroring metadata. The Gold→agent and agent→operator decision steps are LEDGER rows (the rows Purview can't natively walk). Together, the chain reconstructs every decision down to its source-system byte.

1B.8 Multi-Source Silver — The Merge Pattern

When a business entity exists in multiple Bronze sources, Silver merges them. The merge follows three rules:

  1. Authoritative source designation per field — for each Silver column, one Bronze source is declared authoritative (e.g., D365 Sales is authoritative for customer_email; POS is authoritative for last_purchase_ts). The authoritative source-config lives in YAML alongside the conformance Notebook.
  2. Fallback chain — when the authoritative source has a null value, fall back to a documented chain (POS → D365 Sales → CRM master). Every fallback is logged with its source so the lineage walk can retrieve the actual contributor.
  3. Conflict-resolution policy — when sources disagree on a value, the conformance Notebook records all conflicting values in a _source_conflicts column · uses the authoritative value · raises a Sentinel detection if conflict rate exceeds a threshold (Service-specific).

The merge enables Silver to maintain a single-truth canonical view without erasing the underlying source diversity. The diversity is preserved in Bronze and in the merge metadata; Silver just chooses how to present one canonical row downstream.

1B.9 Quality Gates per Tier

TierQuality gatesFailure response
BronzeSchema validation against Mirroring contract · PII classification applied · ingest timestamp present · row count sanityQuarantine table; alert ingest team · Sentinel detection on volume anomaly
SilverCanonical schema validation · merge integrity (no dangling source rows) · authoritative-source available · field-level non-nulls per contract · Silver row count vs Bronze row count expected ratioHalt Gold rebuild · alert data engineer · LEDGER row flagging silver_quality_check_failed
GoldMart-shape validation · query latency budget · Direct Lake refresh success · row-hash consistency across MCP refreshHalt MCP serving for affected mart · failover to previous-day snapshot · Sentinel detection

1B.10 Schema Evolution Discipline

Silver schemas evolve. The discipline:

  • Additive only by default — new optional columns added; existing columns never renamed or retyped. Old Gold builds keep working.
  • Deprecation cycles for any breaking change — a column slated for removal is marked deprecated_at · downstream Gold builds emit a Sentinel warning when reading deprecated columns · two-quarter deprecation period minimum before the column is dropped.
  • Schema version stamped on every Silver row — the schema_version column is preserved; consumers can reason about behavior across versions.
  • ADR required for breaking changes — irreducible breaking changes need an architecture-decision-record approved by the schema-family owner (per Ch 9) and the service-architects of every consuming Service.
  • Backward-compatible reads — Gold build pipelines reading older Silver versions use defaults for new columns; pipelines reading newer Silver versions ignore unknown columns.

Key Takeaways

  • Bronze preserves source variance · Silver dissolves it · Gold answers decision-questions. The three layers solve three different problems.
  • Canonical at Silver is the only placement that satisfies forensic preservation, semantic stability, and decision-speed requirements simultaneously.
  • Five variance classes Bronze absorbs: system · schema · semantic · temporal · governance.
  • 1:N fan-out: one Silver row supports 3–8 Gold marts; one Gold mart joins 2–6 Silver schemas.
  • Read discipline: agents read Gold only · humans read Gold only · Silver is producer-internal · Bronze is forensic.
  • Per-tier contracts enforced by OneLake security · canonical-schema validators · quality gates with explicit failure responses.
  • Schema evolution is additive by default · breaking changes require ADR + two-quarter deprecation.

Catalog Drills

  1. For your engagement's primary Service, identify the five variance classes its Bronze sources exhibit. Which class is the most painful for canonicalisation?
  2. Trace the lineage chain for one operator decision in your engagement — Operator → LEDGER → MCP → Gold → Silver → Bronze → SOR. Identify any step where the chain breaks.
  3. For one Silver schema in your engagement, list every Gold mart that consumes it. Confirm the 1:N fan-out is real; if not, ask whether canonical-at-Silver is over-engineered for that schema.
  4. Run a "what if canonical were at Bronze" thought experiment for one Service. Identify the auditor question that becomes unanswerable. Confirm the architectural choice.
Chapter 2

Canonical Schema Families

What This Chapter Does for You

  • Maps each family to the practices and Services that use it.

60-second read
