2.1 The Schema Families

APEX defines roughly a dozen canonical schema families. Each family corresponds to a functional domain (supply chain, merchandising, pricing, electronic health records, billing & revenue, etc.) and is shared by every Service in any practice that touches that domain. The families are not industry-specific in the conventional sense; SCML serves Retail's RC-E2E-05 (on-shelf availability) and Energy's ER-OG-07 (pipeline leak inventory) and Industrial's ICE-Aftermarket-05 (predictive parts replenishment).

MERMLMerchandisingRC · ICEMarkdown · Elasticity · Competitor · Promotion · Assortment
PROMLPricingRC · TH · TMTPricing · PriceList · DiscountRule · Yield
EHRMLElectronic Health RecordsHLSEncounter · Diagnosis · Procedure · Medication · LabResult

2.2 Naming and Layout Conventions

  • Schema name. Uppercase prefix (3–5 chars) ending in ML for "model layer." SCML, MERML, PROML, EHRML, etc.
  • Entity name. PascalCase, singular: SCML.Lot, MERML.Markdown. Plural-by-default lakehouse table names use lowercase snake_case: scml_lots, merml_markdowns.
  • Bronze table name. br_ prefix + source-system identifier + entity hint: br_pos_transactions, br_sap_inventory_movements.
  • Gold mart name. g_ prefix + question shape: g_markdown_proposal_basis, g_kpi_rc_e2e_03_daily.
  • Foreign keys. APEX-canonical IDs prefixed by entity. customer_id, sku_id, store_id. Source-system IDs preserved as src_*_id for Bronze→Silver lineage.
  • Time fields. event_ts (when it actually happened) vs ingest_ts (when APEX received it) vs silver_ts (when Silver materialized). Always preserve all three.

2.3 Cross-Schema Relationships

The schemas are not islands. RC-E2E-03 reads SCML.Inventory, SCML.Lot, MERML.Markdown, MERML.Elasticity, MERML.Competitor — three different schemas in one Service. Cross-schema joins happen in Silver-to-Gold materialization, not in agent queries.

The relationship graph is documented in Appendix E (Cross-Service Composition Map). The most common joins:

  • SCML.Inventory ⨝ MERML.Markdown on (sku_id, store_id, event_ts) — used in every RC pricing/markdown Service.
  • EHRML.Encounter ⨝ CMSML.Claim on (member_id, encounter_id) — used in every HLS denial-prevention or care-gap Service.
  • WLML.Warranty ⨝ QMSML.Defect on (equipment_id, claim_ts) — used in AXLE / ICE warranty and quality Services.
  • BRMML.UsageEvent ⨝ BRMML.RatedTransaction on (usage_id) with reconciliation against GLML.Posting — TMT-TEL-RAA-04 revenue assurance.

Key Takeaways

  • ~14 canonical schema families serve all 38 Services across 7 practices. SCML, MERML, PROML, EHRML, and the rest are domain-keyed, not industry-keyed.
  • Naming conventions are uniform: Bronze br_, Silver schema-prefixed PascalCase, Gold g_, three timestamps preserved everywhere.
  • Cross-schema joins materialize in Silver→Gold pipelines, not in agent queries; agents see Gold marts, never multi-table joins.
Chapter 3

MCP and the Service Tool Catalog

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Explains how Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the contract between agents and Gold-tier data.
  • Maps the per-Service MCP tool catalog to the Gold marts that back each tool.
  • Walks the access boundary — every MCP call is a managed-identity-authenticated query against Microsoft Fabric Warehouse.
60-second read
  • MCP is a typed RPC contract between agents and Gold; agents call MCP tools, MCP queries Microsoft Fabric Warehouse under mi-apex-merch-mcp.
  • ~165 tools across the 38-Service catalog; Service-scoped role assignments make cross-Service tool access structurally impossible from the wrong agent.
  • Every MCP call writes a LEDGER row with a response row hash; agents verify the hash before reasoning. No agent talks to Fabric directly.
Plain-English primer — MCP is a power outlet

Think of the standard electrical outlet in your home. When you plug in a lamp, you don't have to know whether the electricity came from a wind turbine, a nuclear plant, or your neighbor's rooftop solar. You don't have to splice wires. You don't have to read the utility company's billing system. You just plug in. The outlet is the standardized contract between everything that generates electricity and everything that uses it.

MCP — Model Context Protocol — is the outlet between AI agents and the data tools they need. When an agent needs to read a markdown decision panel, it doesn't write SQL against Microsoft Fabric. It doesn't navigate three levels of database connection. It calls a tool by name (something like rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel) and gets back a typed answer.

Why does that matter?

  • Safety. The outlet only delivers 120 volts (or 240). It doesn't let your lamp pull straight from the high-voltage transmission line. MCP only lets the agent see what the tool definition allows — no agent can "go wider" with free-form SQL.
  • Audit. Every plug-in is logged. Every MCP call writes one LEDGER row, including a hash of the response data, so afterward you can prove what the agent saw.
  • Replaceability. If you replace your generator (Microsoft Fabric → Snowflake, hypothetically), every lamp keeps working as long as the outlet shape stays the same.

The rest of this chapter explains what's behind the outlet (§3.1) · how the catalog of "outlets" is structured across all 38 Services (§3.2) · who plugs in (§3.3) · why we don't let agents bypass the outlet to touch the wires directly (§3.4) · and how Microsoft Agent Framework discovers these outlets and plugs in automatically (§3.5).

3.1 What MCP Is, Operationally

The Model Context Protocol is a typed RPC contract between an agent and a tool host. Each tool has a name, a typed input schema, a typed output schema, and a description string the agent uses for tool selection. Agents call MCP tools instead of writing SQL because MCP gives auditable, scoped, type-safe access — the agent cannot "free-text" a query that pulls more data than the tool definition allows.

In APEX, the MCP host runs as a sidecar to the agent's Container App or as a shared Container App per Service. The host authenticates as the Layer 1 mi-apex-merch-mcp user-assigned managed identity, and every tool's underlying query runs against Microsoft Fabric Warehouse (Gold) under that identity's role assignments.

JSON — example MCP tool definition (RC-E2E-03)
{
  "name": "rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel",
  "description": "Fetch the per-event decision panel for a cold-chain excursion: SKU lot, current inventory position, downstream risk, recent markdown history.",
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "store_id":     { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[A-Z0-9-]{3,32}$" },
      "excursion_id": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" }
    },
    "required": ["store_id", "excursion_id"]
  },
  "output_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "lot_provenance":    { "$ref": "#/definitions/SCMLLot" },
      "inventory_at_risk": { "type": "number" },
      "markdown_history":  { "type": "array", "items": { "$ref": "#/definitions/MERMLMarkdown" } },
      "row_hash":          { "type": "string", "pattern": "^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$" }
    }
  },
  "service_code": "RC-E2E-03",
  "gold_mart":    "g_excursion_decision_panel",
  "audit": {
    "ledger_emit_on_call":   true,
    "row_hash_in_response":  true
  }
}

Every tool definition is per-Service. rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel belongs to RC-E2E-03 and only to RC-E2E-03; HLS-E2E-04 has its own tools that read EHRML/CMSML Gold marts under HLS-E2E-04's name. The Layer 1 mi-apex-merch-mcp identity is granted scoped Microsoft.Authorization role assignments per Service, so cross-Service tool access is structurally impossible from the wrong agent.

3.1.1 What the Code Looks Like — Tool Author Side

The MCP host is a small FastAPI-style server. A tool is a Python function plus three pieces of metadata: a typed input, a typed output, and a description string the LLM uses to pick the tool. Pseudo-code:

Python · MCP tool definition (RC-E2E-03 example)
from apex_m.mcp import tool, MCPHost
from apex_m.identity import managed_identity_token
from apex_m.fabric import query_gold_warehouse
from apex_m.ledger import emit_audit_row, compute_row_hash
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

# === TYPED INPUT — what the agent must supply ===
class ExcursionDecisionInput(BaseModel):
    excursion_event_id: str = Field(description="The canonical event_id_g from §1B.4.1")
    sku_id: str = Field(description="The canonical sku_id_g from MERML")
    store_id: str = Field(description="The canonical facility_id_g from WOSFML")

# === TYPED OUTPUT — what the tool guarantees to return ===
class ExcursionDecisionOutput(BaseModel):
    event_id: str
    sku_name: str
    store_name: str
    units_in_lot: int
    cost_of_goods: float
    days_remaining: int
    velocity_30d: float
    recommended_markdown_pct: float
    row_hash: str   # FORENSIC ANCHOR — agent verifies before reasoning

# === THE TOOL ITSELF ===
@tool(
    name="rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel",
    description="""Fetch the per-event decision panel for a cold-chain excursion:
                    SKU lot, store, days remaining, velocity, cost, recommended markdown.
                    Returns one row per (event, sku, store) tuple.""",
    pattern="read",                # read | decision-emit | hitl-stage
    service_code="RC-E2E-03",
    pii_tiers_touched=[1, 2],      # never 3 or 4 in this tool
)
def get_excursion_decision_panel(input: ExcursionDecisionInput) -> ExcursionDecisionOutput:
    # 1. Query Microsoft Fabric Warehouse using the per-Service managed identity
    sql = """
        SELECT * FROM gold.g_excursion_decision_panel
        WHERE event_id_g = ? AND sku_id_g = ? AND facility_id_g = ?
    """
    row = query_gold_warehouse(
        sql=sql,
        params=[input.excursion_event_id, input.sku_id, input.store_id],
        identity=managed_identity_token("mi-apex-merch-mcp"),
    )

    # 2. Compute the response row hash · this is what the agent will verify
    row_hash = compute_row_hash(row)

    # 3. Audit the call — one LEDGER row per MCP invocation
    emit_audit_row(
        service_code="RC-E2E-03",
        tool="rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel",
        input_hash=hash_dict(input.model_dump()),
        response_hash=row_hash,
        agent_caller=current_agent_identity(),
    )

    # 4. Return the typed response with the hash for agent verification
    return ExcursionDecisionOutput(**row, row_hash=row_hash)

# === BOOT THE HOST ===
host = MCPHost(service_code="RC-E2E-03")
host.register(get_excursion_decision_panel)
# host.register(stage_markdown_approval)        # decision-emit pattern · §13.1.2
# host.register(stage_hitl_card)                # hitl-stage pattern · §13.1.3
# ... 18 more tools per RC-E2E-03 ...
host.run(port=8080)

3.1.2 What the Code Looks Like — Agent Caller Side

An agent in Microsoft Agent Framework consumes the tool through the Loader. The agent's prompt selects the tool by name; the SDK marshals the typed input, calls the MCP host over HTTP, and returns the typed response into the agent's context — invisibly to the agent author:

Python · Agent caller side (Microsoft Agent Framework)
from agent_framework import Agent
from agent_framework.foundry import FoundryChatClient
from agent_framework.tools import MCPStreamableHTTPTool
from apex_m.middleware import (
    ApexClassificationGuard, ApexPromptShield, ApexAuditMiddleware
)

# Discover and wrap the MCP tool · row-hash check is automatic in the wrapper
get_panel_tool = MCPStreamableHTTPTool(
    endpoint=APEX_MCP_HOST_URL,                    # from KV-backed env var
    tool_name="rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel",
    header_provider=managed_identity_token_provider("apex-mcp"),
    row_hash_check=True,                           # APEX extension
)

# Build The Pricer · Microsoft Agent Framework ChatClientAgent
the_pricer = Agent(
    client=FoundryChatClient(),
    name="rc-e2e-03-the-pricer",
    instructions=load_prompt("apps/services/rc-e2e-03/agents/the-pricer/prompt.md"),
    tools=[get_panel_tool],                        # plus 4 more tools
    middleware=[
        ApexClassificationGuard(agent_spec=spec),
        ApexPromptShield(content_safety_endpoint=CS_ENDPOINT),
        ApexAuditMiddleware(agent_spec=spec),
    ],
)

# At runtime: the agent decides to call the tool from its prompt.
# The Loader-wrapped MCPStreamableHTTPTool handles:
#   - HTTP POST to the MCP host with input dict
#   - Microsoft Entra ID claim auth via managed identity
#   - Response deserialization to the typed output
#   - row_hash verification (raises if registry hash != response hash)
# The agent prompt simply sees the typed result in its context window.
result = await the_pricer.run(
    "An excursion fired for event e7c9f12, sku S-4187, store 412. "
    "What's your markdown recommendation?"
)

Two halves · one contract. The author writes the tool once; every agent in every Service that has authorization sees the same shape regardless of which orchestration pattern it's running inside.

Across all 38 Services, the APEX tool catalog runs to roughly 165 tools (Sellers Guide §5.3.4 cites that number). The distribution is uneven by design — pricing-rich Services (RC-E2E-03, TH-HOT-03, TMT-TEL-RAA-04) have more tools because their Gold marts are richer; simpler Services have fewer.

3.3 The MCP Host and the Microsoft Platform

The MCP host is a small FastAPI app (Python in the MVP) that registers tool definitions at startup and dispatches incoming MCP requests to backing Microsoft Fabric Warehouse queries. It runs as a Container App in the same Microsoft.App/managedEnvironments environment as the agents.

The data-plane path:

  1. Agent calls MCP host (HTTP, JSON-RPC framed).
  2. MCP host authenticates as mi-apex-merch-mcp via Microsoft Entra ID.
  3. MCP host issues a parameterized T-SQL query against Microsoft Fabric Warehouse (Gold mart).
  4. MCP host computes the response row hash (SHA-256 over canonical JSON), emits a LEDGER row recording (tool name, agent, input args, output row hash), returns the response.
  5. Agent reads the response, asserts the row hash matches what LEDGER recorded, proceeds with reasoning.
Best Practice — Agents check the row hash

The MCP response includes the row hash and LEDGER also has the row hash. The agent verifies they match before using the data. This catches a category of bugs (cache staleness, mid-flight mart rebuilds) early, while the LEDGER row is still warm. It is cheap to write the check; it pays for itself in the first cross-region post-mortem.

3.4 Why Agents Don't Talk to Microsoft Fabric Directly

An obvious shortcut: skip the MCP host, give the agent the Microsoft Fabric Warehouse connection string and let it write SQL. It works on day one and breaks on day ninety in three ways.

  • Audit becomes free-form. If an agent writes its own SQL, the LEDGER row records "agent ran a query" but the query text is the audit. Reconstruction is by string parsing. With MCP, the audit row is "agent called rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel(store_id=BIGBOX-100, excursion_id=…)"; the call signature is structured.
  • Scope creep. An agent that can write SQL can read any Gold mart; an agent that calls MCP can only call the tools registered for its Service. The MCP catalog is the access policy.
  • Schema drift. An agent's SQL is fixed at prompt-write time; a MCP tool definition is versioned and updated centrally. When a Gold mart is reshaped, you reshape one MCP tool; the agents that call it keep working.
ADR · architecture decision
ADR-003-01 · 2026-04-18 · accepted

Decision: Agents access Gold-tier data only through MCP tools, never via direct Microsoft Fabric Warehouse SQL.

Why: The three reasons above (audit · scope · drift) compound rather than add. Free-form SQL inflates audit cost (string-parse reconstruction), inflates governance cost (every Gold mart is now in the access policy surface), and inflates maintenance cost (every Gold-mart shape change ripples into every consuming agent's prompt). MCP collapses all three to a single typed-RPC contract managed centrally.

Trade-off rejected: Agents authoring SQL with sandboxed Microsoft Entra ID identity scoping. Microsoft Entra ID conditional-access policies could enforce row-level scope; the agent's reasoning could include why it queried what it queried. But it doesn't solve schema drift, and the audit-narrative remains free-form. The cost of MCP is one extra network hop per tool call (~30ms); the benefits are structural.

Caveat: Direct Fabric access remains available for data engineers running Microsoft Fabric notebooks for Silver builds and Gold materialization (§8). The rule applies to agent runtime, not to the data-engineering plane.

3.5 Microsoft Agent Framework as MCP Consumer

Per Microsoft Agent Framework local MCP tools, the SDK ships three MCP transport types. APEX-M's MCP host is built to satisfy all three; the choice is per-substrate:

Agent Framework MCP typeTransportAPEX-M usage
MCPStdioToolLocal subprocess · stdin/stdoutLaptop tier (Lab v0.1) — APEX MCP host runs as a subprocess inside the agent's docker-compose network. Fastest path · zero network · no auth overhead.
MCPStreamableHTTPToolHTTP + Server-Sent EventsDEV / STAGE / PROD — APEX MCP host runs as a Container App reached over a private endpoint. Microsoft Entra ID claim auth · row-hash registry · standard auditable surface.
MCPWebsocketToolWebSocketReserved for streaming-tool scenarios (rare — most APEX MCP calls are request-response with bounded latency).

The .NET equivalent uses the official MCP C# SDK; tools convert to AIFunction via .AsAIFunction() and register on the agent via ChatClientAgent.tools. Either way, the agent code that uses an APEX MCP tool is identical regardless of the substrate the MCP host runs on — the Loader (§14A.8) handles the transport-type selection from env var configuration.

3.5.1 Hosted MCP — Foundry Toolboxes

Beyond local MCP, Microsoft Foundry can host MCP servers itself (per hosted MCP tools). Foundry-hosted MCP servers expose tools as reusable toolboxes — named, versioned server-side tool collections that multiple agents can subscribe to. APEX-M uses hosted MCP for two specific cases:

  • Microsoft-hosted RTI MCP servers — the Eventhouse and Activator remote MCP servers (per §1A.10). Microsoft operates the server; APEX agents subscribe to the toolbox; no APEX-side host code.
  • Tool-approval-required tools — Tier-3 PHI unlock and similar dual-control tools. Foundry's tool-approval workflow pauses execution for human review before invocation; APEX-M maps the approval persona to the Trust envelope's pii-unlock approver list.

3.5.2 The APEX MCP Catalog as an Agent Framework Toolbox

An APEX MCP host can expose its tools as a Foundry toolbox · then any Foundry agent in the same project subscribes to the toolbox and consumes the tools as ordinary FunctionTool instances. This is the integration point that makes APEX MCP tools portable: a Service authored on the canonical pattern can plug into agents authored in either pure Agent Framework code or Foundry's no-code Workflow agent type.

apex_m/host.py · expose APEX MCP catalog as Foundry toolbox
from agent_framework.foundry import FoundryToolbox
from apex_m.mcp_catalog import load_service_tools

toolbox = FoundryToolbox(
    name=f"apex-{SERVICE_CODE}-mcp",
    description=f"APEX-M Gold-mart tools for {SERVICE_CODE}",
    tools=load_service_tools(SERVICE_CODE),   # 8-20 tools per Service
    version=APEX_MCP_CATALOG_VERSION,
)
toolbox.publish(project=FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT)

Once published, every agent in the project — including agents authored outside APEX-M by an engagement team — sees the toolbox in Foundry. Row-hash registry semantics (§13.2) are preserved end-to-end; the agent still gets the same row-hash response and the same LEDGER stamp regardless of whether it consumed the tool via MCPStreamableHTTPTool (direct) or via the Foundry toolbox indirection.

Key Takeaways

  • MCP is a typed RPC contract between agents and Gold-tier data; agents call MCP tools, MCP queries Microsoft Fabric Warehouse under a Service-scoped managed identity.
  • Per-Service tool catalogs (~165 tools across the catalog); Layer 1 mi-apex-merch-mcp identity gets scoped role assignments so cross-Service tool access is structurally impossible.
  • Every MCP call writes a LEDGER row with a response row hash; agents verify the hash before reasoning over the data.
  • Microsoft Agent Framework consumes APEX MCP tools via MCPStdioTool (laptop), MCPStreamableHTTPTool (production), or MCPWebsocketTool (streaming) · same agent code across all substrates · transport selected via env var.
  • The APEX MCP catalog can publish as a Foundry toolbox · downstream Foundry agents (including non-APEX agents) subscribe and consume tools through the same row-hash-anchored contract.
  • Don't let agents talk to Microsoft Fabric directly — audit, scope, and schema versioning all break.
Part II

Bronze Tier — Client Data Sources

Before Marisol's Teams card existed, before the agents had anything to reason about, before Gold had answers to package — the data had to arrive. A temperature sensor on truck TRK-2147 took a reading. D365 Commerce logged a transaction in the western region. A pharmacist's note posted to Epic. An order-management system wrote a fulfillment status to Azure SQL. Every minute, in every client tenant APEX-M serves, thousands of rows from dozens of source-of-record systems land somewhere. Bronze is where they all arrive.

The Bronze contract is severe in its simplicity: preserve every byte exactly as the source system sent it. Don't translate field names. Don't drop fields you think APEX won't need. Don't reconcile inconsistencies between systems. Don't compute. The auditor's question two years from now — "show me the row D365 actually sent at 14:23:07 on Tuesday" — must be answerable with one query against Bronze. Anything you transformed at landing is gone.

The four chapters in this part teach the on-ramp. Chapter 4 inventories the source-of-record systems each practice typically engages — D365 across most practices, Epic and Cerner for HLS, OSS/BSS for TMT-TEL, SAP S/4 for AXLE finance, IoT brokers for everything sensor-driven. Chapter 5 covers the Real-Time Hub pattern — Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence's Eventstream + Eventhouse for the streaming sources that can't wait for batch. Chapter 6 walks ingestion and tokenization — the moment Tier-3 PHI or Tier-4 financial data lands and gets a token, before it ever touches a Silver pipeline. Chapter 7 closes with the PII classification scheme and the pii-unlock identity that gates re-tokenization downstream.

Source-of-Record Inventory by Industry

What This Chapter Does for You

4.1 The SOR Pattern Across the Catalog

Every Service in the 38-Service catalog reads from a small number of client SOR systems. The systems differ by practice, but the categories repeat: operational transaction system (POS, EHR, billing mediation), master-data system (ERP, MDM), customer-or-member system (CRM, payer member master), asset/IoT telemetry (refrigeration, network, manufacturing line), and external feed (competitor pricing, weather, regulatory). RC-E2E-03 hits four of these categories; HLS-E2E-04 hits three; ER-OG-07 hits two with high IoT volume.

4.2 SOR-to-Bronze Connection Pattern

For each SOR, three pieces have to be settled before any Bronze row lands:

  1. Who owns the connection. The client owns the SOR; APEX owns the Bronze landing zone. The connection itself — a Microsoft Fabric Mirroring link, a Microsoft.DataFactory pipeline, an Eventstream connector — is deployed inside the client's Microsoft platform tenant under the Layer 1 substrate, but it reaches into client systems with client credentials. Independence-compliant.
  2. What gets persisted. Always the raw row, in the SOR's native schema, with no enrichment. The Bronze contract from §1.3.1 holds without exception.
  3. How often it lands. Three cadences are common. Streaming (POS, refrigeration, network probes) lands continuously through Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence Eventstream. Near-real-time (1–15 min batches via change data capture) lands through Microsoft Fabric Mirroring or Microsoft.DataFactory. Daily / weekly (master data, competitor feeds, regulatory rate sheets) lands through scheduled Microsoft.DataFactory pipelines.

4.3 Microsoft Fabric Ingestion Paths

Microsoft Fabric exposes four ingestion paths into a Lakehouse, each appropriate for a different SOR shape:

PathMicrosoft Fabric componentSOR shapeTypical APEX use
MirroringMicrosoft Fabric Mirrored DatabaseDatabase SOR with CDC support (Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, Snowflake, Databricks)Mirror SAP S/4HANA tables · payer claims engines · PMS
EventstreamMicrosoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence EventstreamStreaming events (Kafka, Event Hubs, IoT Hub)POS terminal events · refrigeration telemetry · network probes
PipelineMicrosoft Fabric Data Pipeline (Microsoft.DataFactory under the hood)Files, REST APIs, scheduled extractsCompetitor pricing CSVs · daily ERP exports · regulatory rate sheets
ShortcutOneLake Shortcut (Microsoft Fabric)Existing data in another Fabric workspace, ADLS Gen2, S3, GCSCross-tenant Deloitte reference data · shared synthetic fixtures (Lab only)

Most Services use a mix. RC-E2E-03's Bronze layer combines an Eventstream (refrigeration), a Mirrored Database (SAP S/4HANA inventory), and a Pipeline (competitor pricing daily CSV). The medallion contract is uniform regardless of path; the path is just an ingestion choice.

4.4 The SOR Connection Inventory File

For every Service onboarded into a tenant, the delivery team commits a sor-connections.yaml alongside the Service Bicep. This file is the audit-grade record of which client systems feed the Service.

YAML — sor-connections.yaml example (RC-E2E-03)

    landing_path:  bronze/br_erp_inventory
    fabric_component: MirroredDatabase
    cdc_source:    "SAP S/4HANA · /APEX/inventory_position · CDC"
    cadence:       near-real-time
    schema_family: SCML
    pii_classification: tier-2

  - sor_id:        contoso-refrigeration
    description:   "Walk-in refrigeration telemetry · 8,400 sensors"
    landing_path:  bronze/br_refrigeration_telemetry
    fabric_component: Eventstream
    eventstream_name: es-contoso-refrigeration
    cadence:       streaming
    schema_family: SCML
    pii_classification: tier-1

  - sor_id:        nielsen-competitor-pricing
    description:   "Daily competitor pricing feed · top-12 competitor set"
    landing_path:  bronze/br_competitor_pricing
    fabric_component: DataPipeline

    pii_classification: tier-1
    owner:         contoso-merchandising

The MCP catalog editor and the Microsoft Purview catalog both consume this file. The first registers MCP tools that depend on these Bronze landings. The second registers Purview assets so lineage shows up before any Silver build runs.

Key Takeaways

  • Five SOR categories — operational, master/ERP, customer/member, asset/IoT, external — repeat across all 7 practices with practice-specific vendors.
  • SOR connections live in the client tenant under Layer 1 substrate and reach into client systems with client credentials; Independence-compliant by construction.
  • Four Microsoft Fabric ingestion paths (Mirroring, Eventstream, Pipeline, Shortcut) cover every SOR shape; a Service typically uses two or three.
  • sor-connections.yaml is the audit-grade record per Service — Microsoft Purview and the MCP catalog both consume it.
Chapter 5

Real-Time Hub Pattern · Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence (RTI) components used as streaming Bronze.
  • Maps Eventstream → KQL DB → Lakehouse for the streaming Services in the catalog.
  • Shows how the W2-pilot trigger pattern ("Excursion Event Fires · DAG Orchestrator") materializes operationally.
60-second read
  • Microsoft Fabric RTI (Eventstream + KQL DB + Eventhouse) is the streaming-Bronze substrate for any event-shaped source.
  • Eventstream routes events to KQL DB (streaming Bronze) and Lakehouse (batch Silver path) — same events, two consumers.
  • KQL update-policy rules detect trigger conditions; the orchestrator subscribes via Event Grid. Trigger lives in data, not in agent code.

5.1 The RTI Components

Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence is the streaming-data substrate inside Microsoft Fabric. For APEX, three RTI components matter:

  • Eventstream (Microsoft.Fabric/eventstreams) — the entry point. Receives events from Azure Event Hubs, Azure IoT Hub, Kafka, Confluent Cloud, or AWS Kinesis. Routes events to one or more sinks.
  • KQL Database (Microsoft.Fabric/kqldatabases) — the streaming-Bronze store. Holds events with high ingestion rate and fast query (KQL) access. Acts as Bronze for any Service whose source is event-shaped.
  • Eventhouse — the workspace container for KQL DBs in Fabric. Logical grouping per Service or per tenant.

5.2 The Pattern

For every streaming Service in the catalog (RC-E2E-03 cold-chain, ER-OG-07 pipeline leak, TMT-TEL-NET-02 network fault prediction, ICE-Connected-06 dealer telemetry, etc.), the pattern is:

  1. Client streaming SOR (POS, IoT, network probe) emits events to an event broker (Azure Event Hubs, Kafka, etc.). The broker is in the client tenant; APEX does not own it.
  2. Microsoft Fabric Eventstream consumes the broker, routing events to two sinks:
    • KQL DB as streaming Bronze — full-fidelity event store with high cardinality, queryable in KQL.
    • Lakehouse via the Eventstream-to-Lakehouse sink — same events, written as Delta Parquet for batch Silver builds.
  3. An Eventstream rule (KQL-language predicate) detects the trigger condition (e.g., temperature exceeds threshold for >15 minutes) and emits a derived event to a downstream Eventstream sink — typically Azure Service Bus or another Eventstream feeding the orchestrator.
  4. Azure Logic Apps Hybrid (or n8n on the laptop) receives the trigger and starts the W2-pilot DAG.
  5. The DAG calls agents in sequence, each agent reading Gold via MCP, each writing LEDGER rows.

5.3 The Excursion-Trigger Example

RC-E2E-03's "Cold-chain excursion mid-shift" scenario exercises the pattern end to end. The event chain:

KQL — Eventstream rule (excursion detection)
// Eventstream rule: emit an excursion event when a sensor exceeds threshold
// for >= 15 minutes within a single store-zone.
br_refrigeration_telemetry
| where temperature_c > threshold_c
| extend window = bin(event_ts, 1m)
| summarize
    breach_minutes = count(),
    first_breach   = min(event_ts),
    last_breach    = max(event_ts),
    peak_temp      = max(temperature_c)
    by store_id, zone_id, lot_id, hin(event_ts, 30m)
| where breach_minutes >= 15
| project
    excursion_id   = strcat(store_id, "-", zone_id, "-", format_datetime(first_breach, "yyyyMMddHHmm")),
    store_id, zone_id, lot_id,
    duration_min   = breach_minutes,
    peak_temp,
    fired_ts       = now()

This rule is registered as an Eventstream KQL transformation. When it fires, it emits to a downstream Eventstream that Azure Logic Apps Hybrid subscribes to (via Event Grid). Logic Apps starts the workflow, calls The Analyst via HTTP with the excursion payload, and the W2-pilot DAG runs.

Note — Why the rule is at Eventstream, not in the agent

The rule is the trigger. The agent is the decision. Putting the trigger in Eventstream keeps three properties: (1) the agent only runs when something is worth deciding (cost-efficient on Container Apps Consumption profile); (2) the trigger logic is declarative KQL the data team can reason about; (3) the trigger event itself is a row in the KQL DB and on LEDGER, so audit reconstruction starts at the firing condition, not the agent invocation. Ch 5A goes deeper on the threshold taxonomy, Activator as the threshold engine, and the four-tier velocity composition — read it after this chapter for the full picture.

5.4 Streaming-Bronze vs Batch-Bronze in the Same Service

RC-E2E-03 has both streaming Bronze (refrigeration telemetry, POS) and batch Bronze (ERP inventory snapshots, daily competitor pricing). Silver builds run on a hybrid cadence — a continuous 5-minute window for the streaming side, joined against the most recent daily snapshot of the batch side. The Gold mart materializes after both sides are fresh.

This hybrid cadence is the norm, not the exception. About 18 of the 38 Services have at least one streaming source plus at least one batch source. The orchestrator does not see the cadence difference; it just calls MCP tools, and the MCP tools query Gold marts that are fresh.

Key Takeaways

  • Microsoft Fabric Real-Time Intelligence (Eventstream + KQL DB + Eventhouse) is the streaming-Bronze substrate for any Service whose source is event-shaped.
  • Eventstream routes events to both KQL DB (streaming Bronze) and Lakehouse (batch Silver build path) — same events, two consumers.
  • Eventstream KQL rules detect trigger conditions and emit derived events that orchestrators (Logic Apps Hybrid · n8n) subscribe to. The trigger lives in data, not in agent code.
  • Hybrid streaming-plus-batch is the norm: ~18 of 38 Services combine both.
  • Ch 5A picks up here with the four-tier velocity model (streaming · semi-real-time · periodic · Redis hot cache), the threshold taxonomy, and the Microsoft Fabric Activator deep dive — read it next.
Chapter 5A

Data Velocity, Thresholds & Activator — From Signal to Decision

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the four data-velocity tiers APEX-M composes — real-time streaming, semi-real-time, periodic feeds, and the Redis hot cache — with explicit decision criteria for picking among them.
  • Deep-dives Microsoft Fabric Activator as the threshold-evaluation engine: objects, properties, triggers, actions, and the per-Service use cases that pull on it.
  • Teaches a threshold taxonomy (single-metric · windowed · composite · rate-of-change · anomaly · pattern-match) and the canonical threshold-to-action mapping APEX-M Services declare.
  • Shows how a single APEX-M Service often composes three or four velocity tiers at once — and how the trigger-to-decision audit trail stitches them.
  • Names the Redis hot-cache role in the velocity hierarchy and the working/episodic patterns that depend on it (cross-links Ch 25.3 for the full Redis deep dive).
90-second read
  • Four velocity tiers, one composition surface. APEX-M Services don't pick one velocity tier — they compose them. Real-time streaming for "fire on event," semi-real-time for "react within minutes," periodic for "reconcile daily," Redis for "sub-millisecond working memory." Each tier has a Microsoft component, a latency budget, and a cost profile.
  • Thresholds are the bridge from data to action. Without a threshold, a signal is just a row. APEX-M makes thresholds declarative — defined in thresholds.yaml per Service, versioned alongside Bicep, mapped 1:1 to an action and an accountable owner.
  • Activator is the threshold engine for streaming + semi-real-time. Microsoft Fabric Activator (Real-Time Intelligence) watches Eventstreams · Lakehouse tables · Power BI semantic models. It defines objects (truck, store, SKU, agent), aggregates per-object properties, evaluates triggers per object, and fires actions (Teams notification · Power Automate · Logic Apps · custom HTTP webhook).
  • Per-object granularity. 10,000 trucks share one trigger definition; Activator tracks 10,000 independent per-truck states. This is the property that makes Activator viable for APEX-M's per-store, per-SKU, per-agent threshold fan-out — no per-object plumbing to write.
  • Threshold → action is a 1:1 contract. APEX-M's canonical action types: notify · escalate · gate · halt · page · rollback · adaptive. Each threshold owns exactly one. Severity ladders compose by stacking thresholds — same data feed, different cutoffs, different actions.
  • Redis is the runtime hot path. Sub-millisecond reads for the in-flight workflow's earlier steps, the last-N similar decisions, the operator-preference cache, and the MCP-result short-TTL cache. Redis is not a velocity tier for the source data — it is a working-memory layer the agent reaches into between LLM calls.
  • Trigger lives in data; decision lives in agent. The boundary is intentional. Threshold + Activator decide "is this worth waking an agent for." The agent decides "what to do about it." Both write to LEDGER (per Ch 14B.5 audit middleware) so the audit trail starts at the firing condition, not the agent invocation.

5A.1 The Four-Tier Velocity Spectrum

Every APEX-M Service ingests signals at one of four velocity tiers — and most Services compose more than one. The four tiers are not interchangeable; each has a Microsoft component, a latency budget, a cost profile, and a class of decisions it is built for.

TierLatency from event to consumableFreshnessMicrosoft componentsCost driverBest for
1 · Real-time streaming< 1 secondLive (sub-second)Microsoft.Fabric/eventstreams · Microsoft.Fabric/kqldatabases (Eventhouse) · Activator on EventstreamFabric capacity units (per F-SKU) · per-event ingestionExcursion firing · fraud detection · predictive maintenance · network fault detection · IoT telemetry
2 · Semi-real-time1–5 minutesNear-liveDirect Lake on OneLake · Mirrored Database (Fabric · CDC from Microsoft.Sql / Microsoft.DocumentDB) · Activator on Lakehouse/semantic modelFabric capacity units · mirroring trafficOSA gap detection · loyalty offer triggers · supply-chain alerts · sentiment shifts · daily-reset KPIs
3 · Periodic / batch feedsHours to 24hDaily / hourlyFabric Data Pipelines · Fabric Notebooks · scheduled refresh on semantic models · Logic Apps recurrence triggersFabric capacity units · storage (OneLake)Performance attribution · monthly reconciliation · training-data refresh · cohort analysis · compliance reports
4 · Hot cache< 1 msSession-bound · TTL-drivenMicrosoft.Cache/Redis@2024-03-01 PremiumPer-vCore Premium tier · network egressWorkflow session state · last-N similar decisions · operator-preference cache · MCP-result short-TTL cache · rate-limit counters

Tier 4 (Redis) is not a velocity tier for the source data — it is a working-memory layer the agent fleet reaches into between LLM calls. The first three tiers describe how data arrives from the client SOR; Redis describes how the agent remembers what it just did. We include all four in one table because picking the right tier per signal is the architectural decision, and Redis is part of the same decision.

5A.1.1 Picking a Tier — Decision Criteria

The temptation in every engagement is to over-buy real-time. Streaming is expensive in Fabric capacity units and operationally heavier. The decision tree:

QuestionYes → TierNo → Tier
Will a delay of 5+ minutes materially harm the decision? (e.g., refrigeration loss compounds; competitor markdown is wasted)Tier 1 — streaming EventhouseGo to next question
Is the decision time-of-day-bound? (operator opens the dashboard at 9am · weekly planning meeting at noon)Tier 2 — semi-real-time, freshness within minutes is enoughGo to next question
Does the decision require comparison across days/weeks of history? (cohort analysis · attribution · regression)Tier 3 — periodic refresh; latency is dominated by the join window, not the freshnessDefault to Tier 2
Does the agent need this during a workflow run, faster than a Gold-mart query? (last-N similar decisions · in-flight conversation history)Tier 4 — Redis hot cache, always paired with one of Tiers 1–3 as the system of recordUse the underlying tier directly
Best Practice — start in Tier 2, promote to Tier 1 with evidence

APEX-M's default for any new signal is Tier 2 (semi-real-time). It is the cheapest tier that still feels live to an operator. Promote to Tier 1 only when the business case names a specific cost-of-delay (e.g., "every 5 minutes a refrigerator stays warm, 0.3% of inventory is at risk"). The reverse demotion — Tier 1 to Tier 2 — happens twice as often as anyone expects; engagements over-buy real-time because it sounds important, not because it is required.

5A.2 Tier 1 — Real-Time Streaming via Eventhouse

Eventhouse (the Fabric workspace container for KQL Databases) is the streaming-Bronze store for any APEX-M Service whose source emits events. Per Microsoft Learn, Eventhouse provides:

  • High ingestion rates — billions of events per day per KQL DB, sub-second indexing
  • KQL query — the same Kusto query language used in Application Insights, Log Analytics, Sentinel, Defender XDR; reusable analyst skill
  • Streaming ingestion + queued ingestion — streaming for sub-second freshness, queued for higher-throughput batch ingestion at lower per-event cost
  • Update policies — KQL-defined transformations that derive new tables from raw event streams (Bronze → Silver inside Eventhouse, before the data ever lands in Lakehouse)
  • Materialized views — pre-aggregated rollups (per-store · per-zone · per-minute) for fast read paths
  • OneLake availability — every KQL table can be exposed as a Delta Parquet shortcut in OneLake, so Lakehouse semantic models and Notebooks read the same data without a copy

5A.2.1 When Eventhouse Is the Right Answer

The cost of Eventhouse is real (it consumes Fabric capacity units and per-event ingestion is metered). The decision rule is sharper than "it's a stream." A signal belongs in Eventhouse when:

  • Event volume is high. Refrigeration telemetry from 250 stores × 8 zones × 1 reading/30s = ~5.7M events/day. Network probe data from a TMT-TEL-NET-02 carrier-grade fabric runs an order of magnitude higher. Lakehouse Delta tables handle batch fine; they do not handle this ingestion rate.
  • Sub-second queries matter. The Activator trigger has to evaluate within seconds of the event arriving. Lakehouse Direct Lake refresh, even at its fastest, takes minutes.
  • The KQL query language fits the question. Time-windowed aggregations (bin, summarize ... by ...), pattern matching (match_regex), funnel analysis (funnel_sequence), anomaly detection (series_decompose_anomalies) — these are Eventhouse's native idioms.
  • Forensic retention is needed. Eventhouse keeps every event at high resolution. Lakehouse Bronze can keep the same data more cheaply but at a coarser cadence. When the LEDGER points at "the event that fired the decision," Eventhouse is the table that holds it.

5A.2.2 Eventhouse Schema Pattern — APEX-M Canonical

Each streaming Service gets its own KQL DB inside the practice's Eventhouse. The schema convention:

KQL · APEX-M Eventhouse schema pattern
// Bronze tier — raw events, no transformation
.create table BR_RefrigerationTelemetry (
    event_ts:        datetime,
    store_id:        string,
    zone_id:         string,
    sensor_id:       string,
    lot_id:          string,
    temperature_c:   real,
    humidity_pct:    real,
    threshold_c:     real,                  // per-zone target temp
    ingest_ts:       datetime
)
with (folder = "Bronze", docstring = "Raw refrigeration sensor readings; 30s cadence")

// Silver tier — typed, validated, deduplicated via update policy
.create table SI_RefrigerationTelemetry_Conformed (
    event_ts:        datetime,
    store_id:        string,
    zone_id:         string,
    lot_id:          string,
    temperature_c:   real,
    threshold_c:     real,
    breach:          bool,                  // computed: temperature_c > threshold_c
    minute_bucket:   datetime,              // bin(event_ts, 1m)
    _hash:           string                 // for cross-tier reconciliation
)

// Materialized view — per-zone, per-minute aggregation for fast reads
.create materialized-view MV_ZoneMinute on table SI_RefrigerationTelemetry_Conformed
{
    SI_RefrigerationTelemetry_Conformed
    | summarize
        max_temp     = max(temperature_c),
        avg_temp     = avg(temperature_c),
        breach_count = countif(breach),
        latest_ts    = max(event_ts)
      by store_id, zone_id, minute_bucket
}

// Activator reads from MV_ZoneMinute — sub-second queries, pre-aggregated
Note — Eventhouse update policies are the Bronze → Silver path for streams

In the batch medallion (Ch 5), Silver is built by a Notebook job. In streaming, the equivalent runs inside Eventhouse as an update policy — a KQL transformation that runs on every new row in the Bronze table and writes the conformed row to Silver. No orchestration; no separate compute. The job that runs per-row is a single declarative KQL function. Activator then reads Silver (or a materialized view over it), not Bronze.

5A.2.3 Eventhouse Retention & Cost

Eventhouse retention has two dials: hot cache (data physically resident on SSD, sub-second query) and cold retention (data on cheaper storage, slower query). APEX-M canonical:

TierHot cacheCold retentionRationale
Lab v0.1 / DEV7 days30 daysRecent-event debugging window
STAGE14 days90 daysTwo-sprint forensic window
PROD30 days2 years (compliance-driven; PCI / HIPAA / SOX engagements may extend)Operator-friendly hot window + regulatory cold window. Past 30 days, queries route to OneLake-stored Delta Parquet via shortcut — slower but cheaper.

5A.3 Tier 2 — Semi-Real-Time via Direct Lake & Mirrored Database

Semi-real-time is the workhorse tier. Most APEX-M Services live here. The Microsoft Fabric components:

  • Direct Lake mode — Power BI semantic models read OneLake Delta Parquet without import or DirectQuery overhead. Refresh latency from OneLake update to semantic-model freshness: typically < 1 minute on F-SKU capacity above F64. This is "live for the operator" without "streaming" cost.
  • Mirrored Database (Fabric · CDC-based) — replicates an on-prem or cloud transactional database (Microsoft.Sql/servers · Microsoft.DocumentDB · Azure Database for PostgreSQL · Snowflake) into OneLake with near-real-time change-data-capture. The mirror is one Delta table per source table; APEX-M's Silver builds run on the mirror.
  • Activator on Lakehouse / semantic model — Activator can watch a Lakehouse table or a Power BI semantic-model measure. Detection is event-driven (every change triggers a re-evaluation), not poll-based.
  • Scheduled refresh — when the source is too slow for mirroring (a thrice-daily SOR feed), Fabric Data Pipelines run on a recurrence trigger and refresh the Silver tables. Activator then re-evaluates on the new data.

5A.3.1 Direct Lake vs Import vs DirectQuery — APEX-M Choice

Direct Lake (APEX-M default)Import modeDirectQuery
Data locationOneLake Delta Parquet · no copyPower BI in-memory engine (VertiPaq) · copiedSource database · queries per visual
Refresh latencySeconds (Delta version change → semantic model)Minutes to hours (scheduled refresh)Live
Query latencySub-second (VertiPaq over OneLake)Sub-second (in-memory)Source-dependent (often slower)
Capacity SKU floorF-SKU (any)Any Power BI SKUAny Power BI SKU
CostCapacity-bound; no copy storageCapacity + memory footprintSource-database compute per query
APEX-M useDefault for all Gold martsReserved for < 1M-row reference data with rare changesReserved for SOR feeds that cannot land in OneLake (latency-critical compliance flag)

5A.3.2 Mirrored Database — When the SOR Is a Transactional Database

If the client SOR is Microsoft.Sql/servers, Microsoft.DocumentDB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, or Snowflake, Mirrored Database is the right Silver-feed pattern. Per Microsoft Learn:

  • CDC-based replication with no impact on source workload
  • Near-real-time freshness (typically < 1 minute end-to-end)
  • Free of compute charge from Fabric capacity perspective (storage is billed normally)
  • The mirrored Delta tables are first-class OneLake tables — Lakehouse, Notebooks, Direct Lake semantic models all read them directly

APEX-M canonical: mirror the SOR's transactional tables to a Mirrored Database in the Service workspace; run Silver builds against the mirror; promote to Gold for the agents to read. Compliance-driven engagements that cannot mirror (regulatory data residency · contractual SOR isolation) fall back to scheduled Data Pipeline ingestion at the cost of higher staleness.

5A.4 Tier 3 — Periodic Feeds via Data Pipelines & Scheduled Refresh

The batch tier is for signals where freshness within a day (or even within the week) is enough. The Microsoft components are familiar:

  • Fabric Data Pipelines — visual ETL on Fabric capacity. Runs on a recurrence trigger (every N hours / daily / weekly). Pulls from SOR connectors (~150 supported), lands to Lakehouse Bronze, calls a Notebook for Silver conformance, materializes Gold marts.
  • Fabric Notebooks — Spark or Python-on-Lakehouse jobs. Heavy data conformance (multi-source joins · entity resolution · canonical mapping per §1B) lives here.
  • Power BI scheduled semantic-model refresh — refresh the semantic model after Gold marts land, so the Direct Lake-mode reports are fresh at the next operator login.
  • Logic Apps recurrence trigger — for SOR feeds outside Fabric (FTP drops · SaaS connectors · email-attached files), Logic Apps schedules the pull and then triggers the Fabric pipeline.

The output of the periodic tier is, almost always, a fresh Gold mart. The agent fleet reads the Gold mart through MCP (Ch 13); the periodic refresh is invisible to the agent — it just sees fresher data at the next query.

Note — periodic-feed Services still have triggers

"Periodic" describes the data refresh cadence, not the trigger cadence. A Service whose Gold mart refreshes nightly can still fire on the morning's first dashboard open, on a weekly review meeting, or on a specific operator action. The trigger is decoupled from the freshness — Activator on the Power BI semantic model can fire when a daily KPI crosses a threshold, even though the underlying data refreshes only once per day.

5A.5 Tier 4 — Redis Hot Cache (Working & Episodic Memory)

Redis Premium (Microsoft.Cache/Redis@2024-03-01, P-tier) is APEX-M's sub-millisecond working-memory layer. It is not part of the source-data velocity hierarchy — it is the layer the agent fleet reaches into between LLM calls. Ch 25.3 has the full deep dive; the role within the velocity hierarchy:

Redis use patternKey shapeTTLWhy Redis, not Eventhouse / Lakehouse
Workflow session stateapex:session:{service}:{run_id}24 hours (configurable per use case)Agent reads it between LLM calls; sub-ms required; per-session lifecycle
Chat-history providerapex:history:{thread_id} (Redis Stream)24 hoursAgent Framework's ChatHistoryProvider binding; LEDGER carries the durable copy
Last-N similar decisionsapex:similar:{service}:{decision_class} (Sorted Set by recency)30 days · LRU evictionEpisodic memory the agent uses for few-shot examples; LEDGER is the source of truth, Redis is the index
Operator-preference cacheapex:operator:{upn}:prefs (RedisJSON)7 days · refresh on sessionRead on every agent turn; staleness within hours is acceptable; LEDGER captures the durable version
MCP-result short-TTL cacheapex:mcp:{tool_id}:{arg_hash}5 minutes (Service-configurable)Avoids re-querying Gold for the same panel within a workflow run; deterministic key by argument hash
Rate-limit countersapex:rate:{principal}:{window}Window-bound (1m · 1h · 1d)Sub-ms increment + check on every middleware call

Redis is also a threshold substrate for one specific class: rate-limit thresholds (this principal has called this tool N times in the last minute). For everything else, threshold evaluation belongs in Activator (Tier 1 / 2) or in the periodic-refresh Notebook (Tier 3). Cross-reference §25.3 for the durability story (LEDGER) and the learning loop that Redis closes.

5A.6 Thresholds — A Taxonomy

A threshold is the predicate that converts a stream of rows into a decision. Without a threshold, "the temperature was 9°C at 14:32 UTC" is just data. With a threshold ("temperature exceeded 8°C for ≥ 15 minutes in any refrigeration zone"), it is an excursion event. APEX-M classifies thresholds into six families:

FamilyPredicate shapeAPEX-M exampleBest velocity tier
1 · Single-metricmetric > constant"Hub humidity > 80%" (ER-OG-07 air-quality flag)Tier 1 (streaming) — trivial to evaluate
2 · Time-windowedmetric > constant for ≥ duration"Refrigeration temp > threshold for ≥ 15 minutes" (RC-E2E-03 cold-chain)Tier 1 — KQL summarize ... by bin(ts, ...)
3 · CompositeBoolean of multiple single-metrics"Temperature > 8°C AND humidity > 80% for ≥ 15 minutes" (RC-E2E-03 pharma-grade)Tier 1 — same KQL shape, multi-clause where
4 · Rate-of-changeΔmetric / Δtime > constant"Price drop > 30% in < 4 hours" (TMT-MED-03 competitor-price anomaly)Tier 1 — KQL prev() / series_decompose
5 · Anomaly|metric − baseline| / σ > constant"Login volume z-score > 2.5 vs 30-day baseline" (Sentinel agent-identity rule per §32A.2)Tier 1 or 2 — KQL series_decompose_anomalies or Sentinel UEBA
6 · Pattern-matchSequence of events matching a signature"Refund → re-buy → return cycle < 24h × 3+ times in 30 days" (RC-E2E-07 returns fraud)Tier 2 or 3 — pattern matching usually needs cross-day history; Lakehouse + Activator on table works

5A.6.1 The Threshold Object

APEX-M makes thresholds declarative. Every Service ships a thresholds.yaml alongside its agent.yaml and use-case.yaml. Each threshold has eight required fields:

thresholds.yaml · APEX-M canonical shape
# RC-E2E-03 cold-chain — three thresholds, three actions, three owners
thresholds:
  - id: rc_e2e_03.excursion.minor
    family: time-windowed
    predicate: "temperature_c > threshold_c for >= 5 minutes"
    severity: low
    action: notify
    owner: store-manager
    sla_minutes: 60
    runbook_url: https://wiki.client/cold-chain-minor

  - id: rc_e2e_03.excursion.major
    family: time-windowed
    predicate: "temperature_c > threshold_c for >= 15 minutes"
    severity: high
    action: escalate
    owner: merch-director
    sla_minutes: 15
    runbook_url: https://wiki.client/cold-chain-major

  - id: rc_e2e_03.excursion.critical
    family: composite
    predicate: "temperature_c > threshold_c AND lot_class == 'pharma' for >= 5 minutes"
    severity: critical
    action: page
    owner: pharmacy-director
    sla_minutes: 2
    runbook_url: https://wiki.client/cold-chain-pharma

The Bicep deploy reads thresholds.yaml, generates the matching Activator triggers (or KQL update-policy rules), and wires each action to its Logic Apps SOAR playbook or Microsoft Teams adaptive-card flow. Threshold authoring is engagement-team work; threshold realisation is APEX-M framework work.

Independence — thresholds live in the client tenant

Thresholds encode the client's risk appetite. APEX framework code provides the schema, the Bicep generator, and the realisation primitives (Activator triggers · Logic Apps playbooks · Teams adaptive cards) — but the values (15 minutes · 8°C · merch-director) are client decisions, authored by the client's data-product owner or by Deloitte on the client's behalf as part of the engagement scope. The client owns the threshold, the action, and the owner.

5A.7 Threshold → Action Mapping

Every threshold maps to exactly one action. APEX-M's seven canonical action types — pick exactly one per threshold:

ActionWhat happensOwner expectationSLA-tier
notifyInformational message routed to a Teams channel / email distribution / adaptive card. No response required.Read & acknowledgeLoose (hours)
escalateRoute to a specific named persona with workflow context attached. Persona reviews and acts.Triage and decideTight (minutes)
gateBlock a downstream action until a human approver explicitly approves (HITL). Used heavily in agent workflows above a confidence / cost / severity cutoff.Approve or rejectWorkflow-bound (cannot proceed until cleared)
haltStop the in-flight action immediately. The agent workflow is interrupted; downstream agents do not receive the message. Used for safety-critical violations.Investigate before resumeImmediate
pageWake up the on-call engineer / clinician / safety officer. Auto-create Sentinel incident / PagerDuty alert / SMS.Acknowledge within minutesCritical (2–15 min)
rollbackUndo a recent action. For agent decisions: revert the version; for data: snapshot-restore; for pricing: revoke the markdown.Confirm rollback completed cleanlyTight (minutes)
adaptivePass the threshold-breach event to an agent and let the agent decide the response. Used when the action depends on context the threshold cannot encode.Agent decides; LEDGER captures rationaleWorkflow-bound

5A.7.1 Severity Ladders — Stacking Thresholds on One Signal

A single signal often deserves multiple thresholds at different cutoffs, each mapping to a different action. The thresholds.yaml example above shows the canonical pattern — same metric (refrigeration temperature), three thresholds (5 min · 15 min · 5 min + pharma), three actions (notify · escalate · page), three owners. This is the severity ladder. APEX-M's rule:

  • Ladder rungs are monotonic in severity. A higher-severity threshold must be strictly stricter than a lower-severity one.
  • Ladder rungs are monotonic in action escalation. notify < escalate < gate ≤ halt, with page orthogonal (page can attach to any rung).
  • Each rung has its own owner and SLA. A breach of rung 3 does not implicitly trigger rungs 1 and 2 — Activator fires each rung independently, and the action-routing decides whether to suppress lower-severity duplicates.

5A.7.2 Threshold Hysteresis & Debouncing

A threshold that fires and re-fires every few seconds is operationally toxic. APEX-M's hysteresis pattern: every threshold has a paired clear condition stricter than the trigger condition, plus a minimum dwell time.

thresholds.yaml · hysteresis configuration
- id: rc_e2e_03.excursion.major
  predicate: "temperature_c > 8.0 for >= 15 minutes"
  clear_predicate: "temperature_c < 6.0 for >= 10 minutes"  # stricter, plus dwell
  min_silence_seconds: 600                                  # 10-minute debounce
  severity: high
  action: escalate

The first breach fires; subsequent re-breaches within the silence window are suppressed; the clear condition (temp drops below 6°C for 10 minutes — note: stricter than the trigger's 8°C) closes the incident. Activator's per-object state machine handles this natively; KQL update policies require explicit tracking via a state table.

5A.8 Microsoft Fabric Activator — Deep Dive

Microsoft Fabric Activator (Real-Time Intelligence's event-action component, formerly "Data Activator") is the threshold-evaluation engine for Tier 1 and Tier 2 signals. APEX-M leans on it heavily — most of what would otherwise be hand-written KQL update policies or scheduled Power BI subscriptions becomes one Activator object with declarative triggers.

5A.8.1 The Activator Object Model

Activator has four primary concepts:

ConceptDescriptionAPEX-M example (RC-E2E-03 cold-chain)
SourceWhere Activator listens — an Eventstream, a Lakehouse table, or a Power BI semantic modelEventstream sourced from the BR_RefrigerationTelemetry Eventhouse table
ObjectThe "thing" being tracked; Activator partitions the source by an object key and tracks state per objectRefrigeration zone — partition key (store_id, zone_id). ~2,000 distinct objects across the chain.
PropertyA computed value per object — typically a windowed aggregate or a derived flagavg_temp_5min (rolling avg over 5 minutes) · breach_minutes (consecutive minutes over threshold) · lot_class (joined from a lookup table)
TriggerA condition on properties that, when true, fires an action. Conditions are evaluated incrementally as new events arrive.Major excursion trigger: breach_minutes >= 15 AND a 10-minute silence window since the last fire
ActionWhat happens when the trigger fires — Teams message · Power Automate flow · Logic Apps HTTP webhook · Outlook email · Fabric pipeline runCustom HTTP webhook to the APEX-M trigger router (Logic Apps Hybrid), which then starts the W2-pilot DAG

5A.8.2 The Power of Per-Object Granularity

The single property that makes Activator different from "scheduled KQL + alert" is per-object state. One trigger definition ("breach_minutes ≥ 15 with 10-minute silence") tracks 2,000 independent per-zone state machines without any per-zone configuration. Add a new zone in the schema, and Activator picks it up on the next event without re-deploying. Lose a sensor for an hour, and Activator's per-object state resumes from where it left off when telemetry returns.

This is why Activator is operationally lighter than the hand-rolled alternative (state table + KQL window function + cron job + dedup logic). APEX-M's rule: any threshold that requires per-object state should be an Activator trigger, not a KQL update policy. KQL update policies are reserved for stateless transformations (Bronze → Silver typing, schema conformance, single-row enrichment).

5A.8.3 Activator Action Bindings — APEX-M Canonical

Activator ships with several built-in action types. APEX-M's canonical choice for each integration target:

Action targetBuilt-in Activator actionWhen APEX-M picks it
Start a workflowCustom action (HTTP) — POST to a Logic Apps Hybrid endpoint or directly to the agent fleet's /runDefault for any threshold that should start an agent workflow. The trigger router (Ch 16) inspects the payload and dispatches.
Notify a personaMicrosoft Teams action — adaptive card to a channel or chatSeverity = low / notify-action thresholds. No workflow required.
Page an on-callCustom action (HTTP) → PagerDuty / Microsoft Sentinel SOAR playbookSeverity = critical / page-action thresholds. Sentinel correlation is automatic since the action emits to the same workspace.
Email a recipientOutlook actionCompliance-driven thresholds where an emailed audit record is required by policy (e.g., FDA 21 CFR Part 11 deviations).
Trigger a Fabric jobFabric pipeline action — run a specified data pipelineTier 3 cross-tier thresholds: a periodic refresh that detects an anomaly schedules an immediate re-refresh.
Run a Power Automate flowPower Automate actionSaaS-integrated thresholds: post a Salesforce case, create a ServiceNow incident, file an Asana task.
Best Practice — single front door for agent-starting triggers

For thresholds that should start an agent workflow, send the Activator HTTP action to one APEX-M trigger router (Logic Apps Hybrid endpoint), not to per-agent endpoints. The router does the LEDGER pre-row, the auth check, the rate-limit, and the dispatch. Per-agent direct calls from Activator make the audit trail and the rate-limiting per-trigger rather than per-Service — which is the wrong granularity.

5A.9.1 Cross-Cutting Pattern — Activator for Agent Telemetry

Activator is not just for client-data thresholds. APEX-M wires it on its own observability stream too:

  • Agent cost-envelope breach — Activator on the Application Insights cost stream; trigger when a Service's hourly LLM spend exceeds its envelope; action: halt the offending Service's agent versions, page the engagement lead.
  • Grounding-score collapse — Activator on the canary-metric stream (per §14C.5 three-gate evaluation); trigger when grounding score for any Service drops > 10% in a rolling 1-hour window; action: rollback the agent version + pause the promotion pipeline.
  • Agent-identity risk spike — Activator on the Sentinel AIAgentsInfo table (per §32A.4.1); trigger on any new high-risk event for an APEX-M agent identity; action: HTTP → SOAR playbook from §6B.4 (Deployment Guide).

5A.10 Composing Tiers Across a Single Service

Most APEX-M Services compose three or four velocity tiers in one use case. RC-E2E-03 cold-chain excursion is the canonical example:

TierSignalMicrosoft componentRole in the workflow
Tier 1 · streamingRefrigeration telemetry · POS salesEventhouse + ActivatorExcursion-trigger firing (the "wake up the agent" event)
Tier 2 · semi-real-timeMirrored inventory (Microsoft.Sql), Mirrored ERP (Microsoft.DocumentDB)Mirrored Database + Direct Lake semantic modelLot-on-hand + financial-impact lookup at agent decision time (MCP tool reads)
Tier 3 · periodicCompetitor pricing (daily) · weather forecast (3× daily) · lot-class lookup (weekly)Fabric Data Pipeline scheduled refreshGold-mart inputs the Pricing agent reads when proposing markdowns
Tier 4 · Redis hot cacheIn-flight workflow state · last-N similar excursions · operator preference snapshotMicrosoft.Cache/Redis PremiumAgent working memory between LLM calls; episodic-memory retrieval for few-shot

The Service does not "live in" any one tier. It lives in the composition. The architectural skill is picking the right tier per signal — not picking one tier and forcing every signal through it.

5A.11 The Trigger-to-Decision Audit Trail

Every threshold breach must be traceable from firing condition to operator decision. APEX-M's audit trail spans four substrates:

  1. Eventhouse retains the raw event(s) that crossed the threshold (Tier 1 + Tier 2 sources). Retention per §5A.2.3.
  2. Activator retains the trigger-fire event (object id, trigger id, property values at fire time, action attempted, action result). Activator's run history is queryable for ~90 days; APEX-M's Bicep also subscribes Activator events to Sentinel.
  3. LEDGER receives a hash-chained row for every trigger-fired workflow: trigger id, threshold id, owner, action type, agent fleet response, operator decision. The LEDGER is anchored to the Microsoft.KeyVault HSM CMK (§25.2) and is the durable forensic record.
  4. Sentinel correlates Activator firings, LEDGER rows, and operator actions. Detection rule 4 (Service-envelope breach, per §32A.2) cross-checks that every threshold-fired workflow has a matching LEDGER row within SLA; missing rows trigger an incident.
Note — the audit trail starts at the firing condition, not the agent invocation

This is the property the trigger-in-data convention buys APEX-M. If an audit asks "why did the agent decide to mark down lot L-99281?", the answer chain is: Eventhouse row (the temperature reading) → Activator trigger fire → LEDGER workflow.start → agent steps → final decision LEDGER row. The agent does not have to remember why it was invoked; the audit trail does. Cross-reference Ch 32A.1 for the Sentinel KQL that walks the chain end-to-end.

5A.12 Anti-Patterns

Four anti-patterns recur in engagements that miss the tier composition skill:

Anti-patternSymptomCorrection
Tier 1 for everythingStreaming the SOR's customer master table into Eventhouse "for freshness" · capacity-unit bills 3–5× expectedCustomer master is reference data; mirror it (Tier 2) and let Direct Lake handle the freshness. Reserve Tier 1 for event-shaped sources.
Hand-rolled threshold state in agent codeAn agent that "remembers" whether it already escalated this lot · drift in the per-object state · duplicate escalationsMove the state to Activator (per-object state is what it does). Agent code reads the threshold-fired event, decides, writes LEDGER — no per-object memory in the agent.
Threshold logic in n8n / Logic Appsn8n node with an "if temperature > 8" Function block running every minute · misses events · clogged queueThreshold evaluation belongs in Activator or in an Eventhouse update policy. Logic Apps Hybrid is the trigger router, not the threshold evaluator. (Per §14.4 architectural shift.)
Redis as the system of recordEpisodic memory written only to Redis · cache eviction loses operator-correction signal · superagent regressesLEDGER is always the system of record; Redis is the hot index. Every Redis write that matters has a paired LEDGER write at the workflow boundary (per Ch 25).
