Key Takeaways

  • Four velocity tiers (streaming Eventhouse · semi-real-time Direct Lake / Mirrored DB · periodic Data Pipelines · Redis hot cache) — composed per signal, not picked per Service.
  • Default new signals to Tier 2; promote to Tier 1 only with explicit cost-of-delay evidence. Over-buying real-time is the most common engagement-cost surprise.
  • Thresholds are declarative (thresholds.yaml) · six families (single-metric · windowed · composite · rate-of-change · anomaly · pattern-match) · each maps to exactly one of seven action types (notify · escalate · gate · halt · page · rollback · adaptive).
  • Severity ladders stack multiple thresholds on one signal — monotonic in severity, monotonic in action escalation; each rung has its own owner and SLA.
  • Activator is the threshold engine for Tier 1 + Tier 2. Per-object granularity (10,000 trucks share one trigger definition) is the property that makes it operationally lighter than hand-rolled state machines.
  • Every threshold breach is traceable end-to-end: Eventhouse row → Activator fire → LEDGER workflow.start → agent steps → final decision LEDGER row → Sentinel correlation.
  • Redis is the agent's working-memory hot path (sub-ms reads between LLM calls) — not a source-data velocity tier. LEDGER is always the system of record; Redis is the hot index.
Chapter 6

Ingestion and Tokenization

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the ingestion pipeline from SOR to Bronze landing, with Microsoft Fabric component-level detail.
  • Explains tokenization at ingestion time: the deterministic-token pattern that lets Silver/Gold operate on tokens, not raw PII.
  • Maps the tokenization service to its Microsoft.KeyVault HSM root of trust.
60-second read
  • Five-stage ingest: connect · tokenize · land · stamp · emit. Tokenize human-recognizable PII at ingest; opaque join keys pass through.
  • HMAC-SHA256 with Microsoft.KeyVault HSM key — same input → same token; original unrecoverable without HSM access.
  • mi-apex-merch-ingest identity has minimum scope: write Bronze · use tokenization key · read SOR connections · nothing more.

6.1 The Ingestion Pipeline, in Stages

For any single SOR-to-Bronze flow:

  1. Connect. Microsoft Fabric component (Eventstream, Mirrored Database, Pipeline) reaches the SOR with client credentials.
  2. Tokenize. If the source row contains PII fields (per the sor-connections.yaml classification), each PII field is replaced by a deterministic token before persistence. The original value never lands in Bronze.
  3. Land. Tokenized row written to Bronze: KQL DB (streaming) or Lakehouse Delta (batch).
  4. Stamp. Three timestamps and the Microsoft Purview lineage tag added.
  5. Emit. If the row triggers a downstream Eventstream rule, the rule fires and the orchestrator gets notified.

6.2 The Tokenization Pattern

Tokenization replaces a PII value with a deterministic token derived from the value plus a per-tenant secret key held in Microsoft.KeyVault Premium HSM. The same input produces the same token (so joins still work), but the original value is unrecoverable from the token without HSM access.

PYTHON — tokenization sketch
import hmac, hashlib
from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential
from azure.keyvault.keys import KeyClient
from azure.keyvault.keys.crypto import CryptographyClient, EncryptionAlgorithm

# Init once per pipeline; cached cryptography client, MI-authenticated.
credential = DefaultAzureCredential()  # mi-apex-merch-ingest
kv_uri     = os.environ["KEYVAULT_URI"]
key_client = KeyClient(vault_url=kv_uri, credential=credential)
token_key  = key_client.get_key("apex-tokenization-key")  # AES-256-HSM
crypto     = CryptographyClient(token_key, credential=credential)

def tokenize_pii(field_name: str, raw_value: str) -> str:
    """Produce a deterministic token for raw_value, scoped by field_name."""
    if raw_value is None or raw_value == "":
        return raw_value
    msg = f"{field_name}:{raw_value}".encode("utf-8")
    # HMAC-SHA256 with HSM-held key — the digest is the token.
    digest = crypto.sign(SignatureAlgorithm.hs256, hashlib.sha256(msg).digest())
    return f"tok-{digest.signature.hex()[:24]}"

The function runs inside the Microsoft Fabric Pipeline (or the Eventstream transformation) under the mi-apex-merch-ingest identity from Layer 1. The HSM key never leaves the HSM; the tokens are deterministic and joinable across rows and across Services.

Warning — Don't tokenize foreign keys you need to join

The pattern looks attractive for every "ID-shaped" field, but if a field is a join key for downstream Services, tokenizing it here breaks cross-Service joins. The rule of thumb: tokenize anything that is human-recognizable PII (name, email, phone, address). Don't tokenize internal opaque IDs (customer_id, member_id, equipment_serial); they are already identifier surrogates and should join straight through.

6.3 The Ingest Identity

Layer 1 provisions four user-assigned managed identities, one of which is mi-apex-merch-ingest. This is the identity Microsoft Fabric Pipelines and Eventstream transformations authenticate as. It is granted:

  • Storage Blob Data Contributor on the per-Service Bronze landing storage account (or Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse).
  • Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Writer on the per-Service workspace.
  • Key Vault Crypto User on the tenant tokenization key (AES-256-HSM).
  • Reader on the SOR connection objects (the connection itself stays under client ops).

It is not granted access to the LEDGER, to the runtime managed identity scope, or to the PII unlock key. Ingest's job is one-directional: read from SOR (with client-supplied credentials), tokenize, write to Bronze. Anything beyond that is a different identity's responsibility.

6.4 Microsoft.DataFactory Pipeline Patterns

For batch SOR sources, the Microsoft Fabric Data Pipeline activity used most often is Copy Data, augmented by a Notebook activity that runs the tokenization on the landed rows before they are committed to Bronze.

PIPELINE — daily competitor pricing ingest (sketch)
1. Copy Data:    nielsen-pricing-feed → staging/raw/{ds}/competitor_pricing_{ds}.csv
2. Notebook:     run tokenization notebook against staging/raw/{ds}/...
                 writes Delta to bronze/br_competitor_pricing partitioned by date
3. Notebook:     emit Microsoft Purview lineage event
4. Trigger:      kick off Silver-build pipeline for MERML.Competitor

The pipeline is parameterized by date ({ds} in Microsoft Fabric expression language) and runs on a Microsoft.Fabric/dataPipelines-equivalent schedule. Failures route to a Microsoft Sentinel alert via Eventstream → Microsoft Sentinel connector.

Key Takeaways

  • Ingestion is five stages: connect, tokenize, land, stamp, emit. Tokenization is non-negotiable for human-recognizable PII; opaque join keys pass through.
  • Tokenization uses HMAC-SHA256 with a Microsoft.KeyVault HSM-held key (AES-256-HSM); same input → same token, original value unrecoverable without HSM access.
  • The mi-apex-merch-ingest identity has the minimum scope to do its job — write to Bronze, use the tokenization key, read SOR connections — and nothing more.
  • Microsoft Fabric Pipelines + Notebook activities cover batch ingestion; Eventstream transformations cover streaming.
Chapter 7

PII Classification and the pii-unlock Identity

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Establishes the four-tier PII classification scheme APEX uses on every Bronze field.
  • Explains the mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock identity — why it exists, when it is used, how every use is auditable.
  • Walks the just-in-time unlock motion that lets HITL approvers see re-identified data without standing privilege.
60-second read
  • Four PII tiers — Public · Internal · Confidential PII · Restricted PHI/regulated. Tier 3+ tokenized at ingest; Tier 4 adds dual-control unlock.
  • mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock is no-standing-privilege; acquired JIT at the HITL approval moment; every acquisition LEDGER-attributed.
  • Tokenization key (HMAC, ingest-side) and unwrap key (RSA-HSM, JIT) are intentionally separate — different attack surfaces, different lifetimes.

7.1 The Four Tiers

TierField examplesBronze handlingWho can read
Tier 1 — Publicstore_id · sku_id · public-list price · weather observationsStored as-isAll identities
Tier 2 — Internalemployee_id · internal cost · supplier_code · sensor_idStored as-isService identities only
Tier 3 — Confidential PIIcustomer email · phone · loyalty_id · IP address · device fingerprintTokenized at ingestTokenized form to all; raw form requires pii-unlock + LEDGER row
Tier 4 — Restricted PHI / regulated PIISSN · DOB · clinical diagnosis · patient name · payment card number · drivers-license numberTokenized at ingest with separate per-field key · stricter rotationTokenized form only inside Service runtime; raw form gated by HITL approval + dual-control + LEDGER

The classification is set in sor-connections.yaml at field level (or at Bronze-table level if a coarse default is sufficient). Microsoft Purview consumes the classification and applies sensitivity labels to the lineage view.

7.2 The pii-unlock Identity

The fourth Layer 1 user-assigned managed identity, mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock, is intentionally not bound at deployment time to any agent Container App. It lives in Microsoft Entra ID with no standing privileges other than:

  • Key Vault Crypto User on the per-tenant PII-unwrap key (separate from the tokenization key — a different RSA-HSM key in the same Microsoft.KeyVault Premium vault).
  • Storage Blob Data Reader on the per-Service silver layer where re-identification mappings live (encrypted).

An agent that needs to surface real PII to a HITL approver acquires a Microsoft Entra ID token for this identity just-in-time using acquireTokenForUserAssignedIdentity. The acquisition itself writes a LEDGER row before the unlock fires. The token is short-lived (minutes), the unlock is for a single record, and the access window closes when the HITL decision is recorded.

Independence — No standing privilege over PII

The pii-unlock identity is never standing on a Container App. Every replica that started without it cannot escalate; every just-in-time acquisition is audit-attributed. This is the structural enforcement that an APEX deployment running in a regulated client tenant (HLS, financial services, public sector) cannot inadvertently expose PII via prompt injection or agent hallucination — the bytes simply aren't reachable to the agent process unless an audited motion has fired.

7.3 The Just-in-Time Unlock Motion

For RC-E2E-04 (Loyalty Churn) — a Service that touches Tier 3 PII (customer email, loyalty_id) — the motion when a HITL approver wants to see a real customer:

  1. Agent prepares a winback proposal using tokenized customer rows. Decision-grade fact: "this tokenized customer at risk of churn worth $X."
  2. Agent emits a HITL adaptive card to the approver via Microsoft Teams. Card carries the tokenized identifier, not the email.
  3. Approver clicks "see customer details" in the card — UI calls back into the Service's MCP host.
  4. MCP host writes a LEDGER row: pii_unlock_requested with (tokenized id, requesting approver, business reason).
  5. MCP host acquires a mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock token for the next ~5 minutes.
  6. MCP host queries the encrypted re-identification mapping under that token, decrypts the email/loyalty_id for the single tokenized id.
  7. Decrypted values returned to the UI; immediately a second LEDGER row records pii_unlock_completed.
  8. The token expires; the approver decision (apply / decline winback) is captured against the LEDGER row pair.

For Tier 4 PHI, the motion adds a dual-control step: the unlock requires two distinct approver identities to consent before the unwrap key issues a token. This is a Microsoft.KeyVault HSM access policy expressed as a JIT approval workflow.

7.4 Why the Tokenization Key and the Unwrap Key Are Different

One key for both would simplify the architecture by one HSM key. It would also collapse two distinct attack surfaces into one. The tokenization key is used at ingest by the ingest identity on every row; if that key is compromised, the attacker can produce tokens but cannot reverse them (HMAC is one-way). The unwrap key is used at HITL approval time by the pii-unlock identity for one record; it is the only thing that can re-identify. Different lifetimes, different blast radii, different rotation cadences. Two keys.

ADR · architecture decision
ADR-007-01 · 2026-04-22 · accepted

Decision: Tokenization key (HMAC-SHA256, ingest-side) and unwrap key (RSA-HSM, JIT) are intentionally separate Microsoft.KeyVault HSM keys.

Why: Compromise containment. The tokenization key sees every Bronze row at ingest; high-throughput, low blast-radius (HMAC is one-way · stolen key cannot reverse tokens). The unwrap key sees one row per HITL approval; low-throughput, catastrophic blast-radius if compromised (re-identifies all PII). Splitting puts the catastrophic key behind dual-control + JIT acquisition · §7.3, leaving the high-throughput key on a less-restrictive path.

Trade-off rejected: Single shared key with role-based gating. Easier rotation; one HSM rate-limit envelope; but a single compromise reverses every Bronze row ever ingested. Splitting is non-negotiable when the data is Tier-4 PHI.

Cross-volume: Cross-ref Deployment Guide §4.4 (HSM CMK provisioning) · §5 (per-identity Microsoft.KeyVault role assignments).

Key Takeaways

  • Four-tier PII classification (Public · Internal · Confidential PII · Restricted PHI) drives Bronze tokenization decisions and Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels.
  • mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock is a no-standing-privilege identity acquired just-in-time for HITL approval moments; every acquisition is LEDGER-attributed.
  • Tokenization key (HMAC, ingest-side) and unwrap key (RSA-HSM, JIT) are intentionally separate — different attack surfaces, different lifetimes.
  • Tier 4 unlocks add dual-control via Microsoft.KeyVault HSM access policy.
Part III

Silver Tier — Canonical Models

Imagine you've inherited a kitchen from twelve different chefs. One chef labelled their onions "yellow onion." Another wrote "OnionYellow." A third used the Spanish "cebolla." A fourth labelled by supplier code. The onions are the same vegetable — but if your recipe says "two yellow onions, diced," you can't get started until somebody translates all twelve labels into one shared name. That somebody is the prep cook. The prep station is where every chef's onions become your onions.

Silver is APEX-M's prep station. The Bronze landings hold every source system's raw representation — D365's CustomerID, the legacy POS's CustomerKey, Snowflake's customer_id, the Excel master's Cust_No. Same business concept, four different names. Silver translates them all into one canonical schema family (the 14 families from Chapter 9: SCML · MERML · EHRML · CRMML · ...) so that every Gold mart downstream — and every agent prompt that reasons over a Gold mart — refers to the same column the same way regardless of where the data originally came from.

The architects who skip Silver pay later. A Service that reads directly from Bronze couples its prompt to a particular source system's quirks; the next time the client upgrades D365, the prompt breaks. A Service that does the conformance inside Gold does it once per mart, which means re-doing the work for every new mart in every new Service. Silver does the conformance once per business concept and stays out of the way otherwise. The five chapters in this part walk that work. Chapter 8 covers the conformance Notebook pattern itself. Chapter 9 goes deep on each of the 14 schema families' attributes. Chapter 9A shows how the 14 families are used — which Services consume which combinations. Chapter 10 covers quality and lineage through Microsoft Purview. Chapter 10A closes with the Entra + Purview deep dive that governs who can read what.

Chapter 8

From Raw to Silver — The Conformance Layer

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the four conformance moves that turn Bronze rows into canonical Silver entities.
  • Establishes the idempotent-rebuild contract that lets Silver be regenerated from Bronze at any time.
  • Maps the conformance work to Microsoft Fabric notebooks, Microsoft Fabric Warehouse, and the per-tenant Fabric workspace.
60-second read
  • Four conformance moves: type stabilization · naming/unit conformance · canonical-ID resolution · dedup+ordering — all in one Microsoft Fabric notebook per entity.
  • Idempotent rebuild is a hard contract: drop Silver, re-run, get byte-identical output. No out-of-band fixes.
  • Per-Service workspaces hold Silver; cross-Service entity reuse via OneLake Shortcuts + scoped role assignments.

8.1 The Four Conformance Moves

For any Bronze → Silver transformation, four moves do the conformance work. They are usually colocated in a single Microsoft Fabric notebook (PySpark or T-SQL) per Silver entity, but they are conceptually distinct and the notebook is structured by them.

8.1.1 Type stabilization

Bronze preserves whatever the SOR sent. SAP integers may be strings; Epic dates may be MM/DD/YYYY strings; refrigeration sensors may emit Celsius as floats with seven decimal places. Silver gets canonical types: int, decimal(18,4), timestamp. The type table is the schema family's contract.

8.1.2 Naming and unit conformance

SAP calls it MATNR; Oracle Retail calls it item_id; Toshiba POS calls it SKU_NUMBER. APEX SCML calls it sku_id. The renaming happens in Silver. Same for units: temperatures in Celsius, weights in kilograms, currencies stabilized to a per-tenant base currency with the FX rate as of event_ts.

8.1.3 Foreign-key resolution to canonical IDs

Bronze rows reference SOR-internal IDs. Silver entities reference APEX-canonical IDs. The mapping table — id_map — is itself a Silver-tier reference table maintained per tenant per SOR, and the Silver build joins through it. Source IDs are preserved as src_*_id columns for Bronze→Silver lineage but are not used as join keys downstream.

8.1.4 Deduplication and ordering

Streaming SOR sources sometimes deliver the same event twice. CDC sources sometimes produce out-of-order updates. Silver applies a deterministic deduplication rule (typically "max event_ts per natural key, ties broken by max ingest_ts") and emits a single canonical row per business fact. The Bronze layer keeps every duplicate; Silver keeps the last-writer-wins.

8.2 The Idempotent-Rebuild Contract

Silver is rebuildable from Bronze. Always. At any time. This is a contract, not an aspiration:

  • Drop the Silver entity table and run the build notebook. The result must be byte-identical to the running Silver.
  • The build notebook is parameterized by date range; partial rebuilds are routine.
  • No manual fixes, no out-of-band UPDATEs, no Silver rows that aren't traceable to Bronze rows.

Three reasons this matters. First, schema evolution: when MERML adds a column, the existing Silver gets dropped and rebuilt with the new column. Second, conformance fixes: when a unit-conversion bug is found, the fix lands in the build notebook and the back-population is a re-run, not a migration. Third, audit: regulators occasionally ask "show me what Silver looked like on day X with code version Y" — the rebuild contract is what makes that question answerable.

Warning — A Silver row that can't be regenerated is a bug

If you ever find a Silver row that the build notebook doesn't reproduce, that is the bug to investigate, not "an interesting historical artifact to keep." Either Bronze is missing data the original build saw, or the build notebook has drifted, or someone wrote into Silver out-of-band. Diagnose and either back-fill Bronze, fix the notebook, or remove the orphan. The contract has to hold.

8.2.1 A Conformance Notebook in Code

The canonical Silver build is a Microsoft Fabric Notebook · PySpark · idempotent · run on schedule or on-demand. Below is the full structure of a real conformance Notebook (the RC-E2E-03 SCML.excursion_event build) in pseudo-code · the same shape applies to every Silver build across the catalog.

PySpark · silver_scml_excursion_event.ipynb
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
# Conformance Notebook · Bronze → Silver · SCML.excursion_event
# Trigger: scheduled every 5min · Microsoft Fabric pipeline

# === 1. PARAMETERS (set by the orchestrating pipeline) ===
window_start = dbutils.widgets.get("window_start")      # e.g., "2026-05-10T22:00:00Z"
window_end   = dbutils.widgets.get("window_end")        # e.g., "2026-05-10T22:05:00Z"
service_code = "RC-E2E-03"
schema_version = "SCML.excursion_event.v2"

# === 2. READ BRONZE (two sources) ===
iot_df = (spark.read
    .table("bronze_iot_temps")
    .where(f"ingest_ts_t >= '{window_start}' AND ingest_ts_t < '{window_end}'"))

d365_df = (spark.read
    .table("bronze_d365_events")
    .where(f"ingest_ts_t >= '{window_start}' AND ingest_ts_t < '{window_end}'")
    .where("EventType = 'TemperatureExcursion'"))

# === 3. CANONICALISE — IoT is the primary source, D365 is the secondary merge ===
# Resolve canonical surrogate keys via dimension lookups
iot_canon = (iot_df
    .withColumn("facility_id_g", lookup_facility(F.col("store_id"), source=F.lit("iot")))
    .withColumn("asset_id_g", lookup_asset(F.col("device_id"), source=F.lit("iot")))
    .withColumn("observed_at_t", F.to_timestamp("ts").cast("timestamp_ntz"))
    .withColumn("temperature_c_d", F.col("temp_c").cast("decimal(6,2)"))
    .withColumn("severity_score_d", compute_severity_udf(F.col("temp_c"))))

# Find D365 event for same physical asset within ±60 seconds (semantic merge)
merged = (iot_canon.alias("iot")
    .join(d365_df.alias("d365"),
          (F.col("iot.asset_id_g") == lookup_asset(F.col("d365.SourceID"), F.lit("d365")))
        & (F.abs(F.unix_timestamp("iot.observed_at_t") -
                    F.unix_timestamp("d365.Time")) <= 60),
          "left"))

# === 4. BUILD CANONICAL SILVER ROW ===
silver = (merged.select(
    uuid7_udf("iot.observed_at_t").alias("event_id_g"),  # canonical PK
    F.col("iot.facility_id_g"),
    F.col("iot.asset_id_g"),
    F.col("iot.temperature_c_d"),
    F.col("iot.observed_at_t"),
    F.col("iot.severity_score_d"),
    # Forensic array — every source key that contributed
    F.array(
        F.struct(F.lit("iot").alias("system"), F.col("iot.device_id").alias("key")),
        F.struct(F.lit("d365").alias("system"), F.col("d365.EventID").alias("key"))
    ).alias("source_keys_a"),
    F.lit(schema_version).alias("schema_version_s"),
    F.current_timestamp().alias("silver_ingest_t")
))

# === 5. DEDUPLICATE (per §8.1.4) ===
silver_dedup = (silver
    .withColumn("rn", F.row_number().over(
        Window.partitionBy("event_id_g")
              .orderBy(F.desc("observed_at_t"), F.desc("silver_ingest_t"))))
    .where("rn = 1").drop("rn"))

# === 6. MERGE INTO DELTA (idempotent · MERGE on canonical PK) ===
(DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver_scml_excursion_event").alias("tgt")
    .merge(silver_dedup.alias("src"), "tgt.event_id_g = src.event_id_g")
    .whenMatchedUpdateAll()                                 # latest wins
    .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
    .execute())

# === 7. EMIT BUILD-COMPLETE LEDGER ROW (audit) ===
emit_ledger_row(
    service_code=service_code,
    kind="silver.build.complete",
    payload={
        "schema_version": schema_version,
        "window": {"start": window_start, "end": window_end},
        "rows_in_bronze": iot_df.count() + d365_df.count(),
        "rows_in_silver": silver_dedup.count(),
        "notebook_version": NOTEBOOK_VERSION,
    }
)

# === 8. UPDATE MICROSOFT PURVIEW LINEAGE ===
# Microsoft Fabric writes the Bronze→Silver edges automatically
# We add the semantic edge: "this Notebook implements SCML.excursion_event.v2"
purview_register_lineage(
    source_assets=["bronze_iot_temps", "bronze_d365_events"],
    target_asset="silver_scml_excursion_event",
    transformation="silver_scml_excursion_event.ipynb@" + NOTEBOOK_VERSION,
    schema_version=schema_version,
)

Eight steps · always the same eight in every conformance Notebook · only the schema and the source-system rules differ. Step 6 (MERGE on canonical PK) is what makes the idempotency contract hold: re-running the Notebook with the same window produces the same Silver rows. Step 7 (LEDGER emit) is what makes the audit chain hold. Step 8 (Purview lineage) is what makes a regulator's "show me how this Silver row came to be" question answerable.

8.3 Microsoft Fabric Components

Silver builds run on Microsoft Fabric notebooks against the same Lakehouse that holds Bronze. Three patterns dominate:

PatternMicrosoft Fabric componentWhen to use
PySpark notebookMicrosoft Fabric Spark · NotebookLarge fan-out joins, complex deduplication, ML-feature engineering inside the Silver build
T-SQL on WarehouseMicrosoft Fabric Warehouse · Stored ProcedureSchema-stable, foreign-key-rich entities; analyst-readable build logic
KQL update policyMicrosoft Fabric KQL DB · Update PolicyStreaming Silver from streaming Bronze (KQL-DB Bronze with continuous KQL-update-policy materialization)

The choice is per-entity, not per-Service. RC-E2E-03's Silver layer mixes all three: SCML.Inventory is a PySpark notebook, MERML.Markdown is a T-SQL stored procedure, and a streaming-derived SCML.LotMovement is a KQL update policy.

8.4 The Per-Service Silver Workspace

Silver entities live in Microsoft Fabric workspaces named per Service. rc-e2e-03 workspace holds the SCML/MERML Silver entities used by RC-E2E-03. hls-e2e-04 holds the EHRML/CMSML Silver entities used by HLS-E2E-04.

Where multiple Services use the same Silver entity, the entity lives in one Service's workspace and is exposed to others via Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse Shortcuts. SCML.Lot, owned by RC-E2E-09 (Product Tracking), is shortcut-exposed into RC-E2E-03's workspace where the cold-chain agents read it. The Layer 1 mi-apex-merch-runtime identity is granted Storage Blob Data Reader on the source-of-truth workspace by the owner Service's Bicep — this is the Chapter-9-of-Deployment-Guide cross-Service authorization pattern surfacing here.

Key Takeaways

  • Four conformance moves: type stabilization, naming/unit conformance, foreign-key resolution to canonical IDs, deduplication + ordering. They live in a per-entity Microsoft Fabric notebook.
  • Idempotent rebuild is a hard contract: drop Silver, re-run the build, get byte-identical output. No out-of-band fixes.
  • Silver builds use PySpark (Spark notebooks), T-SQL (Warehouse stored procs), or KQL update policies — choice per entity.
  • Per-Service Microsoft Fabric workspaces hold Silver; cross-Service entity reuse via Lakehouse Shortcuts and scoped role assignments.
Chapter 9

Schema Library Deep Dive

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks SCML, MERML, PROML, and EHRML entity-by-entity at the column level.
  • Shows the join shape across schemas that Gold marts build on.
  • Establishes the schema-evolution rules that keep the library stable across Service onboardings.
60-second read
  • SCML · MERML · EHRML · CMSML are concrete column-level entities — DDL-grade, not conceptual. Each is rendered as both DDL and ERD.
  • Every Silver row carries three timestamps · source-system lineage (src_*) · and where appropriate a decision_ledger_id closing the audit loop.
  • Schema evolution is additive by default; practice-specific needs add nullable columns, never fork the schema.
  • The §9A cross-schema view is the materialization spec — keep it synced with Gold-build notebooks for accurate Microsoft Purview lineage.
Concept first — why we drew the dictionary

This chapter is long because it is a dictionary. Every business concept APEX-M's 38 Services reason about — a customer, a SKU, a facility, an order, a patient encounter, a network element — has one canonical representation, named and shaped once, so that the next service architect who needs to model a markdown event in RC-E2E-03 and the architect who needs to model a prior-auth in HLS-E2E-04 reach for the same definition of "customer" without rediscovering it.

If you read the chapter once cover-to-cover, you'll come back to it as reference. If you read it as reference first, you'll find one schema family at a time — pulled up because a Service profile in Part VI named it. Either path works. The order below (SCML first, OEMML last) is alphabetic-by-frequency-of-cross-practice use; the most universally-needed families come first. Skip to the family your engagement needs · read its ERD · note the join keys · keep moving.

The "why we drew it this way" section (§9.0 below) is the legend — read it once and every diagram in this chapter and Appendix A becomes scannable in 30 seconds.

9.0 How to Read the ERDs in This Chapter

Each schema family in this chapter is rendered as both DDL and an entity-relationship diagram (ERD). The ERDs use a compact convention that propagates across all five diagrams in this chapter and Appendix A. Read this section once and the rest is legible at a glance.

9.1 SCML — Supply Chain Model Layer

SCML is the most heavily reused schema family in the catalog. RC, ER, AXLE, and ICE all draw on it. The five headline entities:

DDL — SCML.Inventory
CREATE TABLE SCML.Inventory (
    inventory_id        VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,    -- canonical inventory-position ID
    sku_id              VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,    -- canonical SKU
    location_id         VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,    -- store, warehouse, well, plant
    location_type       VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,    -- 'store' | 'warehouse' | 'plant' | ...
    on_hand_qty         DECIMAL(18,4) NOT NULL,
    on_order_qty        DECIMAL(18,4) NOT NULL,
    reserved_qty        DECIMAL(18,4) NOT NULL,
    available_qty       AS (on_hand_qty - reserved_qty) PERSISTED,
    unit_of_measure     VARCHAR(8)   NOT NULL,    -- 'EA' | 'CS' | 'LB' | 'KG' | ...
    valuation_currency  VARCHAR(3)   NOT NULL,    -- ISO 4217
    valuation_amount    DECIMAL(18,4),
    event_ts            TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,    -- when the SOR observed it
    ingest_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,    -- when APEX received it
    silver_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,    -- when Silver materialized
    src_system          VARCHAR(32)  NOT NULL,    -- 'sap-s4' | 'oracle-retail' | ...
    src_inventory_id    VARCHAR(64),              -- source-system ID for lineage
    PRIMARY KEY (inventory_id, event_ts)
);
DDL — SCML.Lot · FSMA-204 lot provenance
CREATE TABLE SCML.Lot (
    lot_id              VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,    -- canonical lot ID
    sku_id              VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    supplier_id         VARCHAR(64),
    production_date     DATE,
    expiration_date     DATE,
    fsma204_status      VARCHAR(16),              -- 'compliant' | 'pending' | 'recall'
    chain_of_custody    JSONB,                    -- ordered list of custody events
    cold_chain_history  JSONB,                    -- list of (sensor, ts, temp_c)
    event_ts            TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    ingest_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    silver_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    src_system          VARCHAR(32)  NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (lot_id)
);

Other SCML entities — SCML.Movement, SCML.Receipt, SCML.Shipment — follow the same shape: canonical IDs, conformed types, three timestamps, source-system lineage columns. Appendix A lists every entity column.

9.2 MERML — Merchandising Model Layer

MERML is RC-anchored but reaches into ICE-Aftermarket-05 (parts replenishment) and parts of TH-HOT-03 (hotel pricing) where pricing-elasticity concepts apply.

DDL — MERML.Markdown · MERML.Elasticity (sketches)
CREATE TABLE MERML.Markdown (
    markdown_id         VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    sku_id              VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    location_id         VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    base_price          DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    markdown_pct        DECIMAL(5,2)  NOT NULL,    -- 0.00–100.00
    markdown_price      AS (base_price * (1 - markdown_pct/100)) PERSISTED,
    effective_from      TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    effective_to        TIMESTAMP,
    reason_code         VARCHAR(32),               -- 'aging' | 'overstock' | 'excursion' | 'competitive'
    approved_by         VARCHAR(64),               -- HITL approver identity
    decision_ledger_id  VARCHAR(64),               -- LEDGER row that approved this markdown
    event_ts            TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    ingest_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    silver_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    src_system          VARCHAR(32)  NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (markdown_id, effective_from)
);

CREATE TABLE MERML.Elasticity (
    sku_id              VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    location_id         VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    elasticity_coef     DECIMAL(8,4)  NOT NULL,    -- demand-vs-price slope
    elasticity_r2       DECIMAL(5,4),              -- model fit quality
    estimation_window   VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,     -- 'last-90d' | 'last-180d' | ...
    estimated_at        TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    silver_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (sku_id, location_id, estimation_window, estimated_at)
);

Note decision_ledger_id on MERML.Markdown. Every approved markdown carries the LEDGER row that authorized it, which closes the loop between the Service decision and the Silver entity that records the outcome. This is how KPI attribution travels back to the agent that proposed and the human that approved.

9.3 EHRML — Electronic Health Records

EHRML is HLS-only. The schema is shaped to FHIR-equivalent semantics but stored as canonical APEX columns for joinability.

DDL — EHRML.Encounter · EHRML.Diagnosis (sketches)
CREATE TABLE EHRML.Encounter (
    encounter_id        VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    member_id           VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,    -- tokenized — see §7
    provider_id         VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    facility_id         VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    encounter_type      VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,    -- 'inpatient' | 'outpatient' | 'ed' | 'tele'
    admission_ts        TIMESTAMP,
    discharge_ts        TIMESTAMP,
    chief_complaint_code VARCHAR(16),             -- ICD-10 or SNOMED code
    drg_code            VARCHAR(8),
    los_hours           AS (DATEDIFF(HOUR, admission_ts, discharge_ts)),
    event_ts            TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    ingest_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    silver_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    src_system          VARCHAR(32)  NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (encounter_id)
);

CREATE TABLE EHRML.Diagnosis (
    diagnosis_id        VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
    encounter_id        VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL REFERENCES EHRML.Encounter(encounter_id),
    diagnosis_code      VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,   -- ICD-10
    diagnosis_type      VARCHAR(16)  NOT NULL,   -- 'principal' | 'secondary' | 'admit'
    seq                 INT          NOT NULL,
    poa_indicator       CHAR(1),                  -- present-on-admission
    event_ts            TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    silver_ts           TIMESTAMP    NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (diagnosis_id)
);

member_id is tokenized at ingest (§6.2) and the unwrap key sits behind the dual-control HSM access policy (§7.3). The Silver layer never holds raw PHI; the unwrap happens at HITL approval moment for a single record.

9.4 Schema-Evolution Rules

The schema library is a living thing. New Services drive new column requirements; new client SOR variants drive new conformance edge cases. Three rules keep evolution from breaking the library:

  1. Additive only by default. Adding columns is free; renaming columns is a versioned migration. SCML v2 introducing on_consignment_qty next to on_hand_qty is fine; renaming available_qty would be a breaking change requiring a coordinated Service migration.
  2. Practice-specific extensions, not forks. If RC needs a column that ER doesn't, add the column to the shared SCML schema with a nullable default; don't fork SCML into SCML-RC and SCML-ER. The library is one library.
  3. Source-system specifics in src_* columns. If SAP carries an extra field that other ERPs don't, it lands in src_sap_*. Canonical APEX consumers don't read it; SAP-specific Bronze→Silver edge cases use it.

9.5 Cross-Schema Composition for RC-E2E-03 — A Worked View

Individual schema ERDs are the dictionary. The actual data graph a Service traverses cuts across schemas. RC-E2E-03 reads SCML (inventory + lot), MERML (markdown · elasticity · competitor), PROML (pricing · discount rules), composes them through Silver into Gold marts, and exposes those marts to agents via MCP. The diagram below collapses that whole pipeline onto one canvas so an architect can see the joins and the materialization edges in a single view.

9A.1 Cross-Schema Field Map

One last table — the column-by-column map of which Silver columns flow into which Gold mart. This is the practical materialization spec a data engineer reads when building or auditing the Gold-build notebook.

Gold mart · columnSilver source · columnTransformation

Best Practice — Use this view as the materialization spec

The cross-schema field map is what the Microsoft Fabric notebook author refers to when building gold-materialize-pricing-recommendation-basis.ipynb. The spec is also what Microsoft Purview registers as lineage edges when the notebook runs — every Gold-column → Silver-column edge becomes a Purview lineage record. Keep this table in sync with the notebook; if they diverge, lineage drifts and audits get harder.

Key Takeaways

  • SCML, MERML, EHRML (and the rest from Ch 2) are concrete column-level entities — DDL-grade, not conceptual.
  • Every Silver row carries three timestamps (event/ingest/silver), source-system lineage columns (src_*), and where appropriate a LEDGER reference (decision_ledger_id) that closes the audit loop.
  • Schema evolution is additive by default; practice-specific needs add nullable columns, never fork the schema; source-system quirks live in src_* columns.
  • The cross-schema view (§9A) is the practical materialization spec; keep it synced with the Microsoft Fabric Gold-build notebooks so Microsoft Purview lineage stays accurate.
Chapter 9A

Industry Schemas — Deep Dive on How the 14 Families Are Used

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Inventories all 14 canonical Silver schema families (SCML · MERML · PROML · EHRML · CMSML · WLML · QMSML · WOSFML · NETML · BRMML · GLML · CRMML · ECRML · OEMML) with concise definitions and the business concepts each anchors.
  • Maps each schema family to the Services it powers, the Bronze SORs that typically feed it, and the Gold marts it typically supplies — so an engagement can plan the schema bundle a Service needs at scope-time.
  • Walks the cross-schema join patterns that build Gold marts · the per-practice schema overlap matrix · the engagement-specific extension policy.
  • Establishes ownership, evolution discipline, and the worked example of authoring a new Silver schema from scratch.
90-second read
  • 14 schema families, each anchoring one business-concept space across one or more practices. Names are deliberately neutral (Markup Language suffix) to signal that they outlive any particular SOR's representation.
  • Five families are practice-specific: EHRML · CMSML · WLML (HLS) · BRMML (TMT-MED) · ECRML (ICE). Nine cross-cut multiple practices.
  • Three families are nearly universal: CRMML (customers / contacts) · GLML (general ledger / margin) · WOSFML (workforce / operations / shifts / facilities) — used in 5 or more practices.
  • Per Service, typical schema bundle = 3–6 families. One Service rarely needs all 14; one schema family rarely supports only one Service.
  • Cross-schema joins compose Gold marts. Every Gold mart joins 2–6 Silver schemas on canonical keys (entity_id · time bins · facility_id · customer_id).
  • Schema family ownership sits with a named owner (typically a service architect senior in the dominant practice). Cross-practice families have rotating co-owners.
  • Engagement-specific extensions add proprietary columns via a _engagement_* prefix; they coexist with canonical columns but never replace them.

9A.4 Cross-Schema Join Patterns — The Composition Grammar

Gold marts are denormalised joins of 2–6 Silver schemas. APEX-M's canonical join keys (the columns Silver schemas standardise so cross-schema joins compose without translation):

Join keyFamilyJoins to
customer_id_gCRMML (authoritative)MERML.order · CMSML.claim · ECRML.subscription · GLML.revenue_line
sku_id_gSCML / MERML (RC) · OEMML.part_id (AXLE/ICE)MERML.order · MERML.return · WOSFML.lot · SCML.purchase_order
facility_id_gWOSFML (authoritative)SCML.inventory · MERML.store · QMSML.audit · GLML.cost_center
patient_id_gEHRML (authoritative)CMSML.claim · WLML.specimen
contract_id_gPROML (B2B) · ECRML (B2C subscription)GLML.revenue_line · CMSML.benefit_plan
period_id_gGLML (authoritative · fiscal calendar)every margin / forecast / variance join
network_element_id_gNETML (authoritative)WOSFML.alert · CRMML.case · QMSML.outage

The _g suffix marks GUID type (RFC 4122 UUID v7 preferred for time-orderability). Surrogate-key mapping happens at Silver conformance time; original Bronze-source IDs are preserved in _source_keys arrays for forensic walks.

9A.4.1 Worked Example — RC-E2E-03 Pricing Gold mart join

SQL · simplified Gold mart build for RC-E2E-03
SELECT
  sku.sku_id_g,
  sku.sku_name_s,
  fac.facility_id_g, fac.facility_name_s,
  sh.lot_id_g, sh.expiry_date_d,
  ord_30d.units_sold_d, ord_30d.gross_revenue_d,
  cgs.unit_cost_d, gl.margin_pct_d
FROM silver_merml.sku AS sku
JOIN silver_wosfml.facility AS fac
       ON fac.facility_id_g = sku.assigned_facility_id_g
JOIN silver_wosfml.shelf_life AS sh
       ON sh.sku_id_g = sku.sku_id_g
      AND sh.facility_id_g = fac.facility_id_g
JOIN silver_merml.order_aggregate_30d AS ord_30d
       ON ord_30d.sku_id_g = sku.sku_id_g
      AND ord_30d.facility_id_g = fac.facility_id_g
JOIN silver_scml.cost_of_goods AS cgs
       ON cgs.sku_id_g = sku.sku_id_g
LEFT JOIN silver_glml.margin AS gl
       ON gl.product_category_g = sku.product_category_g
      AND gl.period_id_g = current_period_id()
WHERE sh.expiry_date_d - CURRENT_DATE() < INTERVAL 7 DAY

Five schema families compose into one Gold mart row — MERML (sku + order) · WOSFML (facility + shelf_life) · SCML (cost_of_goods) · GLML (margin). The agent reads this mart via MCP; the persona reads it via Power BI Direct Lake; both see the same Parquet bytes.

9A.7 Engagement-Specific Extensions

Every engagement encounters business attributes that don't fit the canonical schema. APEX-M handles this with an extension policy that preserves both canonical and engagement-specific data without dilution:

  • Prefix discipline. Engagement-specific columns are prefixed _engagement_ (e.g., _engagement_loyalty_tier_s) so they sort to the right of canonical columns in IDE views and are obvious in code review.
  • Canonical wins on overlap. If an engagement-specific column conceptually duplicates a canonical column, the canonical column is the read path · the engagement column is for forensic/compat only.
  • Type suffix discipline. Every column ends with a type suffix (_g = GUID · _s = string · _d = decimal · _dt = date · _b = boolean · _i = integer · _t = timestamp · _a = array). Makes KQL and Python typing trivial.
  • Extension lifecycle. An engagement extension may be promoted to canonical (added to the next schema-family version) if 3+ engagements adopt the same extension with the same semantics — promotion is an ADR per Ch 9 ownership.
  • No engagement-only foreign keys. Engagement extensions can't introduce new join keys; only canonical columns may serve as join keys, to keep cross-Service composition tractable.

9A.8 Authoring a New Silver Schema — Worked Example

Steps to author a new schema family (rare · ADR-level event):

  1. Identify the gap. Demonstrate that no existing family covers the concept and that no extension to an existing family suffices. Usually two or more engagements have requested it.
  2. Author the schema spec. YAML in apex-shared-canonical/schemas/<new-family>.yaml defining tables · columns (with type suffixes) · join keys · authoritative source for each column · PII tier per column.
  3. Identify the dominant practice + owner. Name a service architect senior in that practice as the schema-family owner.
  4. Draft Bronze-source map. Identify the typical SORs that will feed it.
  5. Pilot in one Service. Land Bronze · build conformance Notebook · produce Silver · build one Gold mart that consumes it.
  6. ADR review. Submit ADR to the architecture-review board · co-sign by the dominant practice's senior architect + the framework owner.
  7. Add to canonical library. Merge to apex-shared-canonical · update this Ch 9A table · update Sellers Appendix G.

Key Takeaways

  • 14 canonical schema families anchor every business concept APEX-M serves. Names end in "ML" (Markup Language) to signal cross-source neutrality.
  • Three families are nearly universal (WOSFML · GLML · CRMML reach 7 practices each); four are practice-specific (EHRML · CMSML · WLML · BRMML reach 1 practice each).
  • Per Service, the typical schema bundle is 3–6 families. Gold mart joins span 2–6 families on canonical keys with type-suffix discipline.
  • Canonical join keys (customer_id_g · sku_id_g · facility_id_g etc.) are the composition grammar that makes cross-schema Gold marts straightforward.
  • Engagement-specific extensions use the _engagement_* prefix; canonical wins on overlap; only canonical columns can serve as join keys.
  • Authoring a new schema family is an ADR-level event — requires gap analysis · pilot · dominant-practice owner · cross-architect sign-off.

Catalog Drills

  1. For your engagement's primary Service, identify its schema bundle. Confirm 3–6 families. If > 6, is the Service over-scoped? If < 3, is the Service mart-light?
  2. Write the cross-schema join SQL for one Gold mart in your engagement. Identify every canonical key used and which Silver schema family is authoritative for each.
  3. List every engagement-specific extension your engagement has authored. For each, ask: "is this a one-off, or have 3+ engagements requested similar?" If the latter, propose canonical promotion.
  4. Pick one universal schema (WOSFML or GLML or CRMML). Show how the same Silver row supports two different practice Services with completely different Gold mart shapes.
Chapter 10

Quality, Lineage, Microsoft Purview

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the Microsoft Purview integration that catalogs every Bronze → Silver → Gold artifact.
  • Establishes the Silver-tier data-quality contract: what gets checked, what blocks promotion to Gold, what alerts.
  • Maps lineage to the audit chain so the LEDGER decision links back to the Bronze rows that supported it.
60-second read
  • Microsoft Purview catalogs every Bronze table · Silver entity · Gold mart · MCP tool · LEDGER asset, with lineage edges between them.
  • Sensitivity labels mirror the §7.1 PII tier classification and propagate through lineage automatically.
  • Six classes of quality check gate Silver→Gold promotion (schema · referential · volume · distribution · recency · cross-tier).
  • The LEDGER → Gold → Silver → Bronze → SOR lineage chain is the audit-grade path a regulator can walk.

10.1 Microsoft Purview as the Catalog and Lineage Surface

Microsoft Purview is the catalog. Every Bronze table, every Silver entity, every Gold mart, every MCP tool, every sor-connections.yaml entry is registered there. Microsoft Purview consumes:

  • Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse and Warehouse asset catalogs (auto-scan).
  • Microsoft Fabric KQL DB and Eventstream registrations.
  • Microsoft Fabric Pipeline and Notebook lineage events.
  • The MCP tool catalog (registered via a custom Purview type emitted by the MCP host on startup).
  • The LEDGER write events (registered as a custom Purview asset type).

The result is a single catalog where a service architect can ask "which agents read which Gold marts that derive from which Silver entities that derive from which Bronze tables that come from which client SOR systems?" and get an answer rather than a series of joins across documentation.

10.2 Sensitivity Labels and Classifications

Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels mirror the four-tier PII classification from §7.1. Once Bronze is ingested with a tier-3 or tier-4 field, the sensitivity label propagates automatically through Silver and Gold lineage. An analyst opening the Gold mart in Power BI sees the label; an MCP tool definition that returns a tier-3 column gets flagged.

Auto-classification rules cover obvious patterns (email addresses, SSN-shaped strings, NDC codes) and can run on Bronze samples as part of the ingest pipeline. Manual classification overrides the auto-classification when the data shape doesn't match the regex but the field is sensitive (e.g., a free-text "notes" column that operationally contains member-identifiable information).

10.3 The Silver Quality Contract

Silver promotion to Gold is gated by quality checks. The checks are run by a Microsoft Fabric Notebook activity at the end of each Silver build, before any Gold mart that depends on the entity is rebuilt.

Check classExampleAction on fail
SchemaRequired columns present, types match libraryBlock Gold rebuild · alert on-call
ReferentialEvery EHRML.Diagnosis.encounter_id resolves to a row in EHRML.EncounterBlock Gold rebuild · alert on-call
VolumeSilver row count within 3σ of seven-day moving averageWarn · proceed with Gold rebuild
DistributionMedian on_hand_qty for top SKUs within ±20% of trailing windowWarn · proceed
RecencyNewest event_ts within expected lag for source cadenceBlock Gold rebuild · alert on-call
Cross-tierSilver row count == sum of Bronze rows it derives from (post-dedup)Block · open data-quality ticket

The check results are themselves Purview events; over time a quality timeline accrues per Silver entity. When an architect investigates a Service KPI miss, the quality timeline is the first place to look — KPI deviations correlated to upstream quality alerts is a much faster diagnosis than KPI deviations as a free-floating mystery.

10.4 Lineage to LEDGER

The audit chain in the Deployment Guide (§6.3.1, Ch 5) records every agent decision with a row hash and a backing MCP tool reference. The MCP tool reference points at a Gold mart. The Gold mart's lineage in Purview points at Silver entities. The Silver entities' lineage points at Bronze tables. The Bronze tables' lineage points at the SOR connection.

For any LEDGER row, a six-hop reconstruction reaches back to the source-of-record system and the timestamp at which it produced the supporting fact. That is the audit-grade chain a regulator can walk: "on date X, this Service decided Y; the agent that decided it called this MCP tool; the MCP tool returned this row hash from this Gold mart; the Gold mart was materialized from these Silver entities; the Silver entities were built from these Bronze rows; the Bronze rows came from these SOR systems via this connection at this timestamp."

Independence — Microsoft Purview is the audit-narrative substrate

Microsoft Purview running in the client tenant is what makes the two-contract model defensible to a client's audit committee. The Deloitte authoring artifacts that crossed the Independence boundary (agent images, Bicep, schema definitions) are visible as registered assets; the client SOR systems and client data lineage are visible as the things they connect into. The single picture is what an auditor walks. Without Purview, the picture has to be reconstructed from a half-dozen sources.

Key Takeaways

  • Microsoft Purview is the unified catalog: every Bronze table, Silver entity, Gold mart, MCP tool, and LEDGER row is a registered asset, with lineage edges between them.
  • Sensitivity labels mirror the PII tier classification and propagate through lineage automatically.
  • Silver-to-Gold promotion is gated by six classes of quality check; failures block Gold rebuild and alert on-call.
  • The lineage graph from LEDGER → Gold → Silver → Bronze → SOR is the audit-grade chain a regulator walks.
Chapter 10A

Microsoft Entra ID & Purview — Security and Governance Deep Dive

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the Microsoft Entra ID identity model APEX-M depends on — including the new Microsoft Entra Agent ID platform that Foundry Hosted Agents auto-provision (per Ch 11.5 of the Deployment Guide).
  • Inventories the Conditional Access · PIM · ID Protection · ID Governance controls that wrap APEX agents and operator identities.
  • Drills the two halves of Microsoft Purview — Data Governance (Data Map · catalog · classification · lineage) and Data Security (sensitivity labels · DLP · Insider Risk · DSPM for AI) — and how each binds to the APEX Trust envelope (§30.1.5).
  • Establishes the runtime audit-and-governance loop: Entra issues identity → APEX-M scopes its use → Purview observes and classifies what it touches → Insider Risk + Defender for Cloud Apps watches for anomalies → LEDGER preserves the forensic anchor.
90-second read
  • Five identity types in APEX-M: User (operator) · Group (role / scope) · Workload Identity (single-tenant service principal · APEX MCP host) · Managed Identity (Azure-resource-bound · per-Service UAMI) · Microsoft Entra Agent ID (new · Foundry-issued · per-published-agent · with blueprints and Conditional Access).
  • Microsoft Entra Agent ID is the new platform: every published Foundry agent gets a distinct Entra ID service principal · its own blueprint · Conditional Access policies · ID Protection signals · access reviews. Agents are first-class governance subjects.
  • Conditional Access applies to users, groups, agent identities (preview), and workload identities (Workload ID Premium licensed). Risk-based and location-based controls are the two primary axes.
  • PIM elevates roles just-in-time with approval; ID Protection scores risky identities (workload + agent included); ID Governance runs lifecycle workflows and access reviews.
  • Purview has two halves. Data Governance — Data Map (catalog · lineage · classification) over the entire data estate including Microsoft Fabric. Data Security — sensitivity labels · DLP · Insider Risk Management · Communications Compliance · Audit · DSPM for AI.
  • DSPM for AI (Data Security Posture Management for AI) is Purview's AI-specific surface — captures prompt/response audit, classifies sensitive content in AI interactions, scopes Endpoint DLP to block sensitive paste into third-party AI, surfaces sensitivity labels on Copilot answers.
  • The APEX trust envelope (§30.1.5) is realized by these primitives: Entra grants identity · Purview classifies what flows through it · DLP enforces what cannot leave · LEDGER preserves what did happen.
Plain-English primer — the office-building analogy

Imagine your company's headquarters. To get past the lobby, you need an ID badge. The badge tells security who you are, what floors you're allowed on, and what time you're allowed to be there. That's Microsoft Entra ID — the identity system that knows who every person, app, and AI agent is, and decides what they can access.

But identity is only half the story. The building also has:

  • A filing room with labels on every cabinet — "Public," "Internal," "Confidential — HR Only." That's Microsoft Purview Data Map, which catalogs every piece of data in the company and labels it by sensitivity.
  • Security cameras at every door — recording who entered which floor at what time. That's Microsoft unified audit log plus APEX's LEDGER.
  • A printer that won't print Confidential files outside the office — and a paper shredder at the exit. That's Microsoft Purview DLP (Data Loss Prevention).
  • A behavior monitor — flagging when someone who normally arrives at 9am suddenly tries to badge in at 3am. That's Microsoft Entra ID Protection and Purview Insider Risk Management.
  • A SOC (Security Operations Center) in the back room watching all of the above on monitors. That's Microsoft Sentinel + the Defender suite.

The new piece — and the reason this chapter exists — is that AI agents now get their own ID badges. Until 2025, only humans and apps had identities. Now Foundry-hosted agents are first-class citizens in Entra ID: each agent has its own badge (called a "Microsoft Entra Agent ID"), its own access rules, its own audit trail. Agents can be flagged risky, revoked, reviewed quarterly — just like employees.

The rest of this chapter explains how each piece of the building works in detail, how APEX-M wires them together, and how the "two-contract Independence model" keeps everything in the client's tenant (not Deloitte's). Read the primer once · skim the technical sections as you need them.

10A.1 Microsoft Entra ID — APEX's Identity Architecture

Microsoft Entra ID is the identity boundary for every APEX-M tenant deployment. Per Architecture strategies for identity and access management, Entra is integrated with the management plane of Azure and the data planes of most Azure services — so the same identity that signs into the operator portal is the identity APEX-M's Bicep grants role assignments to.

Three Entra ID surfaces APEX-M consumes:

SurfaceWhat it isAPEX-M binding
Microsoft Entra IDThe workforce identity directory (employees, internal apps, service principals)Operators · engagement teams · APEX MCP host workload identities · Foundry agent identities
Microsoft Entra External IDPartner / B2B / B2C — formerly Azure AD B2B and B2C, unifiedCross-tenant scenarios where a client's external auditor needs read-only LEDGER access; rare but documented
Microsoft Entra Workload IDPremium SKU adding Conditional Access · ID Protection · access reviews · app-health recommendations specifically for workload identitiesRequired-licensed for APEX-M PROD — APEX-M MCP host service principals are scoped by Workload ID Premium Conditional Access policies

10A.2 The Five Identity Types in APEX-M

Each APEX-M call traces back to one of five identity types. Understanding which is invoking is the first step in every troubleshooting and audit conversation:

Identity typeMicrosoft Entra objectAPEX-M roleExample
UserUser principal (interactive sign-in capable)Operators (merchandising director · finance lead · clinical reviewer); engagement teamsDaniel Chen (RC merchandising director) signing into Microsoft 365 Copilot · approving an HITL adaptive card in Microsoft Teams
GroupSecurity group · Microsoft 365 group · dynamic membership groupRBAC scope grouping · APEX persona role assignments · domain delegations in Microsoft Fabricapex-rc-e2e-03-merch-directors · apex-hls-e2e-04-prior-auth-reviewers
Workload IdentitySingle-tenant service principal owned by the tenantAPEX MCP host · APEX harness · CI/CD service principal · cross-Service toolssp-apex-mcp-host-rc-e2e-03 with Conditional Access scoped to the apex-m platform VNet IP range
Managed Identity (UAMI · SAMI)Azure-resource-bound service principal · no manual credentialThe four Layer 1 UAMIs from Deployment Guide §4.3 (runtime · mcp · ingest · pii-unlock); per-Container-App SAMIs for Lab usemi-apex-merch-runtime · mi-apex-merch-pii-unlock
Microsoft Entra Agent ID (new)Specialised service principal type · Foundry-issued · governed by an agent identity blueprintPer-published-agent identity for Foundry Hosted Agents (per Deployment Guide §11.5.6); shared project identity for unpublished/dev agentsagent-the-pricer-rc-e2e-03-prod bound to the apex-m-rc-e2e-03 blueprint

10A.3 Microsoft Entra Agent ID — The New Foundry-Issued Identity

Per Agent identity concepts in Microsoft Foundry, the Microsoft Entra Agent ID platform introduces two new Entra ID object types: agent identity blueprint (the governing template) and agent identity (the per-agent service principal). Foundry auto-provisions both:

  • Shared project identity — created when the first agent in a Foundry project is created. Unpublished / in-development agents share this identity. Simplifies experimentation; centralises permission grants for early dev.
  • Distinct agent identity — created when an agent is published. Bound to the agent application resource. Required when an agent crosses into integration testing · production · per-agent audit trails. The published agent uses the distinct identity to authenticate to all downstream services (MCP · A2A · Microsoft.KeyVault · Microsoft Fabric Gold · Microsoft Graph).

The runtime token exchange for an agent's tool call is a four-step OAuth 2.0 chain — developers don't manage tokens directly, Foundry Agent Service handles it:

Foundry agent identity · runtime token exchange (per Microsoft Learn)
1. Blueprint authentication
   Agent Service presents the blueprint's OAuth credentials to Microsoft Entra ID.
   Federated credential (Foundry project's managed identity) is the recommended
   form — no client secret stored in the blueprint. The token request includes:

       POST https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/oauth2/v2.0/token
         client_id              = {blueprint-app-id}
         grant_type             = client_credentials
         client_assertion_type  = urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer
         client_assertion       = {federated-managed-identity-token}
         fmi_path               = blueprints/{service-code}/{agent-id}/{version}
         scope                  = api://AgentIdentity/.default

   The fmi_path (Federated Managed Identity path) scopes the federated token to
   a specific blueprint instance. Without it the broker cannot resolve which
   agent is asking and the exchange fails with AADSTS70021. APEX-M sets fmi_path
   to the canonical naming convention from §14B.6 (service-code/agent-id/version).

2. Agent identity token issuance
   Microsoft Entra ID validates blueprint credentials AND the fmi_path against
   the registered federated managed identity, then issues a token for the specific
   agent identity (the distinct service principal for a published agent).

3. Scoped token request
   Agent Service exchanges the agent identity token for a scoped access token
   targeting the downstream service's audience. Examples:
     - Microsoft Fabric Gold:    https://storage.azure.com   (OneLake reads via ADLS Gen2 API)
     - Microsoft.KeyVault:       https://vault.azure.net
     - Microsoft.DocumentDB:     https://cosmos.azure.com
     - Microsoft Graph:          https://graph.microsoft.com
     - Azure Logic Apps:         https://logic.azure.com

4. Authenticated tool call
   Agent Service presents the scoped access token to the MCP server or A2A endpoint.
   Downstream service validates the token, checks the agent identity's RBAC role
   assignments, and grants/denies access.

Two authentication scenarios per key concepts:

  • Attended (delegated · OBO). The agent acts on behalf of a human user. Agent Service exchanges the user's token for one carrying both the agent identity and the user's delegated permissions. The agent can only access what the user has consented to — APEX-M uses this for HITL-approved actions where the operator's identity gates the call.
  • Unattended (application-only · client credentials). The agent acts under its own authority. Access is governed entirely by the agent identity's RBAC role assignments — no human in the loop. APEX-M uses this for the Year-2 LEDGER few-shot exemplar reads (no operator session).
Best Practice — distinct identity per published agent

Every APEX-M agent that crosses into DEV / STAGE / PROD must have a distinct Foundry-issued agent identity (not the shared project identity). The Bicep deployment of the Service grants per-agent role assignments to the distinct identity (per Deployment Guide §11.5.6). The shared identity is for unpublished dev work only. This is the pattern that gives APEX-M's four-stamp audit anchor (manifest · policy · prompt · agent version) a clean per-agent forensic trail.

10A.4 Authentication Patterns

Three OAuth 2.0 flows APEX-M uses, and the constraint each carries:

FlowWhenConstraint
Authorization code + PKCEOperator interactive sign-in to Microsoft 365 Copilot · Power BI · Microsoft TeamsMFA required by Conditional Access; PKCE prevents code interception
On-behalf-of (OBO)APEX MCP host calling Microsoft Fabric Gold on behalf of the signed-in operatorApp registration must be configured to allow OBO; the downstream resource must trust the upstream app's identity
Client credentials (application-only)APEX agent (unattended) calling Microsoft.KeyVault for secrets · APEX harness running testsNo user context; permissions are app-only; sensitive operations should still gate via Conditional Access for workload identities
Federated credentialBlueprint → managed identity trust (Foundry agent identity); GitHub Actions → Entra (CI without secrets)Recommended for production. No client secret stored. Azure manages credential rotation.

10A.5 Conditional Access — Users, Groups, Agents, Workload Identities

Per Conditional Access: Users, groups, agents, and workload identities, CA can target each of the five identity types. APEX-M's recommended baseline:

TargetPolicyWhy
All operator users (incl. external auditor B2B)Require MFA · block legacy auth · require compliant device for Tier-3 PHI accessBaseline workforce protection
Privileged roles (PIM-eligible)Require MFA + privileged-access workstation + sign-in risk = cleanBreak-glass and engagement-lead protection
APEX MCP host workload identitiesBlock from outside known IP ranges · block on workload-identity risk = highWorkload ID Premium feature; policy is enforced at token issuance
APEX agent identities (preview)Restrict to apex-m platform VNet · scope by custom security attribute (apex.tier) · block elevated agent-identity riskPer Conditional Access and agent identities — agent identities are first-class CA targets in preview
Cross-tenant accessCross-Tenant Access Settings explicitly permit named external auditor tenants only; no inbound default trustADR-025-01 — A2A and other cross-tenant flows are forbidden

Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) for workload identities — when an APEX MCP host calls Microsoft Graph at least once an hour and is registered as a single-tenant app, it qualifies for CAE: 24-hour long-lived tokens with continuous security checks. APEX-M PROD topology enables CAE.
