Chapter 14

Workflow Design Patterns

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Catalogues the four workflow patterns that recur across the 38-Service catalog.
  • Maps each pattern to the agent composition and HITL gate it implements.
  • Establishes the workflow primitives (trigger · branch · parallel · HITL stage · LEDGER emit) that every Service uses.
60-second read
  • Four workflow patterns — triage-and-decide (~18) · continuous-optimization (~8) · detect-and-attribute (~6) · periodic-digest (every Service) — cover the catalog.
  • Seven primitives — trigger · agent call · MCP call · branch · parallel · HITL stage · LEDGER emit — render identically in n8n and Logic Apps Hybrid.
  • The triage-and-decide pattern is the canonical W2-pilot shape from the APEX scenario chains.
Plain-English primer — workflows are recipes

Think of a recipe. A recipe says: "When the timer rings (trigger), chop the onions (step 1), sauté them while you mix the batter (parallel step), check that the result tastes right (a decision point), serve it (final action)." If you've cooked from a cookbook, you already understand workflows.

An APEX-M workflow is the same idea. Something happens — an event fires, a schedule hits, a webhook arrives — and a sequence of steps runs. Most APEX-M workflows follow one of four shapes we see again and again across the catalog of 38 Services. Like recipes, knowing the shape tells you 80% of what will happen:

  • Triage-and-decide — "something just happened · figure out how bad it is · decide what to do · get human sign-off." Most common. Used when a cold-chain truck loses cooling, a prior-auth comes in, a power outage starts.
  • Continuous-optimization — "every day/hour, look at the data · suggest improvements · get sign-off · apply them." Used for ongoing price adjustments, marketing campaign tuning.
  • Detect-and-attribute — "scan a stream for suspicious patterns · explain what we found · stage a remediation." Used for returns fraud, lot-tracking compliance.
  • Periodic-digest — "at the end of the week/month, summarize what happened · send the right person the right summary." Used everywhere; every Service has at least one.

Each shape is composed of seven building blocks (called primitives): trigger · agent call · MCP call · branch · parallel · HITL stage · LEDGER emit. That's it. Every Service's workflow is some combination of these seven. If you can read a recipe, you can read an APEX-M workflow.

One thing the recipe analogy doesn't capture, which this chapter clarifies (and the callout below underlines): who does the work. The kitchen (the workflow substrate — n8n on laptop, Logic Apps Hybrid on cloud) handles the order of operations. But the cooking — the actual reasoning across multiple AI agents — happens inside Microsoft Agent Framework, not in the kitchen's order-of-operations book.

Architectural shift — Microsoft Agent Framework is the default coordinator

The workflow patterns in this chapter describe what the system as a whole does — from event trigger through operator decision. They do not mean that n8n or Logic Apps Hybrid composes the multi-agent coordination. As of Microsoft Agent Framework GA (2025/2026), the canonical APEX-M pattern is:

  • Workflow substrate (n8n on laptop · Logic Apps Hybrid / Foundry workflows on cloud) — narrowed role: receive the trigger event · authenticate the caller · POST to one agent fleet endpoint · route the agent's response to a Microsoft Teams adaptive card (HITL) or downstream non-agent integration · emit a substrate-level LEDGER row for the workflow start/end. Five n8n nodes total · not fifteen.
  • Microsoft Agent Framework (inside the agent fleet · §14B) — does the multi-agent coordination: Sequential · Concurrent · Handoff · Group Chat · Magentic. The five canonical patterns (per-pattern builder classes per Microsoft Learn) absorb what n8n parallel branches and IF nodes used to do for inter-agent message passing.

The four workflow patterns below (triage-and-decide · continuous-optimization · detect-and-attribute · periodic-digest) describe the end-to-end scenario shape. The multi-agent coordination inside the scenario lives in Microsoft Agent Framework, not in the substrate. See §14.4 (substrate calls into Agent Framework) and §14B (Agent Framework deep dive) for the full integration architecture.

14.1 The Four Workflow Patterns

Across all 38 Services, four workflow shapes account for nearly every orchestration. Knowing the pattern names is shorthand for service architects: when an architect says "this Service is a triage-and-decide," every other architect knows roughly what the workflow looks like before reading the JSON.

14.1.1 Triage-and-decide

An event fires; the Analyst severity-ranks it; the Demand Checker quantifies impact; the Finance Lead checks commercial viability; the Operations Lead stages a HITL approval; the human approves or declines; the decision lands in the canonical decision table.

Used by — RC-E2E-03 cold-chain · HLS-E2E-04 prior auth · ER-PU-04 distribution outage · TMT-TEL-NET-02 fault prediction. Approximately 18 of the 38 Services follow this shape.

14.1.2 Continuous-optimization

A scheduled trigger fires; the Demand Checker proposes optimization candidates from a Gold mart; the Finance Lead scores them; the Operations Lead stages a batch HITL approval; approved actions land in canonical decision tables.

Used by — RC-E2E-03 markdown · TH-HOT-03 pricing · TMT-MED-01 content recommendation. Approximately 8 Services.

14.1.3 Detect-and-attribute

An event fires; the Analyst classifies it; an attribution-mart join determines whether to escalate; if so, a HITL stage; the closing decision lands in an audit-attributed table.

Used by — RC-E2E-07 returns fraud · ICE-Aftermarket-03 warranty fraud · TMT-MED-03 ad fraud · TMT-TEL-RAA-04 revenue assurance. Approximately 6 Services.

14.1.4 Periodic-digest

A scheduled trigger fires; multiple Gold marts are read; the Briefer composes a digest; the digest publishes to operator-facing surfaces (Power BI, Teams). No agent decision; no HITL gate; this is the "what happened" loop.

Used by — every Service has at least one periodic-digest workflow. The Briefer is the most-reused agent across the catalog (~32 Services compose it).

14.2 The Workflow Primitives

Every workflow, regardless of pattern, is built from a small set of primitives. The trigger primitive — the one that decides when a workflow runs — is the bridge to the data-velocity-and-threshold deep dive in Ch 5A; Activator firings, Eventstream rule matches, and scheduled refreshes all manifest here as the substrate-level Trigger row below.

PrimitiveWhat it doesn8n nodeLogic Apps action
TriggerStarts the workflow on an event or schedule — fed by Activator / Eventstream / scheduled refresh per Ch 5AWebhook / ScheduleHTTP Request / Recurrence
Agent callHTTP POST to an agent's /runHTTP RequestHTTP action
MCP callHTTP POST to an MCP toolHTTP RequestHTTP action
BranchConditional routing on a previous step's outputIF / SwitchCondition / Switch
ParallelFan-out to multiple steps in parallel; converge on completionSplit In BatchesParallel branch
HITL stagePause workflow; wait for human approval webhookWait + Webhook resumeApproval connector / custom HTTP wait
LEDGER emitWrite an audit row at a workflow checkpointHTTP Request → harness ledger endpointHTTP action → ledger endpoint

Appendix D documents each primitive at the level of input/output schema and shows how each renders in n8n JSON vs Logic Apps JSON. The Deployment Guide's §2.6.3 establishes the workflow-parity contract; this part lives that contract out at the Service level.

14.3 The Triage-and-Decide Worked Example (RC-E2E-03)

The cold-chain excursion workflow is the canonical triage-and-decide. The shape, in primitives:

  1. Trigger — Eventstream rule (§5.3) emits an excursion event; orchestrator subscribes.
  2. LEDGER emit — workflow start row.
  3. Agent call — POST to The Analyst's /run with excursion payload.
  4. Branch — on Analyst severity score: high → continue, low → close + LEDGER emit.
  5. Parallel — fan out to Demand Checker (forward-demand impact) and Finance Lead (margin-at-risk).
  6. Agent call — Operations Lead synthesizes proposed action (sell-through · markdown · destroy).
  7. HITL stage — adaptive card to the Store Operations Lead via Microsoft Teams.
  8. Branch — on approval: emit decision via rc_e2e_03.commit_markdown_decision; on decline: LEDGER row only.
  9. LEDGER emit — workflow complete row, with hash chain anchor.

Every Service profile in Part VI lists its workflow as primitives. The workflow-intent.md file in the delivery repo is the source; n8n JSON and Logic Apps JSON are derived.

14.4 The Workflow Substrate Calls Microsoft Agent Framework

The seven workflow primitives are orchestration-layer constructs (substrate: n8n on laptop · Logic Apps Hybrid on cloud · Foundry workflows on cloud). Each agent call primitive in a workflow is a single HTTP POST into the agent fleet — and inside the agent fleet, what answers the POST is a Microsoft Agent Framework WorkflowAgent assembled by the APEX-M Loader (§14A.8).

The two layers compose cleanly:

The two-layer composition · workflow substrate + agent framework
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  WORKFLOW SUBSTRATE (n8n / Logic Apps Hybrid / Foundry workflow)│
│                                                                  │
│  trigger ─→ branch ─→  [ AGENT CALL ]  ─→ HITL stage ─→ LEDGER  │
│                              │                                   │
│                              │ HTTP POST /run                    │
│                              ↓                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ MICROSOFT AGENT FRAMEWORK · INSIDE THE AGENT FLEET       │   │
│  │                                                            │   │
│  │  WorkflowAgent (built by APEX-M Loader)                   │   │
│  │    │                                                       │   │
│  │    ├── MagenticBuilder()                                  │   │
│  │    │      .participants(Pricer, Demand, Finance, Ops, ...)│   │
│  │    │      .manager(The Analyst)                           │   │
│  │    │      .build()   # Python SDK · .NET uses fluent API  │   │
│  │    │                                                       │   │
│  │    ├── ChatClientAgent per agent + middleware stack       │   │
│  │    │     (ApexAudit · ApexPromptShield · ApexClassif)     │   │
│  │    │                                                       │   │
│  │    └── MCP tools per agent (via Loader §13.4)              │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

n8n and Logic Apps Hybrid never see inside the Agent Framework workflow — they see one POST, one response. The internal Magentic / Group Chat / Sequential coordination that happens inside the response is the Agent Framework's responsibility (§14A.2 · §14B).

14.4.1 Workflow Primitive ↔ Agent Framework Construct · Mapping

Workflow primitive (§14.2)Maps to in Agent FrameworkSubstrate node
triggerNot Agent Framework — substrate-only (Eventstream / schedule / webhook / Activator)n8n trigger · Logic Apps trigger
agent callWorkflowAgent.run() or ChatClientAgent.run()HTTP node POSTing to /run on the agent app · A2A endpoint
MCP callInside the Agent Framework call — MCPStreamableHTTPTool wrapped by Loader (§13.4)Not a separate substrate node — internal to the agent call
branchOutside Agent Framework — substrate-level conditional based on agent's output. (Inside the agent, branching is the orchestrator pattern's job — Handoff or Magentic.)n8n IF node · Logic Apps Condition
parallelEither substrate-level (Microsoft.Logic parallel branches) or Agent Framework Concurrent pattern (§14A.2.2)n8n parallel branches · Logic Apps parallel branches
HITL stageInside Agent Framework — human_input_request primitive · wired by ApexHITLMiddlewareSubstrate routes to Microsoft Teams adaptive card · waits for callback
LEDGER emitInside Agent Framework — ApexAuditMiddleware emits per invocationSubstrate emits its own LEDGER row for substrate-level events (trigger fire · workflow start / end)

14.4.2 The Anti-Pattern · Decomposing Agent Calls Across n8n Nodes

The most common mistake: implementing what should be one Agent Framework workflow as multiple n8n / Logic Apps nodes, one per agent. For example, modeling RC-E2E-03's Magentic pattern as:

ANTI-PATTERN · agent decomposition in the substrate
n8n flow:
  trigger
    → call The Analyst (agent)
    → branch on severity
    → parallel:
        ├── call The Pricer (agent)
        ├── call The Demand Checker (agent)
        └── call The Finance Lead (agent)
    → merge
    → call The Operations Lead (agent)
    → HITL stage
    → LEDGER

WHY THIS IS WRONG:
  - n8n graphs are not type-safe between agent calls
  - n8n cannot model Magentic's dynamic replanning
  - Each agent call is a fresh ChatClientAgent · no shared context provider
  - The four-stamp audit anchor (manifest · policy · prompt · agent version)
    has to be re-stamped per node manually instead of automatically by
    ApexAuditMiddleware inside the agent fleet
  - Cross-agent reasoning (manager's plan over specialists' results) is
    lost — n8n broadcasts variables but the LLM never sees the plan

The correct pattern: one n8n agent-call node invokes the Magentic workflow as a single agent. The Loader-built WorkflowAgent is responsible for the internal coordination; n8n is responsible for the trigger and the post-workflow HITL routing only.

14.4.3 Substrate Choice · When n8n vs Logic Apps Hybrid vs Foundry Workflow

All three substrates call into Microsoft Agent Framework the same way. The choice is operational:

SubstrateWhenAgent Framework integration
n8n (laptop / dev)Free · runs in docker-compose · zero Azure cost · matches user-approved topology UXHTTP node POST to apex-m agent service URL · Loader runs in stdio mode for MCP
Azure Logic Apps Hybrid (DEV/STAGE/PROD)Same Container Apps environment as the agent fleet · VNet-integrated · enterprise-gradeBuilt-in HTTP action with managed-identity auth · APEX MCP host private-endpoint-reachable
Foundry workflow (PROD · low-code)When engagement teams need to edit orchestration visually without redeploying agent codeFoundry's AgentRefAction directly references the published agent's distinct identity

Regardless of substrate choice, the agent code on the other end is the same Loader-built Agent Framework workflow. Substrate choice is a delivery-team decision; agent authoring is unaffected.

Key Takeaways

  • Four workflow patterns — triage-and-decide, continuous-optimization, detect-and-attribute, periodic-digest — cover every Service.
  • Seven primitives — trigger, agent call, MCP call, branch, parallel, HITL stage, LEDGER emit — render identically in n8n and Logic Apps Hybrid.
  • The triage-and-decide pattern (~18 of 38 Services) is the canonical W2-pilot shape from the APEX scenario chains.
  • Workflow substrate calls into Microsoft Agent Framework. The substrate node is one HTTP POST · the agent fleet's WorkflowAgent handles the internal Magentic / Sequential / Group-Chat coordination.
  • The anti-pattern: decomposing agent coordination into n8n nodes. Magentic and Group-Chat patterns cannot survive that decomposition. Keep agent orchestration inside Agent Framework; keep workflow orchestration in the substrate.
Chapter 14A

Agent Orchestration Archetypes — Deep Dive

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Distinguishes agent orchestration (how agents coordinate inside a scenario chain) from workflow orchestration (the Chapter 14 patterns + Chapter 15 n8n / Logic Apps Hybrid runtimes).
  • Documents Microsoft's 5 canonical agent-orchestration patterns from Microsoft Agent Framework (the GA successor to Semantic Kernel + AutoGen).
  • Resolves: "Is Semantic Kernel enough? Is n8n enough?" — definitively, against current Microsoft Learn citations.
  • Shows which APEX-M services use which archetype, with the RC-E2E-03 cold-chain Magentic example.
60-second read
  • Three layers of orchestration sit on top of each other in every APEX-M deployment, and they answer different questions.
  • Microsoft Agent Framework is the canonical agent orchestrator — it supersedes Semantic Kernel and AutoGen as of 2025/2026 GA. Five built-in patterns: Sequential · Concurrent · Handoff · Group Chat · Magentic.
  • Same Agent Framework code runs on laptop AND on Foundry hosted agents — substrate-awareness is env-var-driven, not code-driven.
  • n8n on laptop = Power Automate / Logic Apps / Foundry workflows on cloud — both are workflow orchestrators (triggers, branches, HITL routing, non-agent workflow steps), not agent orchestrators.
  • Semantic Kernel is now legacy. Existing SK code stays valid; new code uses Agent Framework. Migration guide cited below.

14A.1 Three Layers of Orchestration

"Orchestration" in APEX is overloaded. Three things coordinate at three different levels, and each runs on its own substrate. Confusing them is the most common architectural mistake.

LayerWhat it answersVocabularyRuns on (laptop / cloud)
1. Scenario workflow pattern What's the overall shape of this scenario's flow? Triage-and-decide · Continuous-optimization · Detect-and-attribute · Periodic-digest (per §14.1) n8n / Logic Apps Hybrid / Foundry workflows
2. Agent orchestration archetype Inside the scenario, how do the agents coordinate? Sequential · Concurrent · Handoff · Group Chat · Magentic (Microsoft Agent Framework) Microsoft Agent Framework — same code on laptop AND Foundry hosted agents
3. Workflow runtime substrate What executes the non-agent workflow steps? Triggers, branches, HITL routing, ticket creation, schedule n8n on laptop · Power Automate / Logic Apps / Foundry workflows on cloud

Layers 1 and 3 are the same answer in different vocabulary — the *workflow* concern. Layer 2 is a different concern entirely: how the agent fleet itself coordinates *inside* a scenario step. Microsoft documents Layer 2 as "agent orchestration patterns" and provides 5 built-in implementations in Microsoft Agent Framework Workflows Orchestrations.

14A.2 The 5 Microsoft Agent Framework Canonical Patterns

Per AI agent orchestration patterns on Microsoft Learn, the canonical Agent Framework patterns are:

PatternTopologyWhen to useHITL friendly?
SequentialLinear: A → B → CDependent tasks, document-approval-style flows✓ (per Microsoft Learn HITL tutorial)
ConcurrentFan-out + aggregateIndependent operations, ensemble reasoning, parallel fact-gathering✓ (one HITL gate after aggregation)
HandoffMesh: agents transfer control directlyCustomer support, expert systems, dynamic delegation✓ (per-handoff approval)
Group ChatShared conversation, all agents see all messagesCollaborative problem-solving, brainstorming✓ (HITL as a participant)
MagenticManager agent dynamically coordinates specialistsOpen-ended tasks, plans not known up front✓ (manager surfaces HITL gate)
Note — the previous APEX 47-archetype catalog

APEX's Roadmap.md BL.P.65 references "47 orchestration archetypes." Those entries pre-date Microsoft Agent Framework GA. Most of the 47 are *variants* (different agent counts, different HITL placement) of the 5 canonical Microsoft patterns above. The ongoing reconciliation maps each of the 47 to its canonical Microsoft pattern; future amendments to BL.P.65 collapse the 47 into the 5 with parameterization. See ADR-006 for the decision record.

14A.2.1 All Five Patterns in Code · Side by Side

The architectural point is much clearer when you see how little code separates the five patterns. Same agents · same tools · same model · the only thing that changes is which Microsoft Agent Framework builder class (SequentialBuilder · ConcurrentBuilder · HandoffBuilder · GroupChatBuilder · MagenticBuilder) assembles them. Pseudo-code for all five:

Python · The five patterns, same fleet, different conductor
from agent_framework import Agent
from agent_framework.foundry import FoundryChatClient
from agent_framework.workflows import (
    SequentialBuilder, ConcurrentBuilder, HandoffBuilder,
    GroupChatBuilder, MagenticBuilder,
)

# === BUILD THE FLEET (same five agents for every pattern) ===
client = FoundryChatClient()

the_analyst        = Agent(client, name="the-analyst",         instructions=load("analyst.md"))
the_pricer         = Agent(client, name="the-pricer",          instructions=load("pricer.md"))
the_demand_checker = Agent(client, name="the-demand-checker",  instructions=load("demand.md"))
the_finance_lead   = Agent(client, name="the-finance-lead",    instructions=load("finance.md"))
the_ops_lead       = Agent(client, name="the-ops-lead",        instructions=load("ops.md"))


# === PATTERN 1 · SEQUENTIAL · A → B → C linear pipeline ===
# Use when each agent's output is the next agent's input.
# APEX: RC-E2E-04 Loyalty (score → offer-design → finance → ops)
seq = (
    SequentialBuilder()
        .participants(the_analyst, the_pricer, the_finance_lead, the_ops_lead)
        .build()
)
result = await seq.run("Markdown candidate for SKU S-4187 at store 412")


# === PATTERN 2 · CONCURRENT · run all in parallel · aggregate results ===
# Use when each agent works independently on the same input.
# APEX: RC-E2E-07 Returns Fraud (pattern-match across customer/payment/device graphs)
con = (
    ConcurrentBuilder()
        .participants(the_analyst, the_pricer, the_demand_checker, the_finance_lead)
        .build()
)
result = await con.run("Excursion event e7c9f12")
# Each agent sees the same input · returns independent output · framework aggregates


# === PATTERN 3 · HANDOFF · routing by context ===
# Use when input shape determines which specialist handles it.
# APEX: RC-E2E-09 Lot Provenance (compliance officer hands to per-lot-class specialist)
hand = (
    HandoffBuilder()
        .router(the_analyst)
        .targets({
            "refrigerated":   the_pricer,
            "pharmaceutical": the_demand_checker,
            "produce":        the_finance_lead,
        })
        .build()
)
result = await hand.run("Lot L-99281 needs provenance attestation")
# The router agent inspects the input and dispatches to one specialist


# === PATTERN 4 · GROUP CHAT · iterative collaboration with shared context ===
# Use when agents need to "see each other's work" and refine through rounds.
# APEX: HLS-E2E-04 Prior Auth (iterative clinical review · multiple rounds)
gc = (
    GroupChatBuilder()
        .participants(the_pricer, the_demand_checker, the_finance_lead)
        .manager(the_analyst)
        .max_rounds(5)
        .build()
)
result = await gc.run("Pricing proposal for SKU S-4187 · justify markdown ≥30%")
# Manager broadcasts each turn · all agents see history · iterates until done


# === PATTERN 5 · MAGENTIC · manager-led plan with dynamic dispatch ===
# Use when the plan isn't known up front · manager decides who runs when.
# APEX: RC-E2E-03 (cold-chain) · the canonical APEX-M pattern
mag = (
    MagenticBuilder()
        .participants(the_pricer, the_demand_checker, the_finance_lead, the_ops_lead)
        .manager(the_analyst)
        .hitl_persona("merchandising-director")
        .build()                                # Python SDK · .NET = MagenticWorkflowBuilder()
)
result = await mag.run("Excursion event e7c9f12 · two trucks · 40 stores")
# The Analyst builds a plan · calls specialists as needed · replans on each result ·
# stages HITL approval card · waits for operator approval · returns final decision


# === ALL FIVE WRAP AS AGENTS · same downstream interface ===
# Any of the above can be exposed as an A2A endpoint or called from n8n / Logic Apps:
hosted_agent = mag.as_agent(name="rc-e2e-03-decision", description="Cold-chain markdown")
hosted_agent.publish_to_foundry()

Five patterns · ~50 lines of code · all five visible at once. The pattern selection is a one-builder change (SequentialBuilder() → MagenticBuilder() · per the Microsoft Agent Framework Python SDK; the .NET SDK exposes equivalent fluent builders); the agents themselves are unchanged. This is what the architectural shift from "n8n composes inter-agent coordination" to "Agent Framework composes inter-agent coordination" looks like at the code level: the substrate's job shrinks to the trigger + the single HTTP POST · everything inside is one of these five names.

14A.3 Microsoft Agent Framework — Position vs Semantic Kernel and AutoGen

Per the Agent Framework overview:

Agent Framework combines AutoGen's simple agent abstractions with Semantic Kernel's enterprise features — session-based state management, type safety, middleware, telemetry — and adds graph-based workflows for explicit multi-agent orchestration. The Agent Framework is the direct successor, created by the same teams.

QuestionAnswer
Is Semantic Kernel enough?Existing SK code stays valid. New code uses Microsoft Agent Framework — it's the same teams' next generation, with explicit multi-agent workflow support SK does not have. See Semantic Kernel → Agent Framework migration guide.
Is AutoGen enough?Same answer — Agent Framework is the AutoGen successor too. AutoGen → Agent Framework migration guide.
Is Agent Framework production-ready?Yes. It's the framework Microsoft positions for hosted agents on Foundry Agent Service. See Foundry Hosted Agents.
Can the same Agent Framework code run on laptop?Yes — Agent Framework is open-source and runs anywhere Python or .NET runs. The only thing that changes between substrates is which APEX-Core protocol implementations get injected (mocks on laptop, real Microsoft SDKs on Foundry). See Deploy UX and Substrates.

14A.4 n8n's Role — Workflow, Not Agent Orchestration

The most common confusion. n8n is documented in Deployment Guide §2.6 and Chapter 15 (this book) as the laptop-substrate workflow runtime. Its role on laptop is identical to Power Automate / Logic Apps Hybrid / Foundry workflows on cloud:

  • Run a trigger when an event arrives
  • Route the event through a branch / parallel / HITL stage / LEDGER emit (the seven §14.2 primitives)
  • Make agent calls — but the orchestration of how agents coordinate inside that call is Microsoft Agent Framework's responsibility, not n8n's

n8n is intentionally not used for agent-to-agent coordination. When the cold-chain scenario has The Pricer reading Demand Checker's output and Finance Lead's elasticity opinion in parallel, that coordination happens inside Microsoft Agent Framework's Magentic workflow — not in an n8n graph. n8n's node for the agent call simply POSTs to the agent fleet endpoint and waits for the workflow's response.

Anti-pattern — orchestrating agents in n8n

It is technically possible to write per-agent n8n nodes and chain them in n8n. Do not do this. n8n graphs are not type-safe, lack agent-runtime state management, and can't model the 5 canonical patterns (especially Magentic and Group Chat) cleanly. Agent orchestration belongs in Microsoft Agent Framework code that the n8n agent-call node invokes. See ADR-006.

14A.5 Foundry Workflows — The Cloud Substrate Equivalent

On the cloud substrate, APEX-M can use either Microsoft Agent Framework code OR Foundry Agent Service Workflows — declarative YAML or visual designer in the Foundry portal — to coordinate agents. The choice:

Microsoft Agent Framework (code)Foundry Workflows (visual / YAML)
DeterminismFull deterministic control"Primarily nondeterministic" per Microsoft Learn
CustomizationCode path arbitraryBranching + HITL + sequential / group chat
MaintenanceEngineering team ownsLower-skill operators can edit visually
APEX-M defaultYes (via Foundry Hosted Agents)Optional: use when scenario benefits from visual editing

For RC-E2E-03 (deterministic, audit-required, KPI-attributed), Microsoft Agent Framework is the right choice — APEX uses Foundry's hosted-agent hosting model with Agent Framework code inside. Foundry workflows are reserved for use cases where engagement teams need to edit the orchestration without re-deploying agent code.

14A.6 Worked Example — RC-E2E-03 Cold-Chain Excursion

Mapping the canonical Services Guide §18.1 example through the three layers:

RC-E2E-03 cold-chain excursion · three orchestration layers
Layer 1: scenario workflow pattern
  → Triage-and-decide (per §14.1.1)
  Eventstream Activator fires excursion event → orchestrator dispatches
  agent fleet → HITL gate at decide step → audit row → KPI rollup

Layer 2: agent orchestration archetype (Microsoft Agent Framework)
  → Magentic
  The Analyst is the manager agent. It dynamically dispatches:
    - The Demand Checker  (forward-demand impact)
    - The Pricer          (per-SKU markdown proposal with sim P&L)
    - The Finance Lead    (margin-at-risk scoring)
    - The Operations Lead (HITL Adaptive Card synthesis)
    - The Briefer         (audit-row narrative)
  Order is not predetermined; The Analyst decides who runs based on
  the excursion's classification. HITL gate fires when proposed
  markdown > 30% (per use-case hitl_thresholds).

Layer 3: workflow runtime substrate
  → laptop:  n8n         (per Chapter 15)
  → cloud:   Eventstream + Activator destination + Foundry workflow
              (per Deployment Guide §2.6.2)
  The same workflow primitives (§14.2) render in both — different
  JSON dialect, identical contract.

The three layers are explicit in the use case YAML — see the orchestration_archetype field in services/_use-case.schema.md and the populated example at services/rc/RC-E2E-03/use-cases/_default/use-case.yaml.

14A.7 Per-RC-Service Archetype Assignment

First-iteration RC-only assignment, validated against the Services Guide §18 service profiles:

ServiceScenario workflow (§14.1)Agent orchestration (§14A.2)Why
RC-E2E-03 (Pricing)Triage-and-decideMagenticThe Analyst dynamically picks specialists based on excursion class
RC-E2E-04 (Loyalty)Continuous-optimizationSequentialScore → offer-design → finance → ops · linear approval chain
RC-E2E-05 (OSA)Triage-and-decideSequentialGap-detect → priority-score → task-dispatch · simple linear
RC-E2E-07 (Returns Fraud)Detect-and-attributeConcurrent + HITLPattern-match across customer/payment/device graphs in parallel
RC-E2E-09 (Product Tracking)Detect-and-attribute + Periodic-digestHandoffCompliance officer hands off to specialist sub-agents per FSMA-204 lot class
Best Practice — pick archetype during use-case design

The use-case YAML's orchestration_archetype field must be set when authoring a new use case. The wizard validates it's one of the five canonical patterns. Engagements that need a sixth pattern raise an ADR (per adr/) — extending the archetype list is a framework decision, not a per-engagement decision.

14A.8 The APEX-M Agent Framework Loader · Bridge Between APEX Artifacts and Microsoft Agent Framework

Microsoft Agent Framework is APEX's intended A2A platform — the runtime where ChatAgents are defined, orchestrated through the five canonical patterns (§14A.2), and exposed to peer agents over the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol described in §31.4. The bridge between APEX's authoring artifacts (per-agent agent.yaml · prompts/*.md · MCP tool catalog · HITL config) and the SDK is the APEX-M Agent Framework Loader — module apex_m.agent_framework_loader, validated end-to-end at Sprint 42.

The Loader exists for one reason: to make sure that what an engagement architect authors (a directory of YAML and Markdown files) is what Microsoft Agent Framework runs — verbatim, with no impedance mismatch and no hand-translation step in the middle. It is the answer to the question "is the Microsoft Agent Framework going to work with the agents being created" — provable today via the Sprint 42 architecture-validation suite.

14A.8.1 What the Loader Binds

The Loader is an adapter layer per ADR-006. It reads APEX-side authoring artifacts and constructs Microsoft Agent Framework runtime objects with no impedance mismatch — APEX's pattern names (Sequential · Concurrent · Handoff · Group Chat · Magentic) are deliberately verbatim with the released Microsoft Agent Framework builder classes (SequentialBuilder · ConcurrentBuilder · HandoffBuilder · GroupChatBuilder · MagenticBuilder).

APEX-side artifactMicrosoft Agent Framework bindingPurpose
agent.yaml per agentChatAgent instance · model · capabilitiesOne agent definition → one ChatAgent
prompts/*.mdSystem-prompt body of the ChatAgentAuthored as Markdown for review · injected at construction
MCP tools (e.g. rc_e2e_03_mcp)FunctionTool instances via @function_toolEach MCP tool becomes a discoverable function on the agent
canonical_pattern in use-case YAMLOne of SequentialBuilder · ConcurrentBuilder · HandoffBuilder · GroupChatBuilder · MagenticBuilder (Python) / equivalent fluent builder (.NET)Five-pattern dispatcher selects the builder class verbatim
hitl_gate: true + hitl_personahuman_input_request primitive in the workflow graphAdaptive Card → Microsoft Teams persona → resume token
Three-version stamp (manifest · policy · prompt)ApexAuditMiddleware wrapping every invocationPer BL.P.79 — every agent call hash-chained to the LEDGER
Tier-3 PII unlock (Microsoft.KeyVault dual-control)Pre-invocation guard wired into middlewareJIT pii-unlock identity asserted before the model sees PHI

14A.8.2 Lazy Import — The Same Code Runs With or Without the SDK

The Loader imports agent_framework as a lazy / optional dependency in apex-m's runtime extras. This is the substrate-awareness mechanism for the laptop-vs-cloud parity (Ch 1, §14A.3):

apex_m/agent_framework_loader.py · lazy SDK detection (verbatim sketch)
try:
    import agent_framework as _af
    from agent_framework.tools import function_tool as _function_tool
    from agent_framework.workflows import (
        SequentialBuilder, ConcurrentBuilder, HandoffBuilder,
        GroupChatBuilder, MagenticBuilder,
    )
    _BUILDERS = {
        "sequential": SequentialBuilder,
        "concurrent": ConcurrentBuilder,
        "handoff":    HandoffBuilder,
        "group_chat": GroupChatBuilder,
        "magentic":   MagenticBuilder,
    }
    _HAS_AGENT_FRAMEWORK = True
except ImportError:                       # default laptop / test path
    _af = None
    _function_tool = None
    _BUILDERS = {}
    _HAS_AGENT_FRAMEWORK = False


def has_agent_framework() -> bool:
    """Return True if Microsoft Agent Framework SDK is importable."""
    return _HAS_AGENT_FRAMEWORK
  • SDK absent (default Sprint-1 laptop · CI test runners) — build_workflow() returns a WorkflowSpec dataclass capturing every input the SDK would have consumed; the pattern dispatcher returns the name of the builder class (e.g. "MagenticBuilder") instead of instantiating it. The harness asserts the spec.
  • SDK installed (Lab v0.1+ tenant · Foundry hosted agents · Sprint 42 onward) — the same call paths instantiate the real Microsoft Agent Framework builder (SequentialBuilder, ConcurrentBuilder, HandoffBuilder, GroupChatBuilder, MagenticBuilder) and return a live WorkflowAgent. No code changes; one config flag (the runtime extra is installed in the apex-m container image).
Best Practice — author once, run on either substrate

The Loader's lazy-import dual mode is the operational expression of Ch 1's substrate-parity claim. Engagement teams author agent.yaml + prompts/ + use-case YAML, and ship to both Docker-Desktop laptop (no Microsoft Agent Framework dep) and Microsoft.App/managedEnvironments → Foundry-hosted-agent prod (real Agent Framework runtime) without code branches. Validation came from Sprint 42's architecture-validation suite — see commit 0e8b8e4 feat(apex-m): Agent Framework loader (Sprint 42 architecture validation).

Microsoft Agent Framework SDK — current API surface

Per Microsoft Learn, the Python SDK exposes one builder class per pattern: SequentialBuilder, ConcurrentBuilder, HandoffBuilder, GroupChatBuilder, MagenticBuilder. Each is instantiated as a fluent builder (.participants(...).manager(...).build()) returning a WorkflowAgent. The .NET SDK exposes the same five concepts via the Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows namespace with equivalent fluent APIs. Older Microsoft drafts referenced an AgentWorkflowBuilder.Build* static-method API; that shape did not ship — the per-builder-class form is the released surface. APEX code calls the per-builder-class form; pseudo-code in this guide reflects the released API.

14A.8.3 Why the Loader Is the A2A Platform Anchor

A2A (§31.4) is the open agent-to-agent protocol published under the A2A specification. Microsoft Agent Framework is the canonical Microsoft implementation: it ships ASP.NET Core hosting (Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.A2A.AspNetCore) that exposes any Agent Framework agent at /.well-known/agent-card.json, and an A2AAgent client that wraps remote A2A endpoints as standard AIAgents. APEX inherits both directions through the Loader:

  • Inbound A2A — APEX agent as an A2A server. Loader-built workflows are WorkflowAgent instances. Mounting them under MapA2A on the apex-m host publishes the agent card and the HTTP+JSON binding automatically — peer agents (other APEX Services in the same tenant · Microsoft 365 Copilot extensions · third-party agents) discover and invoke them with no extra plumbing.
  • Outbound A2A — APEX agent calling another agent. The Loader registers A2AAgent wrappers as tools on the calling agent. The Pricer-→-Demand Checker collaboration in §14A.6 is a Loader-instantiated A2A call when the two agents run in separate processes; it collapses to in-process function-tool calls when they share a process. Same authoring artifact, different binding — the engagement architect does not write A2A glue code.
  • Cross-Service composition. RC-E2E-03's Pricing Agent invoking RC-E2E-09's Lot Provenance agent (per §17.4) is an A2A call across Service boundaries within the same Microsoft Entra tenant. The Loader inserts an Entra ID claim check in ApexAuditMiddleware; the call fails before leaving the calling agent's process if the claim does not satisfy the per-Service authorization.
  • ADR-025-01 binding — within-tenant only. Cross-tenant A2A is forbidden (§31.4). Within-tenant A2A is the only path the Loader binds. The protocol is capable of more; the policy is the binding.
Independence — what's running in whose tenant

The Loader is APEX framework code. It runs in the client tenant per the two-contract Independence model — client ↔ Microsoft for the platform, client ↔ Deloitte for the Service-delivery engagement. Microsoft Agent Framework is open-source Microsoft software; the client (or, on the client's behalf, the engagement team) installs it as a runtime dep of apex-m on Foundry hosted agents. A2A traffic crosses agent boundaries within the client's Microsoft Entra tenant only — never between Deloitte and the client, never between two client tenants. This volume documents how the Loader builds the bridge; the Sellers Guide describes the commercial envelope; the Deployment Guide describes the platform on which it runs.

14A.8.4 The Five-Pattern Dispatcher

The dispatcher is the heart of the Loader. It is a verbatim mapping — APEX pattern name → Agent Framework builder method — with no transformation:

apex_m/agent_framework_loader.py · pattern dispatcher (verbatim per ADR-006)
def dispatch_to_builder(spec: WorkflowSpec, *, agents=None):
    """Route a WorkflowSpec to the Microsoft Agent Framework builder.

    APEX pattern names map 1:1 to the released Microsoft Agent Framework
    builder classes — the mapping is verbatim, no impedance mismatch:

      sequential  → SequentialBuilder().participants(agents).build()
      concurrent  → ConcurrentBuilder().participants(agents).build()
      handoff     → HandoffBuilder().participants(agents).build()
      group_chat  → GroupChatBuilder().participants(agents).manager(m).build()
      magentic    → MagenticBuilder().participants(agents).manager(m).build()
    """

Every reference in this book to "the Magentic pattern" or "the Sequential pattern" resolves, at runtime, to the corresponding *Builder class on the live Microsoft Agent Framework SDK (Python) — instantiated and built by dispatch_to_builder() with the agent list assembled by load_use_case_workflow(). The .NET SDK exposes equivalent fluent builders in the Microsoft.Agents.AI.Workflows namespace. There is no separate APEX agent-orchestrator implementation. APEX uses Microsoft Agent Framework; it does not replace it.

14A.8.5 Reading the Loader Source

Engagement architects who want to see the bindings end-to-end should read these files in order:

  1. apex-m/src/apex_m/agent_framework_loader.py — the Loader module. Module docstring mirrors this section. Contains AgentSpec, WorkflowSpec, load_agent_spec(), load_use_case_workflow(), dispatch_to_builder(), wrap_mcp_tool(), ApexAuditMiddleware, and build_workflow().
  2. apex-m/tests/test_agent_framework_loader.py — the Sprint 42 architecture-validation suite. Covers the lazy-mode path (no SDK) and the SDK-installed path. This test is the proof that Microsoft Agent Framework does work with the agents being created.
  3. services/rc/RC-E2E-03/use-cases/_default/use-case.yaml — populated example: orchestration_archetype: magentic + per-agent metadata that the Loader reads.
  4. ADR-006 — the architecture decision record that fixes Microsoft Agent Framework as the canonical orchestrator and the verbatim-name mapping rule.

Key Takeaways

  • Three layers of orchestration: scenario workflow pattern (§14) · agent orchestration archetype (this chapter) · workflow runtime substrate (§15 / Foundry workflows / Logic Apps Hybrid).
  • Microsoft Agent Framework is the canonical agent orchestrator — successor to Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. Five built-in patterns: Sequential, Concurrent, Handoff, Group Chat, Magentic.
  • Same Agent Framework code runs on laptop (Docker Desktop) and Foundry hosted agents (Azure prod) — substrate-awareness is env-var-driven.
  • n8n is the laptop workflow runtime, not an agent orchestrator. n8n calls into Agent Framework code; it does not replace it.
  • Semantic Kernel is now legacy; existing code stays valid, new code uses Agent Framework.
  • Per-service archetype assignment lives in the use case YAML's orchestration_archetype field.
  • The APEX-M Agent Framework Loader (§14A.8) is the verbatim bridge from APEX authoring artifacts (agent.yaml · prompts/*.md · MCP tools · HITL config) to Microsoft Agent Framework SDK objects (ChatAgent · FunctionTool · AgentWorkflowBuilder). Lazy-import dual mode means the same code runs with or without the SDK present.
  • Microsoft Agent Framework is the intended A2A platform; the Loader inherits both inbound (MapA2A) and outbound (A2AAgent) bindings. Cross-tenant A2A is forbidden by ADR-025-01.
Chapter 14B

Microsoft Agent Framework — Deep Dive

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the SDK's pipeline architecture (agent middleware · context · chat client) and the core types (ChatClientAgent · Agent · WorkflowAgent) so you can read Agent Framework code without translation.
  • Drills the five canonical workflow patterns with code-shape sketches, when-to-use guidance, and the APEX archetype each maps to.
  • Inventories the extension points (function tools · MCP tools · middleware · context providers · A2A · Foundry provider · observability) APEX-M wires together.
  • Gives engagement architects a single chapter to hand a new joiner who needs to be productive in Agent Framework within a day.
90-second read
  • Architecture. Agent → Agent middleware layer → Context layer → Chat client (with its own middleware) → model. Three concentric layers; each is independently composable; telemetry rides on every one.
  • Core types. ChatClientAgent (.NET) / Agent (Python) wrap an IChatClient; per-pattern builders (SequentialBuilder, ConcurrentBuilder, HandoffBuilder, GroupChatBuilder, MagenticBuilder) compose multiple agents; WorkflowAgent wraps a workflow as an agent.
  • Five patterns (§14A.2 / §14B.4): Sequential · Concurrent · Handoff · Group Chat · Magentic. All five support human-in-the-loop via approval-required tools and request/response.
  • Tools. @function_tool for inline tools · FunctionTool wrappers · MCPStdioTool/MCPStreamableHTTPTool/MCPWebsocketTool for MCP · hosted MCP via Foundry toolboxes.
  • A2A ships in-box (Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.A2A.AspNetCore · Microsoft.Agents.AI.A2A) so any Agent Framework agent is publishable and any A2A endpoint is consumable as an AIAgent.
  • Microsoft Foundry is the recommended runtime: FoundryChatClient / FoundryAgent for inference; Foundry hosted agents for managed deployment with platform-injected env vars.
  • Observability is OpenTelemetry-native with GenAI semantic conventions; zero-code setup via env vars in apex-m container images.
Plain-English primer — the orchestra analogy

Imagine an orchestra. There's a conductor, a group of musicians (each specialized — violin, percussion, brass, woodwinds), sheet music that defines what each plays, and different styles of conducting — a string quartet's tight chamber piece is conducted differently than a symphony's grand finale.

That's Microsoft Agent Framework.

  • The musicians = the individual AI agents. The Pricer, the Demand Checker, the Finance Lead — each specialized for one thing. In Agent Framework code, each musician is a ChatClientAgent.
  • The sheet music = the prompts and tool definitions. What this agent does, what tools it can use, what it cares about.
  • The conductor = the workflow pattern. Agent Framework gives you five conducting styles — Sequential (musicians play one after another), Concurrent (all play at once), Handoff (lead passes from one to another), Group Chat (musicians improvise together listening to each other), Magentic (a lead musician dynamically calls in the rest based on what the music is doing).
  • The score book = the Loader. APEX-M's Agent Framework Loader is what reads the per-Service YAML files and assembles the right musicians with the right sheet music and chooses the right conducting style — all from configuration, not code changes.

Why this matters: before Microsoft Agent Framework, every multi-agent system was a custom orchestra — different musicians, different unspoken conventions, different sheet-music notation, no consistent way to swap one in for another. Microsoft Agent Framework standardizes the whole musical tradition. A musician (an agent) from one orchestra (one Service) can join another. A conductor (a workflow pattern) can be reused across pieces. The same sheet music format works across .NET and Python orchestras.

The rest of this chapter walks each piece in detail: §14B.1 explains how every musician's instrument is wired (the three-layer pipeline) · §14B.2 introduces the core musician types · §14B.3 walks each conducting style · §14B.4 covers the toolkit (tools and instruments) · §14B.5–7 cover the practical concerns (middleware · context · streaming) · §14B.8 covers how musicians from different orchestras talk (A2A) · §14B.9 covers the concert hall (Foundry) · the rest covers operations.

14B.1 The Three-Layer Pipeline

Per the Agent Framework pipeline architecture, every agent invocation flows through three concentric layers. APEX-M and the Agent Framework Loader (§14A.8) attach behavior at each layer:

LayerConcernAPEX-M binding
Agent middlewareWraps RunAsync / run(). Inspects/modifies inputs and outputs. Independent of agent type — same middleware works on ChatClientAgent, A2AAgent, FoundryAgent.ApexAuditMiddleware emits a hash-chained LEDGER row per invocation; ApexHITLMiddleware intercepts when hitl_gate: true; PII-unlock guard runs here for Tier-3.
ContextBuilds the message history before each LLM call. ChatHistoryProvider (single) + AIContextProviders (list of memory / RAG providers).APEX wires Microsoft.Cache/Redis as the working/episodic store via a custom RedisContextProvider; Year-2 LEDGER few-shot exemplars (§28.4) inject as a separate provider.
Chat clientThe IChatClient (or Python ChatClient). Has its own middleware chain — function-invocation telemetry, retry, content filtering, OpenTelemetry instrumentation.APEX uses FoundryChatClient (Microsoft Foundry) by default; AzureOpenAIChatClient for direct Azure OpenAI; the Cost-envelope router picks model deployment per agent.

The benefit of the three-layer split is composability: agent middleware works against the abstract AIAgent contract (so the same logic wraps a ChatClientAgent, an A2AAgent, or a workflow), while chat-client middleware can encode model-specific concerns (rate limits, sensitive-data redaction) without polluting agent code.

14B.2 Core Types — ChatClientAgent / Agent / WorkflowAgent

14B.2.1 ChatClientAgent (.NET)

The .NET workhorse. Wraps an IChatClient (from Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Abstractions) and adds agent semantics — a name, instructions (system prompt), and a tool list:

.NET — minimal ChatClientAgent
using Microsoft.Extensions.AI;
using Microsoft.Agents.AI;

var agent = new ChatClientAgent(
    chatClient: foundryClient,                 // IChatClient
    name: "ThePricingAgent",
    instructions: "You generate markdown proposals for cold-chain excursions...",
    tools: [
        AIFunctionFactory.Create(McpTools.GetExcursionDecisionPanel),
        AIFunctionFactory.Create(McpTools.SimulatePricingScenario),
    ]
).WithOpenTelemetry(sourceName: "apex.rc-e2e-03");

14B.2.2 Agent (Python)

The Python equivalent. Same shape, idiomatic Python:

Python — minimal Agent
from agent_framework import Agent
from agent_framework.foundry import FoundryChatClient

agent = Agent(
    client=FoundryChatClient(),
    name="ThePricingAgent",
    instructions="You generate markdown proposals for cold-chain excursions...",
    tools=[mcp_get_excursion_panel, mcp_simulate_pricing],
    middleware=[ApexAuditMiddleware(agent_spec)],
)

14B.2.3 WorkflowAgent — A Workflow Wearing the Agent Interface

The composition primitive. Per workflows-as-agents, any built workflow can be wrapped as an AIAgent so other agents call it as a tool, A2A clients invoke it over HTTP, and consumers do not need to know they are talking to a workflow:

Python — RC-E2E-03 Magentic workflow exposed as an agent
from agent_framework.workflows import MagenticBuilder

workflow = (
    MagenticBuilder()
        .participants(the_pricer, the_demand_checker, the_finance_lead)
        .manager(the_analyst)
        .build()
)

# Wrap as an agent — now it has .run() and .run_streaming() like any AIAgent
rc_e2e_03_agent = workflow.as_agent(
    name="RC-E2E-03 cold-chain decision",
    description="Decide markdown action for a cold-chain excursion event.",
)

14B.3 The Five Workflow Patterns — Detail

14B.3.1 Sequential — Pipeline

SequentialBuilder().participants(agents).build(). Each agent passes its output to the next. APEX maps RC-E2E-04 (Loyalty: score → offer-design → finance → ops) and RC-E2E-05 (OSA: gap-detect → priority-score → task-dispatch).

14B.3.2 Concurrent — Parallel Fan-Out

ConcurrentBuilder().participants(agents).build(). Agents run in parallel; outputs aggregate. APEX uses for RC-E2E-07 (Returns Fraud) — pattern-match across customer / payment / device graphs simultaneously, then HITL.

14B.3.3 Handoff — Routing to Specialist

HandoffBuilder().router(r).targets({...}).build(). Control transfers based on context. APEX uses for RC-E2E-09 (Product Tracking / FSMA-204 lots) — a compliance-officer agent hands off to a per-lot-class specialist (refrigerated · pharmaceutical · produce).

14B.3.4 Group Chat — Iterative Collaboration

GroupChatBuilder().participants(agents).manager(m).build(). Multiple rounds; orchestrator broadcasts each turn so all agents see the full conversation. Per group-chat docs, agents do not share session instances — the orchestrator synchronises context per turn. Useful for clinical-review-style collaborative reasoning (HLS-E2E-04 prior-auth).

14B.3.5 Magentic — Manager-Led Plan with Dynamic Dispatch

MagenticBuilder().participants(specialists).manager(m).build(). Inspired by Magentic-One. The manager (in APEX: The Analyst) builds a plan, dispatches specialists, tracks progress in a shared ledger, replans on failure. APEX maps RC-E2E-03 (cold-chain) to Magentic — see §14A.6. Magentic also supports human-in-the-loop plan review (the human can edit the manager's plan before dispatch).

Note — Magentic and language parity

As of the current Agent Framework preview, Magentic is fully implemented in Python; the C# implementation is in development. APEX-M's RC-E2E-03 reference implementation is Python; .NET engagements that need Magentic should track the Agent Framework roadmap — Swarm and SelectorGroupChat are also coming.

14B.4 Tools — Function Tools, MCP Tools, Hosted MCP

14B.4.1 Function Tools — @function_tool / AIFunctionFactory

Inline tools. Decorator-based; schema is generated automatically from type hints + Pydantic Field descriptions:

Python — function tool with auto-generated schema
from agent_framework import tool
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import Field

@tool
def stage_markdown_approval(
    sku_id: Annotated[str, Field(description="The SKU to mark down")],
    proposed_pct: Annotated[float, Field(description="Percent off, 0.0–1.0")],
) -> dict:
    """Stage a markdown proposal for HITL approval."""
    ...

.NET equivalent: AIFunctionFactory.Create(MyMethod). The [Description] attribute on parameters drives schema generation.

14B.4.2 MCP Tools — Three Connection Types

Per local MCP tools:

TypeWhenAPEX use
MCPStdioToolLocal subprocess; e.g., uvx mcp-server-calculatorLaptop dev — APEX MCP servers run as subprocesses in docker-compose with stdio
MCPStreamableHTTPToolRemote HTTP/SSE endpointProduction — APEX MCP host on Container Apps, called over private endpoint
MCPWebsocketToolWebSocket transportReserved for streaming-tool scenarios (rare)

14B.4.3 Hosted MCP — Foundry Toolboxes

Per hosted MCP tools, Foundry can host MCP servers itself and expose them as toolboxes — named, versioned server-side tool collections reusable across agents. Tool-approval workflows pause execution for human review before invocation. APEX uses Foundry-hosted MCP for the Tier-3 PII-unlock dual-control path: the agent must request the tool · approver approves out-of-band · then Foundry permits the call.

14B.4.4 Agent-as-Tool — Hierarchical Architecture

Any agent can be exposed as a tool on another agent via .as_tool() (Python) / .AsAIFunction() (.NET). This composition pattern is how the Operations Lead invokes The Pricer's full reasoning as a single function call rather than via raw A2A — the abstraction is the same, the binding is in-process.

14B.5 Middleware — Cross-Cutting Concerns

Middleware solves the problems that recur across every agent invocation regardless of role: logging, guardrails, retry, telemetry, auth checks, error handling, shared state. Per adding middleware, function-based or class-based:

Python — function-based middleware
async def apex_audit_middleware(context, next):
    """Emit LEDGER row before/after invocation; hash-chain to prior."""
    pre_hash = ledger.tip_hash()
    context["apex_pre_hash"] = pre_hash
    result = await next(context)
    ledger.emit(
        kind="agent.invocation",
        agent_id=context.agent.name,
        prev_hash=pre_hash,
        result_summary=summarise(result),
        manifest_version=context["manifest_version"],
        policy_version=context["policy_version"],
        prompt_version=context["prompt_version"],
    )
    return result

agent = Agent(client=client, instructions=..., middleware=[apex_audit_middleware])

APEX-M ships three middleware classes:

  • ApexAuditMiddleware — three-version stamp (manifest · policy · prompt per BL.P.79) + LEDGER hash-chain. Wraps every ChatClientAgent built by the Loader.
  • ApexHITLMiddleware — when the agent's agent.yaml declares hitl_gate: true, this middleware translates the agent's proposed action into a Microsoft Teams adaptive card and pauses execution via human_input_request until the persona approves or rejects.
  • ApexClassificationGuard — runs before the LLM call. If the request would touch Tier-3 PII without an active pii-unlock identity claim, raises PIIUnlockRequiredError and emits a LEDGER warning row.

14B.6 Context Providers — History, Memory, Retrieval

The context layer runs before each LLM call to assemble the full message history and inject additional context. ChatHistoryProvider (single) manages conversation history; AIContextProviders (list) inject memories, retrieved documents, dynamic instructions.

APEX wires three context providers per agent:

  • RedisHistoryProvider — implements ChatHistoryProvider over Microsoft.Cache/Redis Premium (§25.3). Per-thread keys; TTL = use-case-specific (typically 24h for working memory).
  • LedgerExemplarProvider — Year-2 maturation arc (§28.4). Pulls k-nearest historical decisions from the LEDGER (semantic-similarity over the request embedding) and injects them as few-shot exemplars.
  • PolicyContextProvider — injects the current policy-version's "constraints you must respect" block at the top of every system-prompt assembly.

14B.7 Streaming, Background Responses, Checkpointing

  • Streaming. RunStreamingAsync / run_streaming() yield update chunks. Both clients and agents emit the same shape — read chunk.text in either case. APEX uses streaming for the Briefer agent's narrative output to Microsoft Teams (operator sees the digest assemble live).
  • Background responses. Long-running agent calls (mins to hours) return a continuation token instead of an immediate response. The client polls or reconnects. A2A agents support reconnection from the start of a stream (not arbitrary resume). APEX uses background responses for the Magentic plan-execution path on RC-E2E-09 lot-trace investigations.
  • Checkpointing. Workflows can snapshot state (magentic_checkpoint sample) so a multi-hour reasoning chain can resume after a Container App restart. APEX persists checkpoints to Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts (blob) under per-Service containers.

14B.8 A2A — Hosting and Discovery

Three discovery strategies per A2A Agent docs:

StrategyHowAPEX use
Well-Known URIhttps://{host}/.well-known/agent-card.json resolved by A2ACardResolverCross-Service discovery within a tenant — RC-E2E-03 finding RC-E2E-09's Lot Provenance agent
Catalog-basedAgent card retrieved from a registry; convert with AgentCard.AsAIAgent()APEX MCP catalog (Ch 13) doubles as an A2A agent registry; per-tenant scope
Direct configurationA2AClient(uri).AsAIAgent()Tightly coupled in-tenant agents; e.g., the Pricer always knowing where the Demand Checker lives

Hosting: Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.A2A.AspNetCore exposes any agent over HTTP+JSON or JSON-RPC bindings (HTTP+JSON is the default). Mount under app.MapA2A("/a2a/{agent-name}"). APEX-M's FastAPI variant mirrors this with the a2a-sdk Starlette server and A2AExecutor adapter.

14B.9 Microsoft Foundry Provider — FoundryChatClient and FoundryAgent

Microsoft Foundry is APEX's intended inference plane (§31.6). The Agent Framework Foundry provider gives two integration shapes:

  • FoundryChatClient — an IChatClient bound to a Foundry project + model deployment. APEX agents construct ChatClientAgents over this for the regular pipeline.
  • FoundryAgent — a service-managed agent persisted server-side in Foundry, with conversation state managed by Foundry. Used when APEX needs Foundry's hosted-MCP, hosted-grounding, or persistent-session features.

Configuration is two env vars: FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT and AZURE_AI_MODEL_DEPLOYMENT_NAME. Identity flows via DefaultAzureCredential in dev and ManagedIdentityCredential in production (per Microsoft guidance — see §14B.11).

14B.9.1 Foundry Connected Agents and Computer Use

Two newer Foundry Agent Service capabilities round out the hosted-agent surface area. APEX-M positions each one against an existing Agent Framework pattern so engagement teams know which to pick.

CapabilityWhat it isAPEX-M use vs alternatives
Connected AgentsFoundry-hosted agent-to-agent delegation. A Foundry agent invokes another Foundry agent as a tool, with Foundry managing the call, the session, and the identity exchange — no Agent Framework workflow code required.Use Connected Agents when both agents are Foundry-hosted and the relationship is a simple "Agent A calls Agent B for one task, then continues." Use an Agent Framework Handoff or Magentic workflow when the coordination is many-step, requires shared context, or needs HITL — those constructs give richer control than Connected Agents.
Computer UseAgent-controlled browser and desktop actions — the agent can read a page, click, type, and follow a workflow on a virtual machine that Foundry manages.The escape hatch for legacy SaaS that has no API. APEX-M uses Computer Use sparingly — every Computer Use call is a fragile non-deterministic action and lands in the LEDGER with elevated review. Prefer an MCP tool against a real API; fall back to Computer Use only when no other surface exists.
Best Practice — code-side workflows are the default, Foundry-side shortcuts are situational

APEX-M's default is Microsoft Agent Framework code-side workflow patterns (Sequential / Concurrent / Handoff / Group Chat / Magentic). They are unit-testable, version-controlled, locally runnable, and the Loader binds them verbatim. Foundry Connected Agents and Computer Use are shortcuts for two specific situations (zero-code agent-to-agent delegation; legacy-SaaS-without-API). Don't reach for them as a first move — they trade off testability and observability for setup speed. The Sellers Guide commercial envelope (Ch 12) is more comfortable with code-side patterns for the same reason: a Service whose entire coordination is in Foundry config is harder to audit and harder to scope.

14B.10 Observability — OpenTelemetry + GenAI Semantic Conventions

Per Agent observability, instrumentation is OpenTelemetry-native and follows GenAI semantic conventions. Two configuration modes:

  • Zero-code setup. Set env vars (OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT · OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES · APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING) and instrumentation activates automatically. APEX-M's Container Apps revisions set these from Bicep — no application code change required.
  • Manual configuration. Programmatic setup with custom processors, samplers, exporters. .WithOpenTelemetry(sourceName: "...", configure: cfg => cfg.EnableSensitiveData = true) on the agent or chat client.
Warning — sensitive data in spans

EnableSensitiveData = true captures prompts, responses, function-call arguments, and results in OTel spans. Only enable in development or testing. APEX production environments leave it off; LEDGER carries the audit trail with proper PII tier handling instead.

14B.11 .NET vs Python Parity

Agent Framework targets feature parity across .NET and Python. Differences as of the current preview:

Feature.NETPythonAPEX choice
Sequential / Concurrent / Handoff / Group Chat✓✓Either — match the engagement's stack
MagenticIn development✓Python for engagements that require Magentic today
A2A hostingASP.NET Core (Microsoft.Agents.AI.Hosting.A2A.AspNetCore)Starlette/ASGI via a2a-sdk + A2AExecutorEither; APEX-M Python is the reference
Foundry providerMicrosoft.Agents.AI.Foundryagent_framework.foundryEither
MCP — three transports✓✓ (mcp --pre required)Either
Function tools — auto schemaAIFunctionFactory.Create@tool + Pydantic FieldEither

APEX-M chooses Python as its reference language because the Sprint 32-34 use-case work delivers Python MCP tools, Python YAML loaders, and Python pytest harnesses. .NET-shop engagements can run a parallel apex-m.NET project; the Loader contract, agent.yaml schema, and ADR-006 verbatim-mapping rule are language-neutral.

14B.12 Migration — Semantic Kernel and AutoGen

Per the Semantic Kernel migration guide and AutoGen migration guide:

  • From Semantic Kernel: namespace migration from Microsoft.SemanticKernel.Agents → Microsoft.Agents.AI. Message types unify under Microsoft.Extensions.AI.ChatMessage with Role enum (replaces SK's AuthorRole). Plugins → tools (function tools or MCP). Existing SK code stays valid; new code uses Agent Framework.
  • From AutoGen: the dual-model split (low-level autogen-core + high-level Team) collapses to one Workflow abstraction. Team's GraphFlow (control-flow) → Agent Framework's data-flow Workflow with typed edges and concurrent execution. FunctionTool usage simplifies via @tool. Magentic ports cleanly.
  • For APEX: APEX has no Semantic Kernel or AutoGen legacy in the apex-m line — Sprint 32-34 was authored against Agent Framework directly. The migration guides are for engagement teams with prior SK/AutoGen code being onboarded into APEX-accelerated delivery.

14B.13 What Moved From n8n / Logic Apps Into Microsoft Agent Framework

Architectural shift summary — APEX-M iterations through Sprint 32 had n8n and Logic Apps Hybrid composing multi-agent flows directly (parallel branches per agent · IF nodes routing on agent output · merge nodes aggregating). Since Microsoft Agent Framework GA, that work moved into Agent Framework. The substrate retained only what it does best — trigger handling and external-integration routing. The migration:

Old (substrate-side · n8n / Logic Apps)New (Agent Framework-side)Rationale
Per-agent HTTP nodes (one node per agent in fleet)One HTTP POST to the agent fleet · WorkflowAgent.run() dispatches to all agents internallySubstrate can't model dynamic replanning · type-safe message passing · plan tracking
n8n / Logic Apps parallel branches for concurrent agent callsConcurrentBuilder().participants(agents).build()Concurrency primitive is built-in · shared context provider across branches · aggregation is automatic
IF / Switch nodes routing on agent outputHandoffBuilder().participants(agents).build() · context-driven routingHand-off is a recognized AI orchestration pattern with semantic conventions in Agent Framework · n8n's IF was a leaky abstraction over it
Linear "call A → call B → call C" workflow chains across multiple n8n nodesSequentialBuilder().participants(agents).build()Sequential composition is the simplest case · single node in substrate · multi-agent semantics inside
Manual round-robin loops or stop-condition logic in n8nGroupChatBuilder().participants(agents).manager(m).build() · iterative collaboration with full conversation historyGroup-chat coordination requires shared context · n8n cannot synchronize agent context per turn
Bespoke "plan and dispatch" logic in custom n8n code nodes (the most painful pattern)MagenticBuilder().participants(specialists).manager(m).build()Magentic is the canonical "manager-led plan with dynamic dispatch" pattern · the manager replans on each result · n8n cannot do this
n8n's "Wait For Webhook" + manual approval flowhuman_input_request primitive · wired by ApexHITLMiddlewareHITL is part of the agent workflow's typed contract · resume tokens flow through Foundry sessions · Teams adaptive card delivery is a substrate concern
n8n "set variable" nodes preserving state across agent callsAgent Framework's AIContextProviders · session-based state in Foundry hosted agentsContext providers run inside the agent's pipeline · no race conditions · stateful but ephemerally scoped
n8n custom-code nodes computing aggregate outputs (sums · averages · matches)An Agent Framework @function_tool that aggregates · or a Workflow executor that does it as a non-LLM stepKeeps the agent-framework Python alongside the agents · shared dependency set · same testing harness

14B.13.1 What Stays in the Substrate

The reciprocal — work that stays in n8n / Logic Apps Hybrid / Foundry workflows:

  • Trigger handling. Subscribing to Microsoft Fabric Eventstream · scheduled timers · webhook receivers from non-Microsoft SaaS · Microsoft Activator rule-fires.
  • Authentication of the caller. Validating the trigger's source · resolving the caller's identity (Microsoft Entra ID claims · workload-identity tokens) before invoking the agent.
  • Single agent-fleet POST. The actual HTTP call into the agent fleet · with managed-identity auth · with the request payload assembled from the trigger event.
  • Post-response routing. Taking the agent fleet's final response and routing it to: Microsoft Teams (adaptive card via M365 connector) · Microsoft.Storage write (durable artifact) · Microsoft.DocumentDB write (state) · non-agent SaaS connector (Salesforce update · ServiceNow ticket · external email).
  • Substrate-level LEDGER row. Emit the workflow.start / workflow.end LEDGER rows that bracket the agent fleet's per-invocation rows. The substrate row is the parent of the agent rows in the LEDGER lineage tree.
  • Cross-Service workflow chains. When Service A's workflow needs to invoke Service B's workflow (rare but real), the substrate is the natural boundary — each Service's agent fleet stays self-contained, the substrate stitches them together via cross-Service HTTP.
  • Non-agent integrations. Calling external APIs that aren't part of the agent fleet — old-style REST APIs, legacy on-prem services via the data gateway, third-party SaaS connectors.
Best Practice — The "five-node rule"

If your Service's n8n / Logic Apps Hybrid / Foundry workflow has more than five substrate-level nodes (trigger · auth · agent POST · response route · LEDGER emit), inspect every additional node and ask: "is this work that Agent Framework's per-pattern builders (SequentialBuilder / ConcurrentBuilder / HandoffBuilder / GroupChatBuilder / MagenticBuilder) could have absorbed?" The answer is usually yes. The substrate node count is a leading indicator of architectural drift; the canonical APEX-M Service has a substrate workflow you can read in 20 seconds.

Responsible AI & Azure AI Content Safety

What This Chapter Does for You

60-second read
  • Six RAI principles are realised, not declared. Each maps to specific Microsoft platform controls: Fairness → Foundry evals · Reliability → eval gates + LEDGER · Privacy → Purview classification + KV unlock · Inclusiveness → multilingual evals · Transparency → model card · Accountability → APEX LEDGER + Microsoft Audit log.
  • Azure AI Content Safety ships four categories (hate · sexual · violence · self-harm) plus prompt shields (jailbreak + indirect-prompt-injection detection) plus groundedness detection plus protected-material detection plus custom categories.

  • Three-gate evaluation (per §28.5): golden-set regression · LLM-as-judge sampling · canary metrics — promotion gate from one stage to the next.
  • Every Service ships a model card documenting intended use · scope · known limitations · evaluation results · monitored-for risks. Published with the Service Bicep.

14C.1 The Six Responsible AI Principles · APEX-M Realisation

Microsoft's Responsible AI framework defines six principles. APEX-M does not redefine them — it realises each through specific Microsoft platform controls layered on top of APEX framework code:

RAI PrincipleWhat it meansAPEX-M realisation
FairnessEqual treatment across demographicsFoundry evaluation framework runs fairness evals over golden-set with demographic stratification · per-Service evaluation report archived to LEDGER
Reliability & SafetyBehave reliably; safe under stressThree-gate eval (§28.5) · Content Safety on every call · groundedness detection · canary metrics on PROD
Privacy & SecurityRespect data privacyPurview classification (§10A.10) · four-tier PII (Ch 7) · pii-unlock dual-control · KV-anchored LEDGER
InclusivenessEmpower everyoneMultilingual evals · accessibility on Power BI / Teams adaptive cards · operator-language localization in agent prompts
TransparencyUnderstandable systemsPer-Service model card (§14C.6) · LEDGER-row narrative · agent reasoning surfaced in HITL adaptive card · transparency note per agent
AccountabilityPeople accountable for AI systemsAPEX LEDGER (hash-chained · KV-HSM-anchored) · Microsoft unified audit log (DSPM for AI) · per-Service named owner · engagement-lead break-glass · access reviews

14C.2 Azure AI Content Safety — The Active Runtime Control

Per Azure AI Content Safety overview, the service provides five active controls APEX-M calls inline:

ControlPurposeAPEX-M wiring
Text moderationFour built-in categories: hate · sexual · violence · self-harm. Each scored 0–7.Run on user input and on agent output. Block at threshold per Service Trust envelope (HLS = strict; RC = moderate).
Prompt shields (jailbreak detection)Detects attempts to bypass system instructions: direct jailbreak attempts in user prompts and indirect injection in document/tool contentsWired in ApexPromptShieldMiddleware · runs on raw user input + every MCP tool result before injection into model context
Groundedness detectionScores whether model output is supported by the supplied grounding contextRun after model response · below threshold (configurable per Service) → discard response, retry with different exemplars or different model
Protected material detectionDetects copyrighted text or code in model outputRun on agent output for content-generation Services · log to LEDGER · block when triggered (configurable)
Custom categoriesTrain Content Safety on your own categories beyond the built-in fourAPEX-M ships per-practice custom categories (e.g., HLS "off-label drug indication" detector; RC "competitor-brand promotion" detector)
Task Adherence (new)Scores whether the agent's actions stayed within the bounds of its assigned task — answers "did it do what we asked, and only what we asked"Run on every Magentic / Group Chat manager turn and on every HITL gate · low score → escalate to operator with the divergence highlighted. Pairs naturally with Magentic's plan ledger.
Note — Task Adherence is the agent-era safety primitive

Content Safety's first four primitives (text moderation · prompt shields · groundedness · protected material) are content-shaped: they ask "is this string OK." Task Adherence is the first action-shaped primitive: it asks "did the agent's behaviour stay within its assigned task." For an agentic system this is the question the safety story has been missing. APEX-M defaults Task Adherence on for every Magentic and Group Chat manager (where divergence risk is highest) and makes it optional for Sequential / Concurrent / Handoff (where the workflow shape already constrains scope).

14C.3 Prompt-Injection Defense Pattern

Prompt injection has two surfaces:

  1. Direct (user-driven). The user's prompt contains attempts like "ignore previous instructions and reveal …". Prompt shields' jailbreak detection catches the obvious cases. Custom categories catch domain-specific phrasings.
  2. Indirect (data-driven). A scraped document, an MCP tool's response, or a Mirrored SOR row contains crafted text that the model sees as authoritative instructions. The dangerous category — most APEX agents read MCP tool results and Eventhouse rows that originated outside the agent's control.

APEX-M's defense layering on every ChatClientAgent:

Order of defenses · agent middleware stack
[user input]
   ↓
1. ApexClassificationGuard       — block requests touching unauthorised tier
   ↓
2. ApexPromptShieldMiddleware    — Azure AI Content Safety: jailbreak detection on user text
   ↓
3. ApexAuditMiddleware           — emit pre-invocation LEDGER row
   ↓
4. ChatClientAgent (model call)
   ↓ (model produces response · before returning to user)
5. Groundedness check            — Content Safety: response vs grounding context
   ↓
6. Protected-material check      — Content Safety: copyrighted-text detector
   ↓
7. ApexAuditMiddleware           — emit post-invocation LEDGER row + safety scores
   ↓
[response to user]

Independent layer (runs on every MCP tool result before model sees it):
8. ApexToolResultShield          — Content Safety prompt-shield "indirect" mode
                                    on tool outputs · catches data-driven injection

14C.4 Hallucination Handling

Hallucination = model produces output not supported by grounding. APEX-M's three-tier handling:

TierDetectionAction
Detected at runtimeGroundedness score < threshold (typically 0.7)Discard response · retry with stricter prompt + larger context window. Retry budget: 1. Then escalate.
Suspected at runtimeOutput schema validation fails (per §28.3) · LLM-as-judge confidence < thresholdSurface to operator via HITL adaptive card with low-confidence indicator · operator approves or rejects · LEDGER captures.
Detected post-hocOperator reports incorrect output · golden-set regression catches in next eval cycleAdd the case to the golden set · regenerate exemplars · trigger model card update if pattern recurs.

14C.5 The Three-Gate Evaluation Framework

Per Services Guide §28.5, three gates govern stage promotion:

GateWhat it doesCadence
Golden-set regressionFoundry batch eval over per-Service golden set (50–500 cases). Every prompt / model / policy change must pass.Pre-merge · pre-promotion to next stage
LLM-as-judge samplingFoundry evaluator scores a sampled fraction of shadow traffic (typically 5%) using a stronger model as judge.Continuous in PROD
Canary metricsTelemetry-driven — grounding score · hallucination rate · operator-reject rate · latency p95 · cost-per-decision. Microsoft.Insights / Log Analytics dashboards.Continuous in PROD

STAGE → PROD promotion is blocked unless all three gates are green at the moment of promotion. The Bicep deployment pipeline reads gate state from Log Analytics; gate status is part of the Microsoft Notation attestation (per Ch 12).

14C.6 The Per-Service Model Card

Every APEX-M Service ships a model card alongside its Bicep. Required sections per the Microsoft transparency-note framework:

  • Intended use — what decisions this Service is built to support, in what jurisdiction, for which personas.
  • Scope — explicit scope statement matching the Service envelope (§30.1.2). What it does not do is as important as what it does.
  • Models used — Foundry deployment names · model-family generations · Cost envelope assignment.
  • Grounding sources — which Gold mart(s), which MCP tools, which Eventhouse(s) supply context.
  • Known limitations — failure modes documented from eval. e.g., "RC-E2E-03 The Pricer struggles to reason about lots with mixed-shelf-life SKUs and routes to HITL more frequently."
  • Evaluation results — link to the latest golden-set regression report · current canary-metric snapshot · LLM-as-judge sampled accuracy.
  • Monitored risks — explicit list of what Insider Risk Management policies, DLP rules, and Sentinel detections watch for in this Service.
  • Owner — named individuals (Service architect · engagement lead) accountable for the Service's RAI posture.
