27.10 What Generalized · What Specialized

The whole architecture from Chapter 26 ran unchanged. What specialized:

  • Schemas (Part III) — different families, but the conformance contract was identical.
  • Gold-mart shapes (Part IV) — different decision-panel columns, but the row-hash + materialized_at convention was identical.
  • Agent prompts (Ch 28) — different exemplars, but the four-archetype structure was identical.
  • HITL policy (§13.1.3) — dual-control vs single, but the staging primitive was identical.
  • PII handling (Ch 7) — Tier 4 dual-control vs Tier 3 single-unlock, but the JIT identity acquisition primitive was identical.
  • KPI envelope (Sellers Guide §10) — different metrics, but the attribution mart pattern was identical (or absent — HLS doesn't have an attribution mart in this scope, which is a Year-2 gap to fill).

If you can run Chapter 26 and Chapter 27, you can run any of the 38 Services in Part VI. Each one is a substitution of schemas, agents, prompts, and HITL policy onto the same eight-hour scaffold.

Independence · HLS specifics

HLS Services touch HIPAA-regulated PHI throughout. The Tier-4 dual-control mechanism, the never-in-Bronze tokenization, and the JIT pii-unlock identity together are what make APEX HLS-eligible. None of this is HLS-specific code; the policies that engage it are HLS-specific configuration. The same code paths exist in RC-E2E-04 (Tier 3 customer PII) and TMT-MED-03 (Tier 3 device fingerprints) — the dial is set differently for each Service.

Key Takeaways

  • HLS-E2E-04 ran on the same eight-hour scaffold as RC-E2E-03 — only schemas, prompts, and HITL policy differ.
  • Tier-4 PHI is the consequential delta: dual-control unlock, PHI never in Bronze/Silver/Gold (only tokens), JIT identity acquisition at the moment of approval.
  • The architecture generalizes; running Ch 26 and Ch 27 means you can run any of the 38 catalog Services.

Service Drills

  1. Run a third Service from Part VI (suggested: TMT-TEL-RAA-04 revenue-assurance variance close — it's neither RC nor HLS, and the SOX audit-trail requirement adds a third compliance frame). Confirm the eight-hour scaffold holds.
  2. Diff the workflow.n8n.json files for RC-E2E-03 excursion-triage and HLS-E2E-04 prior-auth-decision. The structural similarity should be obvious — same primitive types, same step ordering, different node parameters.
  3. Modify the HITL stub to emit a Microsoft Teams adaptive card preview (JSON only, no actual Teams). Compare to the §16.1 Logic Apps Hybrid card the production substrate would render.
Chapter 28

Agent Design Patterns

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Names the four agent archetypes that recur across all 38 cataloged Services.
  • Walks the standard prompt structure, tool-selection logic, and few-shot exemplar curation pattern.
  • Establishes the evaluation framework — golden sets, LLM-as-judge, regression detection — that gates promotion of a new agent version.
60-second read
  • Four agent archetypes — Analyst · Specialist · Composer · Briefer — cover the agent population in the catalog. Pick the archetype first; design the prompt second.
  • Prompt structure is uniform: system identity · schema-shaped context · few-shot exemplars · instruction · output JSON schema.
  • Few-shot exemplars come from LEDGER. Year-1: hand-curated. Year-2: top approved decisions per persona. Year-3: similarity-retrieved from Redis episodic memory at runtime.
  • Promotion is gated by golden-set regression (no skip), LLM-as-judge sample (statistical), and live-shadow run before traffic-split (operational).
Concept first — the question this chapter answers

If you were starting from scratch, you'd write each agent as a unique prompt — a custom personality, a hand-crafted reasoning flow, a bespoke output shape. Forty Services in the catalog would mean ~200 unique prompts, ~200 unique evaluation harnesses, ~200 chances for prompts to drift apart from the patterns that work. That doesn't scale.

The thesis of this chapter is that every agent in the catalog fits one of four archetypes — the Analyst (ranks and triages), the Specialist (proposes a domain action), the Composer (assembles a HITL approval card), the Briefer (writes the end-of-shift digest). Once you know the archetype, the prompt's structure is fixed; only the domain content varies. The eval harness is the same. The output schema is the same. The few-shot exemplar source (LEDGER) is the same. What changes is the schema-shaped context and the instruction text — the parts where the Service's actual domain content lives.

Read this chapter once before you author your first agent. After that, the workflow is: pick archetype → fill in the four template slots → ship. The rest of the chapter walks each archetype, the five-section prompt structure, the eval gates that catch drift, and the maturation-aware patterns that grow the agent from Year-1 instinct to Year-3 superagent.

28.1 The Four Archetypes

Across the catalog, every agent fits one of four archetypes. Knowing the archetype tells you the prompt shape, the tool-selection logic, the evaluation framework, and the version-bump cadence.

ArchetypeWhat it doesExamplesPrompt focus
AnalystSeverity-rank, classify, score, prioritize. Reads one or two Gold marts; emits a numeric score plus a recommended action class.The Analyst (in every Service) · UM-Policy-Match (HLS-E2E-04) · Fraud-Score (RC-E2E-07) · Churn-Risk (RC-E2E-04)Calibration · explainability · false-positive control
SpecialistApply domain-specific rules and reasoning the Analyst doesn't carry. Reads multiple Gold marts; emits a structured proposal (price · auth decision · refund · markdown amount).The Pricing Agent (RC-E2E-03) · Clinical Reviewer (HLS-E2E-02) · RCA Specialist (AXLE-QMS-02) · Reconciliation Specialist (TMT-TEL-RAA-04)Domain knowledge · constraint satisfaction · confidence scoring
ComposerSynthesize the Analyst + Specialist outputs into a HITL-ready proposal. Composes the adaptive card body, names the approver, structures evidence.The Operations Lead (in every triage-and-decide Service)Persona alignment · evidence presentation · tone calibration
BrieferCompose end-of-shift, end-of-day, or end-of-cycle digests. Reads time-series and attribution Gold marts; emits Markdown or adaptive-card summaries.The Briefer (in 32 of 38 Services · the most-reused agent in the catalog)Narrative coherence · KPI accuracy · brevity

Note the role of Demand Checker · Finance Lead · Outreach Strategist from the catalog — these are parameterized Specialists, not separate archetypes. The Demand Checker is a Specialist whose constraint is forward-demand forecasting; the Finance Lead is a Specialist whose constraint is margin-at-risk + commercial envelope; etc. The archetype is "Specialist with a domain-specific tool set"; the agent name is the domain.

ADR · architecture decision
ADR-028-01 · 2026-05-09 · accepted

Decision: Recognize four archetypes (Analyst · Specialist · Composer · Briefer) instead of creating a separate archetype per agent role.

Why: Earlier drafts had ten or twelve role-specific archetypes (Analyst, Demand Checker, Pricing, Finance, etc.). The taxonomy was unstable — every new Service introduced a new archetype. Collapsing to four means new Services pick from existing archetypes and parameterize, which keeps the framework finite. The dimension that was inflating the taxonomy — the domain — is captured in the prompt and tool catalog, not the archetype.

Trade-off rejected: A taxonomy with explicit "Demand-Forecasting Specialist" vs "Pricing Specialist" vs "Finance Specialist" archetypes. Easier to onboard, harder to maintain — every catalog addition forces a taxonomy review.

28.2 Prompt Structure — Five Sections, Always

Every APEX agent prompt has five sections, in this order. Variations exist; the five sections do not.

PROMPT — five-section structure
# 1. System identity (who is this agent, what is the bound)
You are "The Pricing Agent" for Service RC-E2E-03 (Pricing & Revenue Decision Service).
Your bound is to recommend a markdown percentage for a single SKU at a single store, given
elasticity, competitor price, current price register, and discount-rule constraints. You do
NOT decide whether the markdown is approved (that is the Operations Lead + HITL approver).
You do NOT consider scenarios outside RC-E2E-03 (cold-chain, dynamic markdown).

# 2. Schema-shaped context (what data the agent has, by Gold mart)
The following Gold-mart row is in scope:
{
  "sku_id": "...",
  "location_id": "...",
  "elasticity": { "coef": -1.42, "r2": 0.81 },
  "competitor_price_median_7d": 12.45,
  "base_price": 14.99,
  "discount_floor_pct": 35.0,
  "recent_markdowns": [...],
  "row_hash": "sha256:..."
}

# 3. Few-shot exemplars (3-7 prior approved decisions of similar shape)
Example 1 — same category, similar elasticity, approved by Daniel Chen on 2026-04-22:
<input> ... </input>
<output> { "markdown_pct": 18.0, "confidence": 0.88, "reasoning": "..." } </output>

Example 2 ...
Example 3 ...

# 4. Instruction (what to produce, with constraints)
Recommend a markdown_pct that:
- Stays at or above the discount_floor_pct
- Beats the competitor_price_median_7d by at least 2% (configurable)
- Maximizes expected gross-margin lift given elasticity
Emit your reasoning briefly. Do not exceed 80 words of reasoning.

# 5. Output JSON schema (typed, validated by the runner)
Respond ONLY with this JSON shape:
{ "markdown_pct": <decimal between 0 and 60>,
  "confidence":   <decimal between 0 and 1>,
  "reasoning":    <string <= 80 words>,
  "evidence_row_hashes": [<sha256: hashes from the input>] }

The runner (build_agent_app from the Deployment Guide §10.1) validates the LLM response against the output schema before returning. Schema-violation responses are rejected and re-tried with a corrective system message.

28.2.1 The Code Behind the Five Sections

The five-section template assembles at runtime from four input pieces (prompt template · agent metadata · MCP tool list · LEDGER exemplars). Pseudo-code:

Python · Prompt assembly · runs at every agent invocation
from apex_m.agents import AgentSpec
from apex_m.mcp import describe_tools
from apex_m.exemplars import retrieve_few_shot
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Type

def assemble_prompt(
    agent_spec: AgentSpec,
    user_input: dict,
    output_schema: Type[BaseModel],
) -> str:
    """Build the full system+user prompt from the five canonical sections."""

    # === SECTION 1 · SYSTEM IDENTITY ===
    # Comes from agent.yaml + prompts/identity.md
    section_1 = agent_spec.identity_block       # ~80 words · who you are, what you do

    # === SECTION 2 · SCHEMA-SHAPED CONTEXT ===
    # The schema for the input + the tool catalog the agent may call
    section_2 = f"""
        # Input shape — you will receive a JSON object matching this schema:
        {agent_spec.input_schema_doc}

        # Tools you may call (typed contracts, response includes row_hash):
        {describe_tools(agent_spec.mcp_tools)}
    """

    # === SECTION 3 · FEW-SHOT EXEMPLARS (Year-2+ pattern) ===
    # Empty in Year 1 · 3-5 retrieved similar decisions in Year 2+
    exemplars = retrieve_few_shot(
        service_code=agent_spec.service_code,
        agent_id=agent_spec.agent_id,
        current_context=user_input,
        k=5,
    )
    section_3 = "" if not exemplars else (
        "# Prior decisions for similar situations (operator-approved):\n" +
        "\n---\n".join(format_exemplar(e) for e in exemplars)
    )

    # === SECTION 4 · INSTRUCTION ===
    # The actual task · domain-specific · authored per-agent
    section_4 = agent_spec.instruction_block.format(input=user_input)

    # === SECTION 5 · OUTPUT JSON SCHEMA (typed contract) ===
    # Generated from the output Pydantic model · enforced by the runner
    section_5 = f"""
        Respond ONLY with valid JSON matching this Pydantic schema:
        {output_schema.model_json_schema()}
    """

    return "\n\n".join([section_1, section_2, section_3, section_4, section_5])


# At runtime · within ApexAuditMiddleware:
async def invoke_agent(spec: AgentSpec, user_input: dict) -> dict:
    prompt = assemble_prompt(spec, user_input, output_schema=ExcursionOutput)
    raw_response = await llm_chat(prompt)

    # === SCHEMA VALIDATION · retry once with corrective message if violated ===
    try:
        parsed = ExcursionOutput.model_validate_json(raw_response)
    except ValidationError as e:
        raw_response = await llm_chat(
            prompt + f"\n\nYour previous response failed schema validation: {e}. "
                     "Respond again with only valid JSON matching the schema."
        )
        parsed = ExcursionOutput.model_validate_json(raw_response)

    # === LEDGER WRITE · per §25.3.3 ===
    append_decision_to_ledger(
        service_code=spec.service_code,
        agent_id=spec.agent_id,
        prompt_version=spec.prompt_version,
        input_payload=user_input,
        output_payload=parsed.model_dump(),
        operator_verdict="pending",   # updated when HITL closes
    )
    return parsed.model_dump()

28.3 Tool-Selection Logic

Within an agent's /run call, the agent has access to a scoped MCP tool catalog. Tool selection follows a three-step pattern:

  1. Read the decision-panel mart first. This is the agent's primary fact source. The MCP tool name maps to the agent's question shape (§13.1.1). Always called.
  2. Optional read tools for context — episodic memory (Redis-backed similarity retrieval, §25.3), cross-Service tool calls (§17.2). Called when the agent's prompt indicates the context is needed (a low-confidence first-pass might trigger an episodic-memory lookup; a cross-Service composition might trigger the data-owner Service's tool).
  3. Decision-emit or HITL-stage tool last (Composer archetype only). Reads-only agents (Analyst, Specialist, Briefer) never call decision-emit tools directly — that's the Composer's responsibility.
Best Practice · tool count

Keep an agent's accessible tool count small — ideally 2–4 tools per agent. Many agent failures trace to tool over-selection (the LLM picks a less-relevant tool because more options confuse selection). The MCP manifest (§13.3) is where you constrain this; the runner enforces it.

28.4 Few-Shot Exemplar Curation — Year by Year

The few-shot block (prompt section 3) is the single biggest predictor of agent quality. Its curation evolves through the three-year arc from §25.1.

YearSourceSelectionRefresh cadence
Year 1 · instinctsHand-authored synthetic exemplars by the agent maintainer3–5 hand-picked covering the expected varianceManually, when prompts evolve
Year 2 · recordTop-N HITL-approved decisions from LEDGER, ranked by realized KPI lift in attribution_outcome5–7 selected by per-persona acceptance + per-category coverageNightly batch; freezes the next morning's exemplar set per Service per persona
Year 3 · superagentRedis-backed similarity retrieval at runtime: nearest-N decisions to the current input across the LEDGER training corpusTop-K by RedisJSON / RediSearch similarity scorePer-decision · <100ms retrieval inside the agent's /run call
ADR · architecture decision
ADR-028-02 · 2026-05-09 · accepted

Decision: Few-shot exemplars come from LEDGER decisions that produced realized KPI lift, not from a hand-curated "gold set."

Why: A hand-curated gold set encodes the maintainer's prior beliefs about good decisions. LEDGER + attribution mart encodes what the operator-plus-system actually decided and the realized outcome. The latter is what we want to reproduce; the former is at best a Year-1 placeholder. Once Year-2 LEDGER is rich enough, the hand-curated set becomes deadweight.

Caveat: Selection bias — exemplars are drawn from approved decisions only, which over-represents the operator's prior preferences. The Year-3 episodic-memory retrieval mitigates this by including declined decisions as negative few-shots in some prompt variants.

28.5 Evaluation Framework — Three Gates

Promoting a new agent version (Layer 3 SemVer bump per Deployment Guide §12.1) is gated by three evaluation phases, each catching a different class of regression.

28.5.1 Gate 1 — Golden-set regression (deterministic, no skip)

Every agent has a frozen golden set of (input, expected-output) pairs maintained by the agent maintainer. The CI pipeline runs the candidate agent against the golden set and fails the build on any mismatch. Golden sets are augmented (never edited) when prompts intentionally change behavior.

Golden-set size: ~30–60 pairs per agent. Coverage: every output-schema field, every branch in the agent's reasoning, every persona-specific adaptation, every cross-Service composition path.

28.5.2 Gate 2 — LLM-as-judge sample (statistical)

A separate "judge" LLM evaluates a sample of 200–500 (input, candidate-output, prior-version-output) triples. The judge is given the rubric (e.g., "for The Pricing Agent, prefer the response with stronger elasticity reasoning, valid markdown_pct within constraints, and shorter reasoning at equal quality"). Statistical preference for the candidate > 60% gates the next phase.

The judge is not the same model family as the candidate (avoid same-family bias). Per the Deployment Guide §10.4 cosign attestation, the judge model and rubric version are recorded as part of the candidate's training-corpus attestation.

28.5.3 Gate 3 — Live shadow + canary (operational)

The candidate runs in shadow on a percentage of live traffic — receives the same input as the production agent, but its output is recorded only, not committed. Shadow telemetry shows divergence: how often does the candidate disagree with the production version, and on which decision class? Material divergence (> 5% on high-cost decisions) triggers maintainer review before canary.

Canary follows the Deployment Guide §15.2 traffic-split pattern (95/5 → 25 → 50 → 100). At each stage, Microsoft.Insights queries verify cost-per-decision, safety-verdict distribution, and HITL-acceptance-rate match production within bounds.

Warning · agent regression is silent

Container Apps will report 100% healthy and Microsoft Defender for Containers will report no anomalies for an agent whose reasoning has regressed. The three evaluation gates are how regression gets caught — there is no platform-level detector for "the agent's recommendations got worse." Skip the gates and you're shipping silent regressions to operators who will quietly stop trusting the system.

28.5.4 The Code · Three Gates in CI

All three gates run as Azure DevOps / GitHub Actions stages on every agent-version PR. Pseudo-code captures the structure:

Python · The three-gate evaluation pipeline
from apex_m.eval import (
    load_golden_set, llm_as_judge, shadow_run, canary_promote
)
from apex_m.foundry import FoundryEvaluator

CANDIDATE_VERSION = "the-pricer:v2.4.0"
PRODUCTION_VERSION = "the-pricer:v2.3.2"


# === GATE 1 · Golden-set regression (deterministic) ===
def gate_1_golden_set() -> bool:
    golden = load_golden_set(agent_id="the-pricer", min_size=30)
    failures = []
    for case in golden:
        actual = run_candidate(CANDIDATE_VERSION, input=case.input)
        if not matches(actual, case.expected, tolerance=case.tolerance):
            failures.append({"case_id": case.id, "actual": actual, "expected": case.expected})

    if failures:
        print(f"FAIL · {len(failures)}/{len(golden)} golden-set mismatches")
        publish_failure_report(failures)
        return False
    print(f"PASS · {len(golden)}/{len(golden)} golden-set cases match")
    return True


# === GATE 2 · LLM-as-judge statistical sample ===
def gate_2_llm_judge() -> bool:
    sample = load_eval_sample(size=300, sampling="stratified-by-decision-class")
    rubric = load_rubric(agent_id="the-pricer")    # markdown reasoning · format · brevity

    # Use a different model family as judge to avoid same-family bias
    evaluator = FoundryEvaluator(judge_model="claude-sonnet-via-foundry-marketplace")

    candidate_wins = 0
    for case in sample:
        candidate_out = run_candidate(CANDIDATE_VERSION, case.input)
        production_out = run_candidate(PRODUCTION_VERSION, case.input)
        verdict = evaluator.compare(
            input=case.input,
            candidate=candidate_out,
            baseline=production_out,
            rubric=rubric,
        )
        if verdict == "candidate":
            candidate_wins += 1

    rate = candidate_wins / len(sample)
    print(f"Judge preference for candidate: {rate*100:.1f}%")
    return rate > 0.60   # statistical threshold


# === GATE 3 · Live shadow + canary promotion ===
def gate_3_shadow_and_canary() -> bool:
    # PHASE A · shadow on 100% of live traffic, but candidate's output is not committed
    shadow_run(
        candidate=CANDIDATE_VERSION,
        production=PRODUCTION_VERSION,
        duration_hours=24,
    )
    div = measure_divergence(window=24)  # % of cases where candidate disagreed
    if div.high_cost_decisions_disagreement > 0.05:
        print(f"FAIL · {div.high_cost_decisions_disagreement*100:.1f}% divergence on high-cost decisions")
        return False

    # PHASE B · canary traffic-split 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% per Deployment Guide §15.2
    for split_pct in [5, 25, 50, 100]:
        canary_promote(CANDIDATE_VERSION, traffic_pct=split_pct)
        await_metrics_window(hours=4)
        metrics = read_canary_metrics()
        if not within_tolerance(metrics, ["cost_per_decision", "safety_verdict_dist", "hitl_accept_rate"]):
            print(f"FAIL · canary at {split_pct}% breached tolerance")
            rollback_canary()
            return False
    print("PASS · canary completed 5→100%")
    return True


# === ORCHESTRATION · Azure DevOps Pipeline stages ===
def promote_agent_version():
    assert gate_1_golden_set(),   "Golden-set regression failed · STOP"
    assert gate_2_llm_judge(),    "LLM-as-judge preference < 60% · STOP"
    assert gate_3_shadow_and_canary(), "Shadow or canary failed · STOP"

    # All three gates passed · sign + publish
    sign_candidate_image(CANDIDATE_VERSION, with_attestation={
        "gate_1": "golden_set_passed",
        "gate_2_judge_preference": "0.67",      # the actual measured rate
        "gate_3_canary": "completed_100pct",
        "gate_3_divergence": "0.02",
    })
    publish_to_authoring_registry(CANDIDATE_VERSION)
    print(f"PROMOTED · {CANDIDATE_VERSION} now production")

Three gates · three different failure modes caught at three different sensitivities. Gate 1 catches obvious regressions deterministically. Gate 2 catches subtle quality regressions that show only on aggregate. Gate 3 catches behavioral regressions that show only against live data distributions. Skip any of them and you ship a silent regression — Container Apps reports 100% healthy while operators stop trusting the system.

28.6 When to Fork an Image vs Evolve a Prompt

The Deployment Guide §11.2 establishes that agent images are reused across Services and parameterized by Service config. Within a Service, when does a prompt evolution warrant a new image vs a same-image config update?

ChangeMechanismLayer 3 version impact
New few-shot exemplars (Year-2 nightly refresh)Config update · Microsoft.KeyVault secret rotationNone · runtime read
Tone / persona adjustment in system identityConfig update or minor image bumpPatch
New constraint added to instruction (e.g., "minimum 2% above competitor")Minor image bumpMinor
New output-schema fieldMinor image bump · MCP tool output schema also evolvesMinor
Different reasoning architecture (e.g., chain-of-thought → tree-of-thought)Major image bump · evaluation gates rerun against full golden setMajor
Different model family (e.g., GPT-class → Anthropic-class)Major image bump · also potentially new agent identity (the-analyst-claude vs the-analyst-gpt) for parallel rolloutMajor or new agent

Key Takeaways

  • Four archetypes — Analyst · Specialist · Composer · Briefer — cover every agent in the catalog. Pick the archetype first.
  • Prompt structure is uniform: identity · schema-shaped context · few-shot · instruction · output schema. Runner validates the JSON.
  • Tool count per agent stays small (2–4); few-shot exemplar source evolves Year-1 hand-curated → Year-2 LEDGER-mined → Year-3 Redis-retrieved.
  • Three evaluation gates — golden set · LLM-as-judge · live shadow + canary — catch regression that platform health checks cannot.

Service Drills

  1. Pick one agent from your favorite Service in Part VI. Identify which of the four archetypes it is and verify by reading its prompt structure (in the MVP repo). If it doesn't match cleanly, the agent is either misclassified or carrying responsibility from a second archetype.
  2. Build a 30-pair golden set for one agent. Run it through the agent. How many mismatches? Each mismatch is either a prompt-quality bug, a golden-set bug, or a real bound-of-the-agent issue worth flagging.
  3. Inspect the LEDGER for one Service over the last 30 days. Pick the top-5 highest-realized-KPI-lift decisions for one persona. Would those make better Year-2 few-shots than what's currently in the prompt?
Chapter 29

Performance and Cost Modeling

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Sizes the Microsoft platform footprint for three workload scenarios — Small, Mid, Enterprise — with monthly cost estimates.
  • Maps cost levers per tier (Bronze ingest · Silver build · Gold materialization · agent runtime · LEDGER · Redis · orchestration).
  • Establishes when to right-size up and when to prune — the cost-engineering mental model.
60-second read
  • Three sized scenarios: Small (1 tenant · 10K events/day · 1 Service) · Mid (1 tenant · 5M events/day · 3 Services · 250 stores) · Enterprise (1 tenant · 100M events/day · 8 Services · multi-region).
  • Layer 1 platform footprint dominates Small. Microsoft Fabric capacity dominates Mid. LLM-call cost-per-decision dominates Enterprise.
  • Right-size when per-decision latency exceeds the sub-200ms Gold target or when Microsoft Fabric F-SKU saturates above 70% sustained.
  • Prune when Container Apps consumption replicas idle ≥80% of the day or when LEDGER chain growth exceeds Azure SQL DB performance tier headroom.

29.3 Microsoft Fabric Capacity

Microsoft Fabric capacity (F-SKU) sizes the Lakehouse + Warehouse + RTI + Pipelines + Notebooks holistically. F-SKUs follow a 2× cost step at each tier; the hard part is choosing the tier that gives ~30% headroom over peak load without over-buying.

ScenarioF-SKU recommendationMonthly capacity cost (pay-as-you-go)Drives
SmallF4~$520/moBronze ingest + Silver builds + 1 Service Gold marts. Eventstream for any streaming Bronze sources.
MidF32~$4,200/moMulti-Service Silver builds in parallel · Direct Lake serving · RTI eventstream rate to ~5K events/sec sustained.
EnterpriseF128 (single region) or 2× F64 (multi-region)~$16,800/mo to ~$17,200/moSustained 50K events/sec RTI · 8-Service Silver parallelism · sub-100ms Gold serving · Sentinel correlation.
Best Practice · F-SKU sizing

Microsoft Fabric F-SKU is reservation-eligible at 1-year and 3-year terms. Mid and Enterprise scenarios should reserve at 1-year (15–25% saving); Small scenarios should stay pay-as-you-go until usage stabilizes (~3 months of telemetry). Reserve too early and you're locked into a tier you may need to outgrow; reserve too late and you've left 20% on the table for a year.

Per-Service costs scale with decision volume. Microsoft.App/containerApps consumption pricing (Mid + Enterprise mix Consumption with Dedicated D4 for The Operations Lead) governs the agent-runtime line.

Note · LLM call cost

The biggest single line item at Enterprise scale is not in the Microsoft platform price list — it's the LLM API call cost per agent decision. At ~80K decisions/day × ~5 LLM calls per decision × ~$0.0008 per call (frontier model, mid-2026 pricing) ≈ ~$320/day or ~$9,600/mo per Service. Aggregate across 8 Services and the LLM line approaches the Microsoft Fabric line. Cost-per-decision recorded in LEDGER (§25.2) is what makes this measurable, not estimated.

Layer 1 + Microsoft Fabric capacity + per-Service runtimes + LLM calls. These are bands, not quotes — actual numbers depend on region, reservation discounts, peak-vs-baseline ratio, and the LLM model family in use.

The cost-per-decision drops two orders of magnitude from Small to Enterprise. That's the engagement-economics curve that makes APEX defensible commercially — first Service expensive, fortieth Service cheap.

29.6 Latency Targets and Right-Sizing Triggers

Performance is measured per tier. Sub-target performance is the right-size signal.

Tier · OperationTargetRight-size triggerRight-size action

Agent /run · MCP Gold read< 200 msp95 > 800 msRedis Premium tier bump · or mart shape problem (Ch 11)

29.7 Cost Optimization Patterns

  1. Container Apps Consumption + scale-to-zero. All read-only agents (Analyst · Specialist · Briefer) on Consumption profile. Only the Composer (Operations Lead) on Dedicated D4 because steady-state HITL throughput justifies it. Saves 30–50% on agent runtime vs all-Dedicated.
  2. Microsoft Fabric capacity reservation (1y at Mid, 3y at Enterprise). 15–25% off pay-as-you-go.
  3. Log Analytics retention tiers. Hot 30d · Cold 90d · Archive 7y for regulated workloads. Archive tier is ~5× cheaper than hot.
  4. Microsoft Sentinel data ingestion volume control. Send only LEDGER mirror events + correlated authority logs to Sentinel. Skip raw container logs (already in LAW). Saves 40–60% of Sentinel cost.
  5. Shared Redis across Services in a tenant. One Premium Redis (P1 / P2 / P3) shared across all Services with key-prefix isolation. Saves 70%+ vs per-Service Redis.
  6. LLM model right-sizing. Frontier models for the Specialist (Pricing Agent · Clinical Reviewer); lighter models for the Analyst (severity scoring); rules-based path for the Briefer (templated digest with model-augmented narrative). Mixed-model agents save 40–70% of LLM-call cost vs all-frontier.

29.8 When to Prune

Cost optimization isn't only sizing-up. Three prune signals:

  1. Container Apps replicas idle ≥80% of the day. Reduce maxReplicas · or move from Dedicated to Consumption profile. Often saves $200–800/mo per Service.
  2. Bronze tables that no Silver build reads. Bronze retention is "≥1 year STAGE, ≥7 years PROD" (§1.3.1) but a Bronze table that's ingested and never read is dead weight on Microsoft Fabric capacity.
  3. MCP tools called < 3× per quarter. Either the tool is misnamed (LLMs don't pick it because the description is unclear), redundant (another tool is doing the same job), or genuinely unused. Audit and prune. Tool-catalog over-population degrades agent tool-selection performance (Ch 28).

Key Takeaways

  • Three sized scenarios (Small / Mid / Enterprise) bracket the cost-and-performance envelope. Cost-per-decision drops two orders of magnitude from Small to Enterprise.
  • Layer 1 amortizes; Microsoft Fabric capacity is the dominant Mid-scenario lever; LLM API calls dominate Enterprise.
  • Sub-200ms Gold reads, <8s LLM calls, <50ms LEDGER appends — eight latency targets to hold for the system to feel responsive.
  • Six cost-optimization patterns and three prune signals — apply them after the first ~3 months of telemetry, not at deployment time.

Service Drills

  1. For your live engagement, calculate the actual cost-per-decision from the LEDGER's cost_per_decision_usd column over the last 30 days. How does it compare to the §29.5 unit-economics row for your scenario? Where's the variance coming from?
  2. Pull the latency table from §29.6 and compare each row against your tenant's Microsoft.Insights p95s for the last week. Any sub-target rows? Pick the worst and propose the right-size action.
  3. Audit your tenant's MCP tool catalog: invocation count per tool over 90 days. Any tool below the prune threshold? Propose retirement (with replacement path documented if there's still a need).
Part IX

Agent Stack & Services Era

By now you've followed one decision — Marisol's cold-chain markdown — through every layer that made it possible. Data flowed through Bronze · Silver · Gold (Parts I–IV). Agents reasoned over it through MCP (Part I). Orchestrations stitched the agents together (Part V). Service-specific implementations and worked examples landed it in operators' hands (Parts VI–VIII). Part IX steps back and asks a different question: given that all this works, what kind of operating system are we actually building?

Three perspectives in this part. The first is governance — the Service envelopes (Commercial · Scope · Data · Schema · Trust · Cost) that bound what each Service can do, plus the Experience plane where humans meet the system through Microsoft 365 Copilot, Microsoft Teams cards, Power BI dashboards. These are the rails. The second is the Microsoft agent stack as a coordinated whole — Semantic Kernel, Microsoft Agent Framework, Foundry Agent Service, Copilot Studio, A2A — five components Microsoft positions for different concerns, and how APEX composes them rather than picks one. The third is the bigger arc: the application era ended; the services era began. The deliverable a Deloitte engagement ships is no longer "an app the client deploys" but "an agent-driven decision capability that lives in the client's tenant alongside the rest of their Microsoft estate."

The seven chapters below settle this picture. Chapter 30 is envelopes + experience plane. Chapter 31 is the Microsoft agent stack panorama. Chapter 31A goes deep on Azure AI Foundry as the inference plane. Chapter 32 contrasts APEX's audited agent context with raw LLM SDKs. Chapter 32A walks Sentinel + Defender as the security-operations companion. Chapter 33A covers the M365 · Power Platform · Dynamics 365 · Graph integration surfaces. Chapter 33 closes with the change-management story — the human side of moving from app-thinking to service-thinking.

Chapter 30

Service Envelopes & the Experience Plane

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Walks the six concentric Service envelopes (Commercial · Scope · Data · Schema · Trust · Cost) from the Sellers Guide Runtime Addendum and operationalizes each in Microsoft platform terms.
  • Maps the Experience plane — Layer 08 of the APEX stacked architecture — where human personas meet APEX agents through Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Power BI Direct Lake, and Microsoft Teams.
  • Establishes how envelopes constrain the experience plane and how the experience plane realizes the envelopes for operators.
60-second read
  • Six envelopes nest from outside-in: Commercial (money & time, Wave 1/2/3) → Scope (which Services/agents/tools/Gold views/KPIs) → Data (what the agent may read/write, enforced at MCP + Microsoft Purview + Microsoft Entra ID).
  • Three envelopes overlay the nest: Schema (canonical-entity subset · derives the data envelope), Trust (classification + identity + DLP + HITL · governs everything above), Cost (FinOps boundary · metered per service_code, bound to cost_per_decision).
  • Layer 08 Experience plane is where humans meet agents: Microsoft 365 Copilot · Copilot Studio · Power BI Direct Lake · Microsoft Teams adaptive cards. Each surface is identity-scoped to the signed-in principal.
  • The envelopes constrain the experience plane: a Microsoft Teams approver only sees what the Trust envelope allows; Copilot only invokes MCP tools the Scope envelope registers.

30.1 The Six Service Envelopes

The Sellers Guide §6.12 (Runtime Addendum) introduced the envelope framework as the structural shape of every commercial offering. The Services Guide operationalizes it: each envelope is enforced by specific Microsoft platform components, and the architectural choices in Parts II–VII are deliberate satisfactions of these constraints.

30.1.1 Commercial Envelope · the outermost

The money & time boundary. Wave 1 (Foundation · 4–8 weeks · ~$500K–$2M). Wave 2 (Pilot · 6–15 months · ~$5–15M). Wave 3 (Scale & Fuse · multi-year · ~$8–30M). Every Service deployed in a tenant carries a commercial envelope; the envelope sets the maximum cost the Service can incur and the maximum time before realized KPI lift must be visible.

Microsoft platform realization: Microsoft Cost Management aggregation by apex:service-code tag; Microsoft Fabric capacity reservation pricing (Ch 29 §29.3); per-tenant Bicep parameters expressing Wave selection. Cost dashboards in Power BI Direct Lake surface the Commercial envelope's burn rate to the engagement lead.

30.1.2 Scope Envelope · nested in Commercial

The functional-scope boundary. Within the money/time bound, which Services run · which agents compose those Services · which MCP tools each agent may call · which Gold views are exposed · which KPIs are committed. The Scope envelope determines what the Service does; the Commercial envelope determines how much it can do.

Microsoft platform realization: Service Bicep modules deploy only the Container Apps named in the Scope envelope (Deployment Guide Ch 7); the MCP manifest (§13.3) lists only the Scope-permitted tools; Gold marts are materialized only for Scope-named questions; Microsoft Purview registers only Scope-relevant assets.

30.1.3 Data Envelope · nested in Scope

The read/write boundary. What Bronze sources may land · what Silver entities are accessible · what Gold marts are queryable · what decision tables the Service may write to · what cross-Service tools may be invoked. The Data envelope is the most fine-grained of the nested set.

Enforced at three Microsoft platform layers: MCP tools (each tool's input/output schema is the data interface boundary) + Microsoft Purview (sensitivity labels, classification rules, asset-level access policies) + Microsoft Entra ID (managed-identity scoping; the four user-assigned identities from Deployment Guide §4.3 each carry different Data-envelope grants). The triple enforcement is what makes Data-envelope violation structurally impossible — no single component is the whole defense.

30.1.4 Schema Envelope · derives Data

The canonical-entity subset the Service depends on. RC-E2E-03 derives from SCML.Inventory · SCML.Lot · MERML.Markdown · MERML.Elasticity · MERML.Competitor · PROML.Pricing · PROML.DiscountRule. HLS-E2E-04 derives from EHRML.Encounter · EHRML.Procedure · CMSML.Authorization · CMSML.Member. The Schema envelope is the subset of the §2.1 canonical schema library the Service participates in.

Microsoft platform realization: Per-Service Microsoft Fabric workspace contains exactly the Silver entities the Schema envelope names. Cross-Service entity reuse via OneLake Shortcut is permitted only when both Schema envelopes intersect on the entity (and the data-owner Service grants access via Microsoft.Authorization role assignment per Ch 17).

30.1.5 Trust Envelope · governs all above

The governance overlay. PII tier classification (Ch 7) · Microsoft Entra ID conditional-access policies · DLP (Microsoft Purview Information Protection) · HITL gating policy. Trust propagates downward through every envelope: a Tier-4 PHI field at the bottom of the Data envelope causes Microsoft Defender for Cloud alerts at the Commercial envelope if exfiltration is suspected.

Microsoft platform realization: Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels (Ch 10) · Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access (HLS Tier-4 dual-control · §27.8) · Microsoft Defender for Cloud (subscription-level alerting) · Microsoft Sentinel UEBA (cross-identity behavioral anomaly detection). The Trust envelope is the only envelope with platform-level enforcement spanning every Microsoft service in scope.

30.1.6 Cost Envelope · the FinOps boundary

The per-decision cost ceiling. Tokens consumed by LLM calls · Microsoft Fabric Capacity Units (CUs) consumed by Silver/Gold builds · MCP invocation count · Microsoft Storage I/O · Microsoft Network egress. Metered per service_code, bound to cost_per_decision on every LEDGER row (§25.2). Service P&L is a query, not a reconciliation — pull SUM(cost_per_decision) grouped by service_code and the answer is exact, not estimated.

Microsoft platform realization: Microsoft Cost Management exports tagged by apex:service-code (Ch 29 §29.4) · LEDGER's cost_per_decision column populated at runtime · Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app for CU breakdown · Power BI Direct Lake "Service P&L by month" semantic model.

ADR · architecture decision
ADR-030-01 · 2026-05-09 · accepted

Decision: Cost is treated as a first-class envelope, not a measurement after the fact. cost_per_decision is a mandatory column on every LEDGER row; apex:service-code is a mandatory tag on every Microsoft platform resource a Service deploys.

Why: Reconciling cost after the fact (the "FinOps reconciliation" practice common in cloud-native applications) is incompatible with W3 outcome-based commercial envelopes. The W3 contract requires a defensible per-decision cost at decision time, not three months later in a billing review. The audit row records cost; the audit row is queryable; therefore P&L is a query.

Trade-off rejected: Cost-attribution as a downstream Microsoft Cost Management report. Easier to implement (no LEDGER schema change); incompatible with the commercial commitment. The decision is structural: the Cost envelope is built into the audit row, not bolted onto Microsoft Cost Management.

30.2 The Experience Plane · Layer 08 · Where Humans Meet Agents

The APEX stacked architecture is eight layers. Layers 01–07 are everything this book has covered: data plane, semantic plane, agent plane, runtime plane, Service plane, deployment plane, governance plane, learning plane. Layer 08 is the experience plane — the surfaces where human personas (operators, approvers, executives, analysts) actually interact with APEX agents and the Services they compose.

Four Microsoft surfaces realize Layer 08:

30.2.1 Microsoft 365 Copilot · persona-shaped, channel-adaptive

Microsoft 365 Copilot surfaces APEX agent outputs inside Outlook · Microsoft Teams · Word · Excel. A Merchandising Director asking Copilot in Outlook "what markdowns are pending my approval?" gets a Copilot response that invokes RC-E2E-03's stage_markdown_approval via MCP — same agent, same Service, different surface.

Every Copilot surface is identity-scoped: the signed-in Microsoft Entra ID principal determines what the user sees. Daniel Chen sees pending markdowns for his stores; Marisol Reyes sees excursion alerts for hers. Identity-scoping is enforced at the Microsoft Graph layer; the APEX MCP host receives the scoped identity claim and applies it to the Data envelope.

30.2.2 Microsoft Copilot Studio · custom copilots embedded in LOB apps

Microsoft Copilot Studio is the low-code surface for building custom copilots. Where the operator workflow lives inside a non-Microsoft line-of-business surface (Salesforce · Workday · ServiceNow · a homegrown app), Copilot Studio hosts a custom copilot that speaks MCP to the same Gold-view tools. One governance plane, many experiences.

Why this matters for APEX: the Service architecture (Layers 01–07) is invariant; the experience the operator sees is a deliberate choice per persona per channel. A Store Operations Lead might prefer Microsoft Teams adaptive cards (next subsection); a Field Service Dispatcher might prefer a Salesforce-embedded custom copilot. Both invoke the same MCP tools; both write to the same LEDGER; both stay within the Service envelopes.

30.2.3 Microsoft Teams · HITL approvals via adaptive cards

The HITL stage primitive (§13.1.3 · §15.4 · §27.8) renders in production as a Microsoft Teams adaptive card. Approvers see the card in a Teams channel · approve · modify · or deny inline. The decision writes back through the agent's manifest into the LEDGER row, closing the workflow's HITL pause (§14.2).

Adaptive cards are identity-bound: the approver's Microsoft Entra ID identity is captured at card-resolution time and recorded as approved_by in the decision row (e.g., MERML.Markdown.approved_by). For Tier-4 PHI dual-control unlocks, two adaptive cards in two Teams channels (or two Microsoft Entra ID principals' personal queues) gate the workflow until both approve.

30.2.4 Power BI Direct Lake · semantic models over Gold

Operators and executives consume the system's outputs through Power BI dashboards built on semantic models served via Microsoft Fabric Direct Lake. Sub-second queries · zero data duplication · audit-row reviews live here. The Steering Committee and the CFO walk attribution-mart rollups in Power BI before signing W3 outcome-based milestones.

The Gold marts the agents read (§11.2) are the same Gold marts Power BI semantic models materialize from. One Gold tier, two consumers — agents via MCP, humans via Direct Lake. The convergence is the key economic insight: building Gold once serves both consumers, and the unification is what makes the §29.5 cost-per-decision math defensible.

30.3 How Envelopes Constrain the Experience Plane

The two abstractions in this chapter — six envelopes and four experience surfaces — are not independent. The envelopes constrain what the experience plane can show; the experience plane realizes the envelopes for the operator.

EnvelopeConstraint on the Experience planeMicrosoft platform mechanism
CommercialCost-aware UI · "this Copilot answer cost $0.18" optionally surfaced for high-cost queries · cost dashboards visible to engagement lead onlyMicrosoft Cost Management role assignments · Power BI row-level security
ScopeCopilot only invokes Scope-listed MCP tools · Power BI dashboards only show Scope-listed Gold views · Custom copilots cannot reach beyond ScopePer-Service MCP manifest · Microsoft Purview asset registration · Microsoft Entra ID app registration scopes
DataPersona sees only the data their identity is granted · Tokens stay tokens unless an HITL pii-unlock fires · Power BI semantic model honors RLSMicrosoft Entra ID conditional access · Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels · Microsoft.KeyVault JIT pii-unlock
SchemaCross-Service Power BI dashboards must compose at the data-owner's permission level · Copilot grounding stays within the Schema-envelope subsetOneLake Shortcut + Microsoft.Authorization role assignments at workspace scope
TrustHITL adaptive cards include the Trust-envelope policy summary · approver's Microsoft Entra ID identity captured · DLP runs on the Copilot outputMicrosoft Purview Information Protection · Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps · Microsoft Sentinel UEBA
CostPer-decision cost surfaced to the engagement lead's Power BI · cost-bound queries blocked when Cost envelope exhaustedMicrosoft Cost Management thresholds · Microsoft Fabric Capacity throttling

The reverse — how the experience plane realizes envelopes for operators — is what the human actually sees:

  • An operator never sees a token they shouldn't (Trust envelope realized via tokens-in-Bronze + JIT unlock).
  • An approver never approves a decision the Service shouldn't make (Scope envelope realized via Microsoft Teams adaptive-card content restrictions).
  • An executive never quotes a cost they can't reproduce (Cost envelope realized via LEDGER-backed Power BI P&L).
  • A regulator never finds an audit gap (Trust envelope realized via Microsoft Purview lineage walks).

Key Takeaways

  • Six Service envelopes: Commercial (money/time) · Scope (functional-scope) · Data (read/write) · Schema (canonical-entity subset) · Trust (governance overlay) · Cost (FinOps boundary).
  • Each envelope is realized by specific Microsoft platform components — none stays at the level of policy slogans.
  • Layer 08 Experience plane has four surfaces: Microsoft 365 Copilot · Copilot Studio · Microsoft Teams adaptive cards · Power BI Direct Lake. Each is identity-scoped to the signed-in Microsoft Entra ID principal.
  • The Gold tier serves two consumers — agents via MCP, humans via Direct Lake — and the convergence is the cost-per-decision economics from §29.5.

Chapter 31

The Microsoft Agent Stack

What This Chapter Does for You
  • Inventories the Microsoft agent stack components — Semantic Kernel · Agent 365 · Agent-to-Agent (A2A) · Copilot Studio · Azure AI Foundry — and what each contributes.
  • Maps each component to where it composes within an APEX Service (agent runtime · inter-agent calls · operator surface · inference plane).
  • Establishes the rule: APEX picks which component for which job, not which framework wins. Multiple components compose; none replaces the others.
60-second read
  • Five Microsoft agent components plug into APEX Services: Semantic Kernel (agent runtime SDK · alternative to plain FastAPI) · Agent 365 (Microsoft 365 surface integration) · A2A (agent-to-agent protocol · complement to MCP) · Copilot Studio (low-code custom copilots over MCP) · Azure AI Foundry (model hosting + agent runtime · the inference plane).
  • MCP (Ch 3, Ch 13) is the agent↔tool protocol; A2A is the agent↔agent protocol. They complement, not compete.
  • APEX picks components per job: Semantic Kernel for agents needing function-calling planners, Agent 365 for M365 surface integration, A2A for inter-agent within a workflow, Copilot Studio for non-Microsoft LOB embedding, Foundry as the always-on inference plane.
  • None of these components replace the Service architecture (Layers 01–07); they realize it in different surfaces and runtimes.

31.1 The Stack at a Glance

The Microsoft agent stack is not one framework; it is five components that compose. Each addresses a different concern. APEX uses each where the concern fits.

ComponentConcernAPEX role
Semantic KernelCross-language agent SDK · function calling · planners · memory connectorsAgent runtime SDK alternative to plain FastAPI · used when planner-style reasoning is needed
Microsoft 365 Agents (Agent 365)Surface integration with Outlook · Microsoft Teams · Word · Excel · PowerPointBring APEX agent outputs into the Microsoft 365 surfaces operators already live in
Agent-to-Agent (A2A)Standardized protocol for agent collaboration across runtime boundariesInter-agent calls within a Service workflow · cross-Service composition through a common protocol
Microsoft Copilot StudioLow-code custom copilot builder · plugs into any MCP-speaking backendBuild Service-specific custom copilots · embed in non-Microsoft LOB apps · governance plane stays unified
Azure AI FoundryModel hosting · evaluation · agent runtime · groundingThe inference plane · where the LLM calls happen · evaluation framework integration (Ch 28 §28.5)

31.2 Microsoft Semantic Kernel · Cross-Language Agent SDK

Semantic Kernel is Microsoft's open-source SDK for building AI agents in .NET, Python, and Java. Its primitives — plugins, functions, planners, memory connectors — give an agent a structured way to reason over tools and accumulated context.

How APEX uses it:

  • Agent runtime alternative. The MVP's build_agent_app(runner=..., agent_id=...) contract from Deployment Guide §10.1 produces a FastAPI app exposing /run and /healthz. For .NET-shop clients or for agents needing planner-style reasoning, the same contract is satisfiable by a Semantic Kernel agent in C# or Python — the HTTP surface is identical, the LEDGER row shape is identical, the MCP tool consumption is identical. The runtime SDK changes; the agent contract does not.
  • Function-calling planners. Where The Pricing Agent's reasoning needs to compose multiple MCP tool calls in a derived sequence (read-elasticity · evaluate · read-similar-decisions · refine · emit-recommendation), Semantic Kernel's FunctionChoiceBehavior.Auto planner can pick tools dynamically. The Year-2 LEDGER few-shot exemplars (Ch 28 §28.4) feed the planner's context.
  • Memory connectors. Semantic Kernel's memory abstraction adapts to Azure Cache for Redis (the §25.3 working/episodic memory). The agent's memory store is Redis · the connector is Semantic Kernel · the read pattern is identical regardless of underlying store.

When to choose Semantic Kernel over plain FastAPI: when the team's primary language is .NET; when the agent's reasoning genuinely needs a planner (most APEX agents are simpler than this); when the same agent must run in both Container Apps and a desktop / non-server context.

31.3 Microsoft 365 Agents · Surface Integration

Microsoft 365 Agents (the agent infrastructure that lives inside the Microsoft 365 ecosystem and that operators sometimes refer to as "Agent 365") brings APEX agent outputs into the Microsoft 365 surfaces — Outlook · Teams · Word · Excel · PowerPoint. The agent definition lives in the Microsoft 365 admin center and respects all of Microsoft 365's existing identity, compliance, and licensing models.

How APEX composes with it:

  • Surface registration. An APEX Service registers a Microsoft 365 Agent that points at the Service's MCP host as its tool source. From the Microsoft 365 user's perspective, asking Copilot in Outlook for "show me pending markdowns" produces a Copilot answer that invokes rc_e2e_03.stage_markdown_approval via the registered M365 Agent.
  • Identity flow-through. The Microsoft Entra ID identity of the signed-in user passes through Microsoft Graph to the M365 Agent to the MCP host. The agent's /run sees the user's Entra ID claims in its request context · scope-checks against the Service's Trust envelope · returns content the user is allowed to see.
  • HITL surfaces in Microsoft Teams. The HITL adaptive card from §15.4 / §16.2 is rendered by Microsoft 365 Agents when the workflow stages an approval. Same orchestration; native Teams surface.

When to use Microsoft 365 Agents vs Copilot Studio: M365 Agents for first-party Microsoft 365 surfaces (Outlook · Teams · Word). Copilot Studio for custom or non-Microsoft surfaces (next section). Both can speak MCP to the same Service.

31.4 Agent-to-Agent (A2A) · The Inter-Agent Protocol

Where MCP standardizes how an agent calls a tool, A2A standardizes how an agent calls another agent. The two protocols are complementary: an agent reads its data via MCP, then collaborates with peer agents via A2A, then writes its decision via MCP again.

How APEX uses A2A:

  • Within a Service workflow. The Operations Lead (Composer archetype, §28.1) needs the Specialist's proposal · the Demand Checker's forecast · the Finance Lead's commercial scoring before composing the HITL adaptive card. Classic implementation routes these through the orchestrator's parallel-step primitive (§14.2). With A2A, the Operations Lead can directly invoke peer agents under the same protocol, with the orchestrator providing only the workflow shell.
  • Cross-Service composition. RC-E2E-03's Pricing Agent invokes RC-E2E-09's Lot Provenance agent (cross-Service example from §17.4). The cross-Service call traverses A2A; the per-Service authorization (data-owner grants role assignment) holds through Microsoft Entra ID claims passed in the A2A envelope.
  • Multi-tenant agent collaboration is forbidden by ADR-025-01. A2A within a tenant: yes. A2A across tenants: no. The protocol is capable; the policy is the binding.
  • Implementation — Microsoft Agent Framework is the intended A2A platform for APEX. The actual binding from APEX agent definitions to A2A endpoints (inbound via MapA2A · outbound via A2AAgent wrappers as tools) is done by the APEX-M Agent Framework Loader documented in §14A.8. Engagement architects do not write A2A glue code — they author agent.yaml + prompts/*.md + use-case YAML, and the Loader produces A2A-compliant WorkflowAgent instances at runtime.

The choice between A2A and orchestrator-mediated calls (n8n / Logic Apps Hybrid) is per-pattern:

PatternUse orchestratorUse A2A
HITL gating · cross-Service scheduling · branch-on-result✓ (workflow shape needs the orchestrator)
Agent-pair collaboration mid-decision · low latency · same-Service✓
Parallel fan-out where each branch is independent✓
Synchronous reasoning across two agents that must converge before HITL✓ (orchestrator's parallel + merge is heavier)

31.5 Microsoft Copilot Studio · Custom Copilots over MCP

Copilot Studio is the low-code surface for building custom copilots. Where the operator's natural workflow lives in a non-Microsoft LOB application — Salesforce · Workday · ServiceNow · a homegrown app — Copilot Studio hosts a copilot embedded in that app, speaking MCP to the same Gold-view tools the M365 Copilot speaks to.

How APEX composes:

  • Per-Service custom copilots. Each Service can ship a Copilot Studio definition that registers the Service's MCP tools as its action set. The custom copilot is identity-scoped through Microsoft Entra ID app registration; it inherits the Service's Scope and Trust envelopes.
  • One governance plane, many experiences. The Trust envelope (§30.1.5) propagates regardless of the surface. Microsoft Purview tracks lineage from Bronze through to the Copilot Studio response. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps watches for anomalous prompt injection.
  • Same Year-1 → Year-3 trajectory. A Copilot Studio custom copilot still calls MCP tools, still emits LEDGER rows, still feeds the §25.3 Redis episodic memory. The maturation arc is invariant under surface choice.

31.6 Azure AI Foundry · The Inference Plane

Azure AI Foundry is where the LLM calls actually happen. Model hosting · grounding · evaluation framework · prompt-flow tooling. APEX's agent runtimes (FastAPI, Semantic Kernel) all eventually issue chat-completion requests to a model deployed in Azure AI Foundry.

How APEX uses Foundry:

  • Model deployments per Service. The Cost envelope (§30.1.6) constrains which model family each agent uses. Frontier models for the Specialist (Pricing · Clinical Reviewer); lighter models for the Analyst (severity scoring); rules-based path for the Briefer where viable. Foundry hosts the deployments; the agent code names them in its config (Microsoft.KeyVault secret · per Service).
  • Evaluation framework. Foundry's built-in evaluation tooling integrates with the §28.5 three-gate framework. Golden-set regression runs as a Foundry batch evaluation; LLM-as-judge sampling runs as a Foundry evaluator on shadow traffic; canary metrics export to Microsoft.OperationalInsights for the §28.5.3 telemetry-driven promotion gate.
  • Grounding to Microsoft Fabric Gold. Foundry's grounding feature lets the model reason over a specified data source. APEX uses Foundry grounding selectively — most agent reasoning is over Gold-mart MCP responses (the canonical APEX path), but for unstructured-document grounding (clinical guidelines for HLS-E2E-02 oncology CDS · regulatory text for ER-MN-02 environmental compliance), Foundry's grounding pulls from Microsoft Fabric OneLake unstructured stores into the agent's context window at runtime.

31.7 The Composition Pattern · A Worked Example

RC-E2E-03's cold-chain excursion workflow uses several stack components together. Trace the data flow once:

  1. Eventstream fires the excursion event (§5.3 KQL rule).
  2. Azure Logic Apps Hybrid (§16) receives the trigger · POSTs to the agent fleet's single A2A endpoint · emits LEDGER workflow.start row. (Multi-agent coordination then runs inside Microsoft Agent Framework, not Logic Apps — per §14.4.)
  3. The Analyst agent runs in Container Apps · runtime SDK is FastAPI (could be Semantic Kernel) · LLM call lands at Azure AI Foundry.
  4. The Analyst calls MCP tool rc_e2e_03.get_excursion_decision_panel · Gold mart query · row hash returned.
  5. The Analyst's severity score triggers the parallel fan-out. The Operations Lead invokes The Pricing Agent and The Demand Checker via A2A for synchronous collaboration · they converge on a recommendation.
  6. Operations Lead composes a Microsoft Teams adaptive card via Microsoft 365 Agents · Marisol Reyes sees it in her Teams channel.
  7. Marisol approves · the resolution flows back through Microsoft 365 Agents → Logic Apps → MCP commit_markdown_decision.
  8. Daniel Chen the Merchandising Director reviews the day's outcomes in Power BI Direct Lake over the same Gold marts the agents read. He can also ask Outlook Microsoft 365 Copilot for the day's KPI-attribution summary; the answer is grounded by another MCP call to rc_e2e_03.get_kpi_daily.

Six Microsoft components compose · the agent contract is invariant · LEDGER captures every step · the operator never knows which framework runs where.

Best Practice · pick per concern, not per fashion

The temptation to "standardize on Semantic Kernel" or "go all-in on Copilot Studio" recurs in every engagement. Resist. The five components solve five different concerns; standardizing on one means re-implementing the others poorly. Pick Semantic Kernel for planner-needing agents · M365 Agents for first-party surfaces · Copilot Studio for non-Microsoft LOB · A2A for agent collaboration · Foundry for inference. The agent contract (Ch 28) is what stays uniform; the realization is what flexes.

Key Takeaways

  • Five Microsoft agent components plug into APEX: Semantic Kernel (runtime SDK) · Microsoft 365 Agents (M365 surfaces) · A2A (inter-agent protocol) · Copilot Studio (custom copilots) · Azure AI Foundry (inference plane).
  • MCP and A2A are complementary protocols — agent↔tool and agent↔agent — not competitors.
  • APEX picks components per concern, not per framework loyalty. Six components in one workflow is normal.
  • The agent contract from Ch 28 (five-section prompt structure · output schema validation · LEDGER emission) is invariant under runtime/surface choice.
  • Microsoft Agent Framework is the intended A2A platform; the APEX-M Agent Framework Loader (§14A.8) is the verbatim bridge from APEX authoring artifacts to ChatAgent · FunctionTool · per-pattern builder classes (SequentialBuilder / ConcurrentBuilder / HandoffBuilder / GroupChatBuilder / MagenticBuilder). Same code runs with or without the SDK present.

Catalog Drills

  1. For one Service in your engagement, identify which of the five Microsoft agent components compose into its delivery. Which agents are FastAPI and which are Semantic Kernel? Which surface gets M365 Agents and which gets Copilot Studio?
  2. Trace one cross-Service composition (e.g., RC-E2E-03 calling RC-E2E-09's Lot Provenance) and identify where MCP fires vs A2A fires. What's the latency cost of each protocol hop?
  3. Audit your Foundry model deployments: which agent uses which model family · what's the cost-per-decision Cost envelope budget · is there a smaller model that would still meet the §28.5.1 golden-set bar?

31A.4 Grounding Mechanisms

Foundry exposes four grounding paths:

  1. File search. Upload PDFs / docs to a Foundry project; Foundry chunks · embeds · indexes · auto-grounds on retrieval. APEX-M uses for Service-specific reference materials (HLS clinical guidelines · ER environmental regulations · TMT contract templates).
  2. Vector index. Bring-your-own embeddings store (Azure AI Search · Cosmos DB vector index · pgvector). APEX-M uses Azure AI Search vectorized indexes for the LEDGER few-shot exemplar retrieval (§28.4).
  3. Hosted MCP. Foundry-managed MCP servers (per Services Guide §14B.4.3). Tool-approval workflow built-in; reusable across agents via toolboxes.
  4. A2A. Foundry agents can call other Foundry agents directly (per §14B.8). Inter-agent grounding through agent-to-agent collaboration.

The four are composable. RC-E2E-03 The Pricer typically grounds via: hosted MCP (Gold mart reads) + vector index (LEDGER exemplars) + A2A (Demand Checker collaboration). Three grounding sources, one model call.

31A.5 Prompt Flow

Prompt Flow is Foundry's authoring tool for composable prompt-orchestration logic (multi-step reasoning · branch logic · custom Python nodes · evaluation hooks). APEX-M uses Prompt Flow selectively:

  • Used for: Year-1 / Sprint-0 prototype agents before they're rewritten into Agent Framework. Visual authoring helps SMEs critique reasoning paths.
  • Not used for: production agents. Agent Framework's ChatClientAgent + middleware is the canonical runtime (per §14B).
  • Migration path: Prompt Flow YAML → Agent Framework Python is largely mechanical. Per-step instructions become prompt blocks; eval hooks become middleware.
